  - Rotate your hand so that your first finger points in the direction of the magnetic field (north to south) and so that your second finger points in the direction of the current in the wire
  - Your thumb will point in the direction of the force on the wire ![Diagram of a left hand showing Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule. Thumb indicates motion, first finger shows magnetic field, second finger represents current.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/011-diagram-of-a-left-hand-showing-fleming-s-left-ha.png) Don’t be afraid of using the left-hand rule during an examination. Just put your thumb and first two fingers in the correct positions and align them with the field and current directions in the diagram. Make sure you use your left hand! **A** and **B** are incorrect because these directions are not perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of the magnetic field. **D** is incorrect because this direction is not perpendicular to the direction of the current.

Arrows indicate axes directions.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/008-graph-showing-a-sinusoidal-wave-with-voltage-bet.png)

![Four diagrams, labelled A to D, show different mechanical lever and piston configurations with labels X and Y on dual pistons below a lever.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/009-four-diagrams-labelled-a-to-d-show-different-mec.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- At point P in the graph, the magnitude (size) of the p.d. is greatest
- The coil must be parallel to the magnetic field to produce the maximum p.d. (figures A and C)

  - Therefore, options **B** and **D** can be eliminated
- A positive value of p.d. indicates that X is more positive than Y
- Therefore, a negative value of p.d. indicates that Y is more positive than X

**A** is incorrect as this corresponds to a maximum p.d., but the polarity is opposite (X would be more positive than Y), so it matches a positive peak, not point P, which is a negative peak.

parts.problemMd:
A rectangular coil is dropped between a pair of opposite magnetic poles, as shown.

![A rectangular coil entering the gap between two magnetic poles, labelled 'N' and 'S' to indicate north and south.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/003-a-rectangular-coil-entering-the-gap-between-two-.png)

In which position is the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. in the coil the greatest?

![A: The bottom edge of the coil has just entered the magnetic field.
B: The entire coil is inside the uniform magnetic field.
C: The top edge of the coil is still in the field, but the bottom edge has left it.
D: The entire coil has left the magnetic field.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/004-a-the-bottom-edge-of-the-coil-has-just-entered-t.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- An e.m.f. is induced in the coil only when its horizontal wires are cutting through the magnetic field lines
- The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. depends on the speed at which the magnetic field lines are being cut
- As the coil falls, it accelerates due to gravity, meaning its speed increases at each successive position $( v_{C} > v_{B} > v_{A} )$
- In position **C**, the top wire of the coil is cutting the field lines while the coil is moving at a higher speed than it was in position **A**

**A** is incorrect because although an e.m.f. is induced, the coil is moving more slowly than at position **C**.

**B** is incorrect because when the entire coil is within a uniform magnetic field, the e.m.f. induced in the top wire cancels out the e.m.f. induced in the bottom wire, so, the induced e.m.f. is momentarily zero.

**D** is incorrect because the coil has completely left the magnetic field and no field lines are being cut; therefore, the induced e.m.f. is zero.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember that an e.m.f. is only induced when there is a change in the magnetic flux through the coil. When the coil is entirely within a uniform field, there is no change in flux, so no e.m.f. is induced. Also consider that a falling object accelerates, so the coil moves faster at lower positions, which affects the rate of cutting field lines.

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The proton number of helium is two. This means it must have two protons.
- The charge on a proton is positive. Since an atom is neutral, this means it must have two electrons.
- The nucleon number of this atom is 4. The number of neutrons is the nucleon number minus the proton number (4 - 2 = 2). This means there are two neutrons in this atom.

**A** is incorrect as this atom has three electrons, so this atom is not neutral.

**B** is incorrect as this atom has four protons, so this atom is not helium, and it is not neutral.

**D** is incorrect as this atom has four protons and four electrons. This atom is not helium.

**B **is incorrect as this is the nucleon number. This tells us the number of *protons *plus the number of *neutrons *in the nucleus of an aluminium atom*.*

**D **is incorrect as this number does not represent the number of neutrons. We never add the proton number to the nucleon/mass number.

- **Nuclear equations must be balanced**, which means the sum of the nucleon numbers on the left of the equation must equal the sum on the right. The same goes for the proton numbers.

**B** is incorrect as in this answer the numbers are correct, but since the proton number has changed then this element is no longer uranium (U).

**C** is incorrect as this equation does not describe the decay. Uranium is the nuclide which decays into **α**-particle and another nuclide. Therefore, the **α**-particle should be on the right hand side. You should also notice that this equation is not balanced.

parts.problemMd:
The background count rate measured by a radiation counter is 40 counts per minute (cpm).

With the counter close to a radioactive source, the counter reading is 960 cpm.

The half-life of the source is 20 minutes.

What is the counter reading one hour later?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The corrected count rate at the start of the experiment is

960 cpm – 40 cpm = 920 cpm

- One hour is three half-lives (3 × 20 minutes), so the count rate due to the radioactive source will halve three times in one hour
- Therefore, the detector will record a count of

920 × ½ × ½ × ½ = 115 cpm

- The background count needs to be added to this, so the detected count rate is

115 cpm + 40 cpm = 155 cpm

**A** is incorrect because the background count has not been added back into the count rate.

**B** is incorrect because the background count has been ignored completely in the calculation.

**D** is incorrect because the background count in the first stage was omitted, even though it was added back in at the end.

parts.problemMd:
The count rate due to a sample of a radioactive isotope is measured for 80 minutes. | **time**

**(minutes)** | ** count rate **** **
**(counts / second)** | |---|---| | 0 | 480 | | 20 | 380 | | 40 | 300 | | 60 | 240 | | 80 | 190 | What is the half-life of the isotope?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The half-life of an isotope is the time it takes for half of its active nuclei to decay
- As there will be half of the active nuclei, the activity will have fallen to half of its initial value
- The count rate is proportional to the activity, so the half-life of the isotope is the same as the time for the count rate to fall to half of its initial value
- The initial count rate is 480 counts / second; half of this is 240 counts / second
- The count rate has fallen to 240 counts / second after 60 minutes, so the half-life is 60 minutes

The half-life of an isotope is constant; therefore, it does not depend on the number of active nuclei remaining. You should know the definition of half-life based on the number of active nuclei, but you should also realise that half-life can be defined in terms of activity and even count rate.

parts.problemMd: What creates the periodic nature of the seasons?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The tilting of the Earth's axis means that certain hemispheres (halves) of the Earth tilt towards the Sun for one half of the year, and away from the Sun from the other half

  - When the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, this is spring and summer
  - When it is tilted away from the Sun, this is autumn and winter
- The orbiting of the Earth around the Sun means that different sides of the Earth face the Sun at different parts of the year, every 365 days

  - Therefore, the combination of both creates the seasons

The tilting of the Earth's axis and its orbit around the Sun is why when it is winter in Europe (in the northern hemisphere), it is summer in Australia (in the southern hemisphere). Whilst Europe is facing away from the Sun during that time, this means Australia is facing towards the Sun, because of the tilt.

Make sure to remember it is the **mass** of the planet that affects its gravitational field strength the most, not so much its surface area or diameter or density.

parts.problemMd:
Which line in the table best describes the angle of the Earth’s axis from the vertical, and the effect of this tilt?

|   | **Angle of tilt** | **Effect of tilt** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 23.4° | Rising and setting of the Sun |
| **B** | 23.4° | Changing of the seasons |
| **C** | 66.6° | Rising and setting of the Sun |
| **D** | 66.6° | Changing of the seasons |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The Earth’s axis tilts 23.4° from the vertical
- The effect of this tilt is a change in intensity of the sunlight falling on the surface of the Earth at different times of year

  - Therefore, the tilt of the Earth’s axis causes the changing of the seasons

**A** and **C** are incorrect as the rising and setting of the Sun are caused by the rotation of the Earth on its axis

**D** is incorrect as the angle is too large

It’s a common misconception to think that the seasons are caused by the Earth being closer to the Sun during the summer.

But, when it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere it is winter in the Southern Hemisphere!

Although the Earth **is **slightly closer to the Sun at certain times, the distances are so huge that it makes virtually no difference to the heat and light energy received.

What **does **make a big difference is the tilt, so that sometimes the Earth ‘leans into’ the sunlight, and at other times, ‘leans away’.

parts.problemMd:
Which line in the table correctly identifies the length of one year, one day and daylight hours during an equinox, all as experienced on Earth?

|   | **One Earth year / days** | **One Earth day / hours** | **Daylight hours during an equinox / hours** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 356 | 8 | 8 |
| **B** | 364 | 12 | 12 |
| **C** | 365 | 12 | 8 |
| **D** | 365 | 24 | 12 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- A **year **is defined as the amount of time it takes for a planet to complete one orbit of its star

  - In this case the Earth is usually said to orbit the Sun once every 365 days
  - Only **C** or **D** could be correct

- A **day **is defined as the amount of time it takes for a planet to complete one full rotation on its axis

  - The Earth rotates once every 24 hours
  - **D** must be correct

- An **equinox **(meaning ‘equal night’) happens twice a year (21st March and 23rd September) when the daylight and night-time hours are equal

  - Therefore, daylight hours during an equinox are half of 24, or 12 hours
  - This confirms that answer** D** is correct

In fact the Earth takes 365.25 days to orbit the Sun.

These extra 6 hours are ‘saved up’ for four years, then added to February in leap years. This prevents the calendar getting out of synch with the seasons (which otherwise it would eventually) and creates that extra day in February.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

The orbit of the Earth around the Sun can be thought of as following a circular path with a circumference of 942 × 10<sup>6</sup> km.

What is the approximate orbital speed of the Earth?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- To find the orbital speed use the equation for speed
$v=\frac{d}{t}$
- Where *v* = average velocity, *d* = distance and *t *= time
- From the question:

  - Circumference, or distance, *d* = 942 × 10<sup>6</sup> km
  - Time of one orbit, *t* = 365 days
  - Time can be converted using *t *= (365 × 24) hours = **8760 hours**

- Therefore, the orbital speed,
- $v=\frac{(942\times10^{6})\mathrm{km}}{8760h}=107534\mathrm{km}/h$
- This can be written as 100 000 km /h when rounded to one significant figure

Notice that if a more accurate value for time is used, 365.25 days = 8766 hours, the final answer still rounds to the same value.

parts.problemMd:
The radius of Jupiter's orbit is 778 × 10<sup>6 </sup>km. What is the time taken for light from the Sun to reach the surface of Jupiter?

The speed of light is 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s.
parts.solutionMd:
The answer is **B** because:

- The time is calculated by:

  - $speed=\frac{distance}{time}\Rightarrow time=\frac{distance}{speed}$
- The speed is the speed of light = 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s
- Converting the distance into metres (m) gives:

  - 1 km = 1000 m
  - 778 × 10<sup>6</sup> km = (778 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × 10<sup>3</sup> m = 778 × 10<sup>9</sup> m
- Substituting these values into the time equation gives:

  - $timetaken=\frac{778\times10^{9}}{3\times10^{8}}=2593=2600s$

**A** is incorrect as the distance has not been converted from km into m

**B** is incorrect as the time has been calculated as 
$\frac{speed}{distance}$instead of $\frac{distance}{time}$ and the distance has not been converted into m

**D** is incorrect as the time has been calculated as $\frac{speed}{distance}$instead of $\frac{distance}{time}$

For the time to be in s, the distance must be in m and the speed in m/s. Make sure to look out for unit conversions, as units on both sides of the equations must be equal

parts.problemMd:
**Extended Tier Only**

The orbit of the Moon around the Earth is modelled as a circular path of radius $3.8\times10^{5}$km.

The orbital period is 29.5 days (710 hours).

What is the orbital speed of the Moon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- To find the speed of the Moon, the distance it covers each orbit and the time of each orbit are both needed
- The distance is the circumference, *C*, of its circular orbit

$C=2πr$

- The orbital time is given as 710 hours (h) and the radius is 3.8 × 10<sup>5</sup> km
- Speed is distance per unit time

$v=\frac{2π\times(3.8\times10^{5})}{710}=3360$   km/h

- Written in standard form to two significant figures, this is

$v=3360$  km/h = 3.4 $\times$10<sup>3</sup>  km/h

It is possible to memorise the equation $v=\frac{2πr}{T}$ , but a little physical reasoning and understanding of where this equation comes from could save you having to learn one more equation (and potentially mis-remembering it under exam pressure!).

parts.problemMd:
A comet is at the point in its orbit where it is furthest from the Sun.

Which row is correct?

|   | orbital speed | energy in gravitational potential store |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | at its maximum | at its maximum |
| **B** | at its maximum | at its minimum |
| **C** | at its minimum | at its maximum |
| **D** | at its minimum | at its minimum |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Comets travel in highly elliptical orbits around the Sun
- As a comet moves further away from the Sun, the distance between them increases, which means energy is transferred to its gravitational potential store

  - Therefore, at the point furthest from the Sun, the energy in the gravitational potential store is at its **maximum**
- The total energy of the comet remains constant throughout its orbit
- Due to the principle of conservation of energy, an increase in gravitational potential energy results in a decrease in kinetic energy
- When the gravitational potential energy is at its maximum, the kinetic energy is at its minimum

  - Since kinetic energy depends on speed, a minimum kinetic energy means the orbital speed of the comet is also at its **minimum**

**A** is incorrect as it assumes the orbital speed is at its maximum when the comet is furthest from the Sun

**B** is incorrect because the comet has its minimum orbital speed and maximum gravitational potential energy at this point, not the other way around

**D** is incorrect as the energy in the gravitational potential store is at its maximum, not its minimum, when the comet is furthest away

> **[exam-tip]**
> A great way to remember this is to apply the principle of conservation of energy. When a comet approaches the Sun, it "falls" towards it, losing gravitational potential energy and gaining kinetic energy, causing it to speed up. As it moves away, it travels "uphill" against the Sun's gravity, losing kinetic energy and gaining gravitational potential energy, causing it to slow down.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

The orbit of Venus around the Sun is treated as a circular path with an average radius of 108.2 million km. The orbital period of Venus is 225 days.

What is the orbital speed of Venus?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- Average orbital speed is defined by the equation $v=\frac{2πr}{T}$

  - Where *r *is the average radius of the orbit and *T* is the orbital period

- From the question

  - Average radius, *r* = 108.2 million km = 108.2 × 10<sup>6</sup> km
  - Orbital period, *T* = 225 days = 225 × 24 = 5400 hours

- Therefore, average orbital speed,
- $v=\frac{2π\times(108.2\times10^{6})}{5400}=125896\mathrm{km}/h$ Rounding to 3 significant figures gives 126 000 km/h

**A** is incorrect as the value of π has been left out of the calculation

**B** is incorrect as the 2 was left out of the calculation

**D** is incorrect as the answer is derived from dividing the distance by the number of days, rather than hours

What is the orbital speed of Mars?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The average orbital speed, *v* is calculated by: $v=\frac{2πr}{T}$

  - Where *r* is the orbital radius and *T* is the orbital time period

- Convert the orbital radius (distance) from km into m

  - 227.9 million km = 227.9 × 10<sup>6</sup> km = 227.9 × 10<sup>9</sup> m
  - orbital radius, *r*  = 227.9 × 10<sup>9</sup> m

- Convert the time period (orbital duration) from days into hours:

  - 1 day = 24 hours

parts.problemMd:
A student is investigating the factors that affect the size of the crater (hole) a ball makes when it is dropped into sand.

Plan an experiment which would enable you to investigate one factor which might affect the size of the crater.

The apparatus available includes

- metal balls of different sizes
- a tray of sand

Write a plan for the experiment.

In your plan you should:

- state which factor is being investigated,
- state the key variables that you would control,
- list any additional apparatus needed,
- explain briefly how you would carry out the experiment including what would be measured and how this would be done,
- state the precautions which should be taken to obtain reliable results,
- suggest a suitable graph which could be drawn from the results.

You may draw a diagram if it helps to explain your plan.
parts.solutionMd:
State the factor to be tested:

- Clear statement of an appropriate variable to test;** [1 mark]**

Name the control variable:

- A named variable which should be kept constant;** [1 mark]**

Set out the apparatus:

- A metre rule and any apparatus essential to variable under test;** [1 mark]**

State the method:

- measure factor under test **AND **drop ball **AND** measure diameter / depth of depression;** [1 mark]**

State any repetitions:

- Repeat for new value of variable under test;** [1 mark]**

State any additional points:

**Any one from:**

- Repeat experiment or each value of factor and average;** [1 mark]**
- Means of measuring depth;** [1 mark]**
- Means of diameter of crater accurately;** [1 mark]**
- Apparatus for measuring diameter of ball accurately;** [1 mark]**
- Measure diameter of ball / crater in different places (and take mean);** [1 mark]**
- Smooth / flatten sand surface;** [1 mark]**
- At least 5 sets of data taken;** [1 mark]**
- Reliable means of releasing ball;** [1 mark]**
- Sensible values for factor quoted;** [1 mark]**

Draw a graph:

- Graph of diameter / depth of depression vs appropriate continuous variable;** [1 mark]**

**An example of an answer which would score 7 marks is:**

![img-706c5be35428-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/006-img-706c5be35428-1.jpeg)

Drop the smallest ball from a height of 1 m above the tray of sand. Remove the ball and measure the crater diameter in the sand using the 30 cm ruler.  Repeat for 7 metal balls of different sizes; **[1 mark]**

Repeat the experiment for each size of metal ball at least 3 times and calculate the mean diameter of the crater **AND **record the results in a table; **[1 mark]**

The height of the ball must be measured perpendicular to the ruler to ensure it is dropped at the same height each time and to avoid parallax error; **[1 mark]**

Plot a graph of the diameter of the crater vs. the diameter of the metal ball; **[1 mark]**

![img-da7fe464224b-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/008-img-da7fe464224b-1.jpeg)

Calculate the average time between two drops falling.

average time = ..................................................... s
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average time between two drops:

- List the known quantities:

  - Number of drops = 50
  - Time for 50 drops, $t = 20 \text{s}$
- Divide the total time by the number of drops:

$\text{average time} = \frac{\text{time for 50 drops}}{\text{number of drops}} = \frac{20}{50}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$\text{average time} =$$0 . 4 \text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for $20 \div 50$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $0 . 4 \text{s}$
> 
> - Accept 0.40 s
> - Both marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> The time between drops is the total time shared between the drops, so divide the time by the number of drops. Dividing the other way round gives 2.5, which is the number of drops per second: a rate, not a time.

parts.problemMd:
Four students P, Q, R and S each attempt to measure the time period (the time for one complete oscillation) of a pendulum. The arrows in Fig. 2.1 show the movements of the pendulum that each student times.

![screenshot-2022-10-12-at-13-28-02](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/049-screenshot-2022-10-12-at-13-28-02.png)

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Student S **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is easy to confuse students Q and S because both start and finish timing at the centre. One complete oscillation ends only when the pendulum returns to its starting position moving in the same direction as when it started. Student Q's pendulum is moving in the opposite direction at the end, so Q has timed only half an oscillation. Student S's pendulum swings to both sides and returns moving in its original direction, which is one full period.

parts.problemMd:
Another student uses a stopwatch to measure the time taken for 50 periods of a pendulum.

Fig. 2.2 shows the time taken on the stopwatch.

![screenshot-2022-10-12-at-13-30-36](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/050-screenshot-2022-10-12-at-13-30-36.png)

Calculate the time for one period of the pendulum. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

time for one period = ...................................................... s
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the time for one period of the pendulum:

- List the known quantities:

  - Total time = 1 minute 23.37 s
  - Number of periods = 50
- Convert the total time into seconds:

$1 \text{minute} = 60 \text{s}$

$\text{total time} = 60 + 23 . 37 = 83 . 37 \text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

- Write down the equation for the time of one period:

$T = \frac{\text{total time}}{\text{number of periods}}$

- Substitute the known values:

$T = \frac{83.37}{50}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer and give it to 3 significant figures:

$T = 1 . 6674 \text{s}$

$T =$$1 . 67 \text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for converting the total time to seconds: $83 . 37 \text{s}$
> 
> 1 mark for dividing the total time by the number of periods: $T = \frac{83.37}{50}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $1 . 67 \text{s}$
> 
> - Must be given to 3 significant figures; do not accept 1.6674 or 1.7
> - ecf from an incorrectly converted total time (e.g. reading the stopwatch as 123.37 s gives 2.47 s)

> **[exam-tip]**
> A stopwatch display of 1:23.37 means 1 minute 23.37 s. Convert the total time to seconds before dividing — a common error is to read the display as 123.37 s. Give your final answer to the 3 significant figures the question asks for; leaving it as 1.6674 s loses the final mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Side lengths from part (a): A = 7.5 cm, B = 4.0 cm, C = 2.0 cm. Expected answer 0.075 times 0.040 times 0.020 = 6.0 × 10<sup>-5 m³ (accept 0.00006 m³ or 0.000060 m³). volume = .................................... m<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:

$\text{side A} = \frac{7.5}{100} = 0 . 075 \text{m}$

$\text{side B} = \frac{4.0}{100} = 0 . 040 \text{m}$

$\text{side C} = \frac{2.0}{100} = 0 . 020 \text{m}$

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Convert each side to metres before multiplying, or your volume will be in cubic centimetres. If you multiply in centimetres first, remember that 1 m<sup>3</sup> = 100<sup>3</sup> cm<sup>3</sup>, so divide by 10<sup>6</sup>, not by 100.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A teacher investigates the reaction time of five students. A 0.50 m ruler is held above the hand of a student before being allowed to fall. The arrangement is shown in Fig. 3.1.

As soon as the ruler falls the student closes their hand, catching the ruler. The further the ruler falls, the greater the reaction time of the student. The results obtained are shown in Fig. 3.2.

In a similar investigation, a ruler drops a distance of 11.0 cm and has an average speed of 16 cm / s.

Calculate the reaction time.

reaction time = ...................................................... s
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the reaction time from this data:

Recall the equation for speed:

- $\mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{time}}$ **OR  **$v=\frac{s}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make time the subject:

- $\mathrm{time}=\frac{\mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{speed}}$ **OR  **$t=\frac{s}{v}$

Substitute the values:

- $t=\frac{11}{16}$ **[1 mark]**
- *t* = 0.69 s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The key to this question is simply to remember that the reaction time is the amount of time that passes before the person catches the ruler. If you were confused by the description then just remember that you will never be asked to invent or discover anything new in an exam. The questions will always use only the physics you learned in class.*

parts.problemMd:
A student has a piece of metal that has an irregular shape. The weight of the metal is 3.0 N.

Calculate the mass of the metal.

mass = ..................................................... kg
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the mass of the metal:

List the known quantities:

- Weight of metal, *W *= 3.0 N

Recall the value of gravitational field strength on Earth:

- *g *= 9.8 N/kg

Recall the equation for mass, *m* and weight, *W *and rearrange to make mass the subject:

- $W=mg$
- $m=\frac{W}{g}$
- $m=\frac{3.0}{9.8}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the mass of the metal:

- *m *= 0.306 kg = 0.31 kg (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *For your physics examinations, the gravitational field strength on Earth is 9.8 N/kg.*

Fig. 1.1 shows a dripping tap and a measuring cylinder. The water drops all have the same volume. The drops fall from the tap at equal time intervals.

![Diagram showing a dripping tap with drops falling into a measuring cylinder. Labels indicate "dripping tap" and "measuring cylinder".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/030-diagram-showing-a-dripping-tap-with-drops-fallin.png)

(i) The student collects 200 of the drops in a measuring cylinder. The total volume collected is 60 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the average volume of **one** drop of water.

volume = .................................................. cm<sup>3</sup> [3]

(ii) Another student uses a stop-watch to measure the time taken for the tap to produce 200 drops. Fig. 1.2 shows the time reading on the stop-watch.

![Illustration of a stopwatch showing a time of 3 minutes, 46.50 seconds; marked as Fig. 1.2.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/031-illustration-of-a-stopwatch-showing-a-time-of-3-.png)

Determine the time, in seconds, for the tap to produce 200 drops.

time = ...................................................... s [2]

(iii) Determine the average time interval between one drop starting to fall and the next drop starting to fall.

time interval = ...................................................... s [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the average volume of one drop of water:

- Total volume = number of drops × average volume of one drop; **[1 mark]**
- Where:

  - Total volume of water = 60 cm<sup>3</sup>
  - Number of drops = 200

Rearrange to find the average volume of one drop:

- Average volume of one drop = $\frac{total volume of water}{numberofdrops}$
- Average volume of one drop = $\frac{60}{200}$ **[1 mark]**
- Average volume of one drop = 0.3 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) Determine the time for the tap to produce 200 drops:

- The stop-watch shows a time reading of 3 minutes and 46.5 seconds
- To convert 3 minutes into seconds, multiply by 60 s
- 3 minutes = 3 × 60 = 180 s

The time reading, in seconds, is:

- Time = 180 + 46.5 **[1 mark]**
- Time = 226.5 s **[1 mark]**

(iii) Determine the average time interval between each drop:

- Time interval = $\frac{total time}{numberofintervals}$ **[1 mark]**
- Time interval = $\frac{226.5}{200}$
- Time interval = 1.1 s **[1 mark]**

**Total: [7 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A student uses a stopwatch in a timing experiment.

Fig. 1.1 shows the stopwatch readings.

![screenshot-2022-10-27-at-12-07-39](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/055-screenshot-2022-10-27-at-12-07-39.png)

Calculate the time interval between the two readings.

time interval = ...................................................... s
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the time interval between the two readings:

List the known quantities:

- Start time = 1 minute 22.1 seconds
- Final time = 3 minutes 46.5 seconds

Convert the times to seconds:

- $1\mathrm{min}=60s$
- $\mathrm{start} \mathrm{time}=1\mathrm{minute}22.1s$

  - $\mathrm{start} \mathrm{time}=60s+22.1s=82.1s$
- $\mathrm{final} \mathrm{time}=3\mathrm{minutes}46.5s$

  - $\text{final} \text{time} = ( 3 \times 60 ) + 46.5 = 226.5 \mathrm{s}$

Calculate the time interval:

- The interval is the difference between the start time and the final time
- $interval=final time-starttime$
- $interval=226.5-82.1$ **[1 mark]**
- interval = 144.4 s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *You could have answered this question without converting both times first. You may have subtracted the minutes and seconds separately and given your answer in minutes and seconds before converting to seconds. However, you needed to give your final answer in seconds, because the answer space gives units of seconds.*

parts.problemMd:
A device has a light-emitting diode (LED) that flashes briefly at regular intervals.

Describe how to determine accurately the average time for each interval, using a stopwatch.
parts.solutionMd:
Describe how to determine accurately the average time for each interval, using a stopwatch:

- Start the stopwatch as the LED flashes; **[1 mark]**
- Time a large number of flashes, such as 10 (or more); **[1 mark]**
- Stop the stopwatch on the 10th flash (or any integer value greater than 1); **[1 mark]**
- Divide the time on the stopwatch by 10 (or the integer value written in the previous point); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Make sure you start the timer on a flash. This flash is t = 0. The next flash is the first flash you count. *

> *Just timing  the duration between two consecutive flashes would give an inaccurate value. There is error involved when using a stopwatch, because the **reaction time** of the experimenter affects the time between the LED flashing and the stopwatch starting. *

> *We want the uncertainty to be a small fraction of the measurement itself, so a longer measurement of time gives a more accurate result. Dividing this by the number of flashes then gives a more accurate value for the length of a single flash. *

> *It is important to state that the stopwatch needs starting as the first marking point. *

parts.solutionMd:
To measure the volume of one of the coins:

Any **four** from:

**Method 1: use a measuring cylinder**

- Measuring cylinder partially filled with water; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of water recorded; **[1 mark]**
- Coin(s) placed in water; **[1 mark]**
- New volume noted; **[1 mark]**
- (Average) volume of a coin = increase in volume **OR**** **Increase in volume ÷ number of coins = average volume of one coin; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

Any **four** from:

**Method 2: use a displacement can**

- Displacement can filled with water; **[1 mark]**
- Empty measuring cylinder under spout; **[1 mark]**
- Water covers all coin(s); **[1 mark]**
- Displaced water collected in measuring cylinder; **[1 mark]**
- (Average) volume of a coin = increase in volume **OR**** **Increase in volume ÷ number of coins = average volume of one coin; **[1 mark]**

**An example answer which would score 4 marks:**

Take a measuring cylinder and add water, **[1 mark] **noting the starting volume (call this *V*<sub>*1*</sub>) **[1 mark]**

Put five coins in the water, **[1 mark] **the volume will increase.

Note the new volume (call this *V*<sub>*2*</sub>) **[1 mark]**

Find the volume of five coins by calculating, volume *V* = *V*<sub>*2*</sub> - *V*<sub>*1*</sub>

Find the volume of one coin by calculating the average, so $\frac{V}{5}=volumeonecoin$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You can see from the example that by writing a detailed explanation, step by step, you will often get more of the 'marking points' than there are marks for the question.*

> *You will still only be given four marks, but don't take this as a sign you should write less! Remember that you won't know exactly what the examiner is giving marks for. You do know that they are looking for good physics, so practice covering all the steps in short bullet points.*

> *You do not need to write in full paragraphs or sentences in your physics exam, unless the command word specifically asks for it. For this question, bullet points of the main points are better. Make sure you understand what the command words mean so that you can answer the questions fully. *

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the magnitude of the downward force acting on the bucket of water:

Determine the vertical resultant tension force of the ropes:

- Construct a vector diagram using the parallelogram method

![BVH6pu5I_ma-vector-tension-bucket](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-1-physical-quantities-and-measurement-techniques/assets/060-bvh6pu5i-ma-vector-tension-bucket.png)

- $F_{R}=\frac{T}{\mathrm{cos}θ}$ **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, $F_{R} = \frac{ 31}{\cos ( 45 )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $F_{R}=44N$** [1 mark]**

Determine the downward force acting on the bucket:

- The downward force is balanced by the vertical resultant tension force

  - Therefore, the forces are equal and opposite

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The downward force on bucket = 44 N

The bucket has a mass of 0.65 kg.

Calculate the mass of the water in the bucket.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the mass of the water in the bucket, $m_{w}$:

List the known quantities:

- Weight, $W$= 44 N (from part (a))
- Mass of bucket, $m_{b}$= 0.65 kg
- Gravitational field strength, $g$ = 9.8 N/kg

Recall the equation for weight and rearrange to make $m$ the subject:

- $W=mg$
- $m=\frac{W}{g}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the combined mass of the bucket, $m_{b}$, and the water, $m_{w}$:

- $( m_{b} + m_{w} ) = \frac{W}{g} = \frac{ 44}{9.8}$
- $( m_{b} + m_{w} ) = 4.49 \text{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the mass of the water:

- $m_{w}=4.49-0.65=3.84=3.8\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You will be expected to remember the value of the gravitational field strength, **g** = 9.8 N/kg or 9.8 m/s. Sometimes, it may be given to you in the question.*

parts.problemMd:
During part of a race, a skier travels a distance of 200 m in a time of 6.4 s.

Calculate the average speed of the skier.

average speed = ................................................ m/s
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average speed of the skier:

- List the known quantities:

  - Distance travelled, *s* = 200 m
  - Time taken, *t* = 6.4 s
- State the equation linking average speed, distance and time:

$\mathrm{average} \mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled}}{\mathrm{time} \mathrm{taken}}$**[1 mark]**

- Substitute values into the average speed equation:

$\mathrm{average} \mathrm{speed}=\frac{200}{6.4}$ **[1 mark]**

average speed = 31.25 = **31 m/s** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for $\mathrm{average} \mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled}}{\mathrm{time} \mathrm{taken}}$ **OR****  **$v=\frac{s}{t}$
> 
> 1 mark for calculating $200\div6.4$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 31 m/s (2 s.f.)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Regularly in CIE exams, there is a mark for stating the correct equation. Therefore, don't just jump straight into substituting in values. If you are unsure of the symbols for average speed, distance, and time, write the equation out in words, as this is also accepted!

**Extract:**

- At P accept "speed is increasing" or "speeding up"; at R accept "speed is decreasing" or "slowing down" for the mark.
- Do not accept "decreasing acceleration" or "non-uniform/decreasing in acceleration" for "decelerates" at R.

Fig. 4.1 shows a speed–time graph for the skier in another part of the race.

![IPRqRWuG_cie-2020-31-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-2-motion/assets/095-iprqrwug-cie-2020-31-6.png)

Describe the motion of the skier at each point **P**, **Q**, **R **and **S **on the graph.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> At **P**:
> 
> - The skier (constantly) accelerates (from 5 m/s) / speed is increasing / speeding up **[1 mark]**
> 
> At **Q**:
> 
> - The skier is at constant speed (of 17.5 m/s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> At **R**:
> 
> - The skier decelerates (from 17.5 m/s to rest) / speed is decreasing / slowing down **[1 mark]**
> 
> At **S**:
> 
> - The skier is at rest / stationary **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> On a speed-time graph a horizontal line means constant speed, not stationary — the skier is still moving
> 
> Don't confuse decelerating (slowing down) with decreasing acceleration (still speeding up, just less quickly)
> 
> Make sure you recognise the key aspects of a speed-time graph:
> 
> - The area under the graph is the distance travelled
> - A horizontal straight line is constant speed
> - A diagonal straight line with a positive gradient is acceleration and with a negative gradient is deceleration
> - A curved line directed upwards is non-constant acceleration and directed downwards (like at R) is non-constant deceleration

parts.problemMd:
An elevator in the Empire State Building is travelling at constant speed downward as it passes three levels.

This takes 5.0 seconds and each level has a height of 4.0 m. Calculate the speed of the elevator. State the correct units in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the speed of the elevator:

List the known quantities:

- Height of each level, $h$ = 4.0 m
- Number of levels  = 3
- Time taken, $t$ = 5.0 s

Recall the speed equation:

- $v=\frac{s}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the total distance covered:

- $s=3\times h=3\times4.0$
- $s=12m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the speed and give its units:

- $v=\frac{12}{5.0}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v=2.4$ **[1 mark]**

State the units:

- Units are m/s **OR** metres per second **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *If you got this question wrong, you most likely did not spot that the elevator travels the distance of **three** levels*

  - *You could have missed **two** marks by not reading the question fully*
  - *You were also awarded a mark for giving the units - **always** go through a question and **underline** crucial information **before** you start*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Calculate the speed of the elevator:

List the known quantities:

- Height of each level, h = 4.0 m
- Number of levels  = 3
- Time taken, t = 5.0 s

Recall the speed equation:

- v = s / t

Determine the total distance covered:

- s = 3 × h = 3 × 4.0
- s = 12 m

Calculate the speed and give its units:

- v = 12 / 5.0
- v = 2.4

State the units:

- Units are m/s OR metres per second

**Extended tier only**

From this constant speed, it takes the elevator 1.5 s to come to rest.

Calculate the deceleration of the elevator.

deceleration = ...................................................... m/s<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the deceleration of the elevator:

List the known quantities:

- Time taken to stop, $t$ = 1.5 s
- Initial speed, $u$ = 2.4 m/s (from part **(a)**)

Determine the change in speed:

- Elevator comes to **rest** so the final speed = 0 m/s
- $Δv=v-u=0-2.4=-2.4m/s$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation for acceleration:

- $a=\frac{Δv}{Δt}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the deceleration:

- $a=\frac{-2.4}{1.5}$ **[1 mark]**
- $a=-1.6m/s^{2}$

State the deceleration:

- $\text{deceleration} = 1.6 ( \mathrm{m} \div \mathrm{s}^{2} )$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *If your final answer had a negative sign, you may still have gained the marks*

  - *However, it is important to know the distinction between **acceleration** and **deceleration*
  - *They have opposite signs to one another, so if acceleration is −8.0 m/s*<sup>*2*</sup>* then deceleration is 8.0 m/s*<sup>*2*</sup>
- *Change in speed =** final speed − initial speed**, not the other way round*

  - *The order is important, **swapping** initial and final speeds changes the **sign** of change in speed!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Once everyone has left the elevator, the cable breaks. A device which measures speed over time was found in the elevator when a team investigated the incident.

The data from this are shown in Fig. 1.1.

![1-2-q4c-e-speed-time-freefall-stop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-2-motion/assets/098-1-2-q4c-e-speed-time-freefall-stop.png)

**Fig 1.1**

(i) Calculate the gradient of the speed-time graph.

[3]

(ii) When the elevator's cable completely snapped, the elevator is in freefall. Explain how the gradient shows this.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the gradient of the speed-time graph:

Recall how to calculate gradient:

- $\mathrm{gradient}=\frac{Δy}{Δx}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the gradient of the graph:

![screenshot-2023-02-07-at-15-49-42](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-2-motion/assets/099-screenshot-2023-02-07-at-15-49-42.png)

- $Δy=49-0=49$
- $Δx=5.0-0.0=5.0$
- $\mathrm{gradient}=\frac{49}{5.0}$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{gradient}=9.8m/s^{2}$ (range of 9.7 to 9.9 m/s<sup>2</sup> accepted) **[1 mark]**

(ii) Explain how the gradient shows the elevator is in freefall:

- 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> is the acceleration due to gravity; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The simplest way to calculate this gradient was to use a triangle covering the **whole** diagonal line, giving the values shown in the mark scheme*

  - *It is important to notice that the line goes up to 49 m/s, not 50 m/s - differences likes this are crucial when reading data from a graph*
- *To answer part (ii) correctly, you must recognise that the value you calculated for **gradient** is **similar** or **identical** to the value of acceleration due to **free fall **/ gravity*

  - *This means the cable is no longer supporting the elevator, which is **falling** under the force of its own **weight** **only*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the speed–time graph of a person on a journey.

On the journey, he walks and then waits for a bus. He then travels by bus. He gets off the bus and waits for two minutes. He then walks again. His journey takes 74 minutes.

![may-june-2020-42-q1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-2-motion/assets/096-may-june-2020-42-q1.jpg)

For the whole journey calculate:

(i) the distance travelled

distance = ......................................................... [3]

(ii) the average speed.

average speed = ......................................................... [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the distance travelled:

Recall the equation for calculating distance, *s:*

- $s=vt$* ***OR**** **$distance travelled=area under graph$; **[1 mark]**

Use the graph to obtain the time for each section of movement:

![pbBl25G4_file-000-35](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-2-motion/assets/097-pbbl25g4-file-000-35.png)

- Section (A) = 20 minutes
- Section (B) = 20 minutes
- Section (C) = 22 minutes

Convert the time from minutes to hours:

- This is because the speed is measured in km/h (not km/min)
- $1hour=60minutes$

  - $SectionsAandBare20minutes=\frac{20}{60}=\frac{1}{3}of an hour$
  - $SectionCis22minutes=\frac{11}{30}of an hour$

Calculate the area under each part of the graph:

Any **one **from:

- $areaundersectionA=5\times\frac{1}{3}=1.667km$ **[1 mark]**
- $areaundersectionB=40\times\frac{1}{3}=13.33km$ **[1 mark]**
- $areaundersectionC=6\times\frac{11}{30}=2.2km$ **[1 mark]**

- *No additional marks for further correct areas*

Calculate the total area under the graph:

- $total area=areaofsectionA+areaofsectionB+areaofsectionC$
- $total area=1.667+13.33+2.2$
- total area = 17 km **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the average speed:

Convert the total time from minutes into hours:

- $totaltimeofjourney=74minutes=\frac{74}{60}=\frac{37}{30}hours$

Recall the equation to calculate the average speed:

- $averagespeed=\frac{total distance}{total time}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the average speed:

- $averagespeed=\frac{17}{\frac{37}{30}}=13.78=14km/h$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *You can give the equation for distance in words or symbols and in any rearrangement to score 1 mark. *

> *Look carefully at the **units** on the axes of the graph. Time is measured in **minutes**. Don't try to convert to seconds, as the units for speed are km / h. Convert the time into **hours**.*

**Extract:**

When marking this answer:

A high-speed train travels along a straight track and passes four stations, A, B, C and D.

The distance between each pair of neighbouring stations is 12 km.

The train takes 30 minutes to travel from station A to station D.

Calculate the average speed of the train. State the unit of your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average speed of the train:

- List the known quantities:

  - Distance between neighbouring stations = $12 \text{km}$
  - Time taken, $t = 30 \text{minutes}$
- Determine the total distance from station A to station D (three sections of 12 km):

$d = 3 \times 12 = 36 \text{km} = 36  000 \text{m}$ **[1 mark]**

- Convert the time into seconds:

$t = 30 \times 60 = 1800 \text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

- Write down the equation:

$\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$

- Substitute the known values:

$\text{average speed} = \frac{36000}{1800}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$\text{average speed} =$$20 \text{m/s}$ **[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a total distance of 36 km **OR** 36 000 m
> 
> 1 mark for converting the time to 1800 s **OR** 0.5 hours
> 
> 1 mark for dividing the total distance by the total time
> 
> 1 mark for the correct value of 20
> 
> 1 mark for the unit m/s **OR** metres per second
> 
> You may also gain full marks by working in kilometres and hours: 36 km ÷ 0.5 h = 72 km/h

> **[exam-tip]**
> Count the gaps, not the stations. Four stations have only three sections of track between them, so the train travels 3 × 12 km, not 4 × 12 km.
> 
> Always sense-check a time conversion. Thirty minutes is half an hour, and an hour is 3600 s, so the answer must be 1800 s. If your value is ten times bigger or smaller than this, look again at your working.

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates how the material of a surface affects the height to which a ball bounces.

The following apparatus is available to the student:

- a selection of balls of similar size
- a clamp, stand, and boss
- samples of different surface materials (e.g., wood, carpet, rubber, tile)

Plan an experiment to investigate how the surface material affects the bounce height of the ball.

In your plan:

- list any additional apparatus needed
- explain briefly how you would carry out the investigation
- state the key variables to keep constant
- draw a table, with column headings, to show how you would display your readings (you are **not** required to enter any readings in the table)
- explain how you would use your readings to reach a conclusion.

You may draw a diagram if it helps your explanation.
parts.solutionMd:
**Apparatus**

Use a metre ruler to measure bounce height and a set square to ensure the metre rule is vertical.

**Method**

1. Set up the metre rule vertically using the stand and clamp
2. Place the first surface material (e.g., wood) on the bench at the base of the ruler
3. Hold the ball at a fixed drop height (e.g., 50.0 cm) and release it
4. Observe the maximum height reached by the ball on its first bounce and record it in the table
5. Repeat the drop from the same height at least two more times for this surface and calculate an average bounce height
6. Repeat the entire procedure for at least four other different surface materials

**Control variables**

The variables to be controlled are the drop height of the ball and the type of ball used (i.e. use the same ball each time).

**Table**

| surface material | bounce height 1 / cm | bounce height 2 / cm | bounce height 3 / cm | average bounce height / cm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |   |   |

**Conclusion**

Compare the average bounce heights for each material by plotting a bar chart with surface material on the x-axis and average bounce height on the y-axis. The tallest bar shows which surface results in the highest bounce.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The plan is marked out of 7, with one mark awarded for each of the following points:
> 
> **Apparatus**
> 
> - Metre rule **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Method**
> 
> - Valid procedure, e.g. dropping the ball from a fixed point and measuring the bounce height using the ruler **[1 mark]**
> - Repeat the experiment for at least 3 different surface materials **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Control variable**
> 
> - Drop height **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Table**
> 
> - Table with columns for surface material and bounce height with appropriate units **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Conclusion/analysis of the data**
> 
> - Compare readings in the table to see if different surfaces produce a change in the dependent variable (average height)** ** **OR** Plot a bar chart of material vs bounce height **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Additional points**
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Method to ensure the metre ruler is vertical / perpendicular to the bench, e.g. use of a set square
> - Method to measure the bounce height more accurately, e.g. use of a video camera / slow-motion phone camera
> - Take at least 5 sets of data
> - Repeat each measurement and take the average
> - Use the same ball / diameter / mass of ball each time
>

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate acceleration:

List the known quantities:

- Initial velocity, *u* = 0 m/s
- Final velocity, *v* = 120 m/s
- Time, *t* = 8.0 s

Recall the equation for acceleration:

- $a=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ **OR **$acceleration=\frac{change in velocity}{change in time}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values:

- $a=\frac{120-0}{8}$

Calculate the final answer:

- Acceleration, *a* = 15 m/s<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *A "change in" any quantity means the final value minus the initial value. In the case of velocity, this is often written as **v** − **u**. It is important to get this the right way round, as there is a big difference between gaining 120 m/s and losing 120 m/s.*

parts.problemMd:
An athlete runs 630 m in 130 s on a flat section of a road and then 254 m in 40 s on a downhill slope.

Calculate the average speed for the total distance run by the athlete.

average speed = ...................................................m/s
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the average speed for the total distance run by the athlete:

List the known quantities:

- Distance travelled on flat road,* s*<sub>1</sub> = 630 m
- Distance travelled on downhill slope,* s*<sub>2</sub> = 254 m
- Time taken on flat road, *t*<sub>1</sub> = 130 s
- Time taken on downhill slope, *t*<sub>2</sub> = 40 s

State the equation for average speed, *v*:

- $averagespeed=\frac{total distance}{total time}$ **OR** $averagespeed=\frac{s_{1}+s_{2}}{t_{1}+t_{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $v=\frac{s_{1}+s_{2}}{t_{1}+t_{2}}$
- $v=\frac{630+254}{130+40}=\frac{884}{170}$ **[1 mark]**

- *v* = 5.2 m/s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Equations with multiple values of the same quantity can sometimes look intimidating or confusing, but once you understand the notation, they are not that complex.*

> *For example, this question has **two** values for distance and **two** values for time. The easiest way to deal with this is to give the variables a number. Distance 1 and distance 2, time 1 and time 2. The short way to write this is just **d*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **d*<sub>*2*</sub>*, **t*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **t*<sub>*2*</sub>*. Try not to be overwhelmed by the notation, just read it as distance 1 and distance 2. *

**Extract:**

Density = W times k divided by V1 = 1.944, expected answer 1.9 g/cm³. 1 mark for the value rounded to two significant figures (error carried forward from the candidate's own W and V1); 1 mark for the unit g/cm³. Do not accept 1.944 or 1.94 for the value mark.

Calculate a value *ρ*<sub>1</sub> for the density of the modelling clay, using your results from **(a)(ii)** and **(c)** and the following equation:

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the density of the modelling clay:

- List the known quantities:

  - Weight, $W = 1 . 4 \text{N}$ (from part (c))
  - Volume, $V_{1} = 72 \text{cm}^{3}$ (from part (a)(ii))
  - $k = 100 \text{g/N}$
- Substitute into the given equation:

$ρ_{1} = \frac{W\times k}{V_{1}} = \frac{1.4\times100}{72} = 1 . 944$

- Round to two significant figures and give the unit:

$ρ_{1} =$$1 . 9 \text{g/cm}^{3}$ **[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a value of 1.9, given to two significant figures
> 
> - ecf: accept the candidate's own $W \times 100 \div V_{1}$ correctly evaluated and rounded to two significant figures
> - Do not accept 1.944 or 1.94 (too many significant figures)
> 
> 1 mark for the unit g/cm<sup>3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The value mark can only be gained at two significant figures, because an answer cannot be more precise than the data used to calculate it: the forcemeter reads to two significant figures and the ruler gives each length to two significant figures. CIE has become stricter about this, so for every calculation: find the piece of data with the fewest significant figures, write your answer to more figures than that, then round it to match.
> 
> ![screenshot-2022-11-10-at-12-21-00](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/018-screenshot-2022-11-10-at-12-21-00.png)

> Write the full calculator value (1.944) in your working and then round it: this shows the examiner both the correct arithmetic and the correct rounding. The unit is a separate mark, so g/cm<sup>3</sup> must be written on the answer line.

To find the volume of a piece of modelling clay of irregular shape:

- Record the (initial) volume of water (in the measuring cylinder); **[1 mark]**
