> *This part of the practical is a very common question and one that often trips students up. Practice explaining the steps in a logical fashion.*

> *You could also try answering with a diagram if that suits you better. The one below would get all four marks **as long as** all of the labels and the calculation are included.*

![irregular shape volume](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/043-irregular-shape-volume.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows laboratory equipment used to find the density of an irregularly shaped solid.

The volume of the modelling clay is found to be 64 cm<sup>3</sup>.

State the volume in m<sup>3</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
To convert cm<sup>3</sup> to m<sup>3</sup>:

Calculate the number of cubic centimetres in one cubic metre by imagining a large cube with sides of 100 cm:

- $1 \mathrm{m}^{3} = ( 100 \times 100 \times 100 ) = 1 000 000 = 1 \times 10^{6} cm^{3}$

Find the reciprocal (do 1 divided by) to find the number of m<sup>3</sup> in one cm<sup>3</sup>:

- $1\mathrm{cm}^{3}=\frac{1}{1\times10^{6}}=1\times10^{-6}m^{3}$

Calculate the answer:

- $64\mathrm{cm}^{3}=\frac{64}{1\times10^{6}}=64\times10^{-6}m^{3}$
- Volume = $64\times10^{-6}m^{3}$**OR**** **$0.000064m^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Many students find these conversions difficult to begin with but they are essential, so, practice!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The volume of the modelling clay is found to be 64 cm^3.
To convert cm^3 to m^3:
...
Calculate the answer:
- 64 cm^3 = 64 × 10^-6 m^3
- Volume = 64 × 10^-6 m^3 OR 0.000064 m^3

The mass of the modelling clay is 60 g.

(i) Determine the mass in kg.

[1]

(ii) Calculate the density of the modelling clay, stating your answer in terms of S.I. units.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The mass in kg is:

Use the fact that 1 kg = 1000 g:

- $\frac{60}{1000}$
- $=0.060\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate density in S.I. units:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 0.06 kg
- Volume, *v* = 0.000064 m<sup>3</sup> (from part (c)

Use the density equation and calculate:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{v}$ **[1 mark]**
- $ρ=\frac{0.06}{0.000064}$** [1 mark]**

Write the answer to two sig figs and include the units:

- $ρ=940\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Calculations like these are almost always what examiners call 'error carried forward' (you will see it written 'ecf' in mark schemes).*

> *This means that even if you got the conversions from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to m*<sup>*3*</sup>*, or from g to kg, wrong, as long as you have correctly calculated density in the final part, you will get those marks because you used the right method.*

> *Another reason to always show your working!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Expected answer: density (only one box should be ticked).

Fig. 1.1 shows a set of masses made from the same material.

![2019-feb-mar-q1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/045-2019-feb-mar-q1.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Identify the quantity that is the same for all the masses.

Tick **one** box.

`square` density

`square` volume

`square` weight
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Density **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The clue is "made from the same material": density is a property of the material, so every mass has the same density however big it is. The masses have different sizes, so their volumes and weights cannot be the same.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Expected answer: 2500 g.

The largest mass is 2.5 kg.

State the number of grams in 2.5 kg.

2.5 kg = ...................................................... g
parts.solutionMd:
To convert the mass into grams:

- $1 \text{kg} = 1000 \text{g}$

$2 . 5 \text{kg} = 2 . 5 \times 1000 =$$2500 \text{g}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The prefix kilo means × 1000, so kilograms to grams is a multiplication. If you are unsure which way to convert, remember that a gram is a smaller unit, so the number of grams must be larger.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

g = 9.8 N/kg is given in the stem. Combined mass 4.0 kg. Expected value 39.2 (accept 39). Accept 40 only if g = 10 N/kg has been used. The unit N (newtons) earns its own independent mark; a bare number scores the value mark but not the unit mark. Error carried forward from an incorrect combined mass.

The three largest masses are 2.5 kg, 1.0 kg and 0.5 kg.

The gravitational field strength *g* is 9.8 N/kg.

Calculate the combined weight of these three masses. Include the unit.

weight = .........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the combined weight of the three masses:

- List the known quantities:

  - Masses: $2 . 5 \text{kg}$, $1 . 0 \text{kg}$ and $0 . 5 \text{kg}$
  - Gravitational field strength, $g = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$
- Add the masses to find the combined mass:

$m = 2 . 5 + 1 . 0 + 0 . 5 = 4 . 0 \text{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

- Write down the equation linking weight, mass and gravitational field strength, and substitute the known values:

$W = m g = 4 . 0 \times 9 . 8$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$W=39.2=$$39$ **[1 mark]**

- Give the unit:

**N** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the combined mass of $4 . 0 \text{kg}$ (accept 4 kg)
> 
> 1 mark for the equation $W = m g$ or $g = \frac{W}{m}$ in words or symbols, **OR** correct substitution $4 . 0 \times 9 . 8$ (accept the three weights calculated separately and added: $24 . 5 + 9 . 8 + 4 . 9$)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final value of 39
> 
> - Accept 39.2
> - Accept 40 if $g = 10 \text{N/kg}$ is used
> - ecf from an incorrect combined mass
> 
> 1 mark for the unit N (or newtons), awarded independently of the value

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Include the unit" is a signal that the unit is credited separately, so write N, not kg. You can add the masses first or multiply each mass by *g* and add the three weights: both routes score full marks. Rounded to two significant figures, 39.2 N is 39 N, not 40 N.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Question stem:

- Eight logs, average mass of each log 65.0 kg
- The stem gives g = 9.8 N/kg

---

When marking this answer:

- A correct final answer of 5100 N or 5096 N with no working scores all three marks
- Accept any correct substitution for the second mark, for example 8 × 65.0 × 9.8, 637 × 8 or 520 × 9.8
- Only 5100 N (or 5.1 × 10<sup>3</sup> N) or 5096 N earns the final mark; 5090 N is not a correct rounding and does not earn it
- An answer of 5200 N (g = 10 N/kg used) earns the W = mg mark only, never the substitution or final mark
- The weight of one log only (637 N) earns the W = mg mark only

Fig. 2.1 shows a wooden raft. The raft is made from eight logs.

The logs are all of the same type of wood.

![A flat raft made of eight logs of equal length lying side by side and held together near each end. One log is labelled log of wood.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/039-a-flat-raft-made-of-eight-logs-of-equal-length-l.png)

The average mass of each log is $65 . 0 \text{kg}$.

The gravitational field strength *g* is $9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$.

Calculate the total weight of the raft.

total weight of the raft = ....................................................... N
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the total weight of the raft:

- List the known quantities:

  - Average mass of each log $= 65 . 0 \text{kg}$
  - Number of logs = 8
  - Gravitational field strength, $g = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$

- Calculate the total mass of the raft:

$m = 8 \times 65 . 0 = 520 \text{kg}$

- Write down the equation for weight:

$W = m g$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the known values:

$W = 520 \times 9 . 8$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$W = 5096 \text{N}$

$W =$$5100 \text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct final answer of $5100 \text{N}$; 5096 N is also accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always use the value of *g* given in the question rather than one you remember: using 10 N/kg here gives 5200 N, which does not match the data you were given. Read the question carefully too. It asks for the weight of the whole raft, so remember to multiply the mass of one log by the number of logs.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Question stem:

- One log: mass 66.0 kg, length 3.0 m, cross-sectional area 0.040 m<sup>2</sup>

---

When marking this answer:

- In part (i), a correct final answer of 550 kg/m<sup>3</sup> with no working scores all three marks
- In part (i), award the final mark for a density correctly calculated from the candidate's own volume (ecf)

(i) The mass of one of the logs is $66 . 0 \text{kg}$. It is $3 . 0 \text{m}$ long and has a cross-sectional area of $0 . 040 \text{m}^{2}$.

Calculate the density of the wood in the log.

density = ............................................... kg/m<sup>3</sup>

[3]

(ii) Explain why the log in **(b)(i)** floats on water.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the density of the wood in the log:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass of the log, $m = 66 . 0 \text{kg}$
  - Length of the log, $l = 3 . 0 \text{m}$
  - Cross-sectional area, $A = 0 . 040 \text{m}^{2}$
- Calculate the volume of the log:

$V = l \times A = 3 . 0 \times 0 . 040$

$V = 0 . 12 \text{m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

- Write down the equation for density:

$ρ = \frac{m}{V}$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the known values:

$ρ = \frac{66.0}{0.12}$

- Calculate the answer:

$ρ =$$550 \text{kg/m}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (ii) The log floats on water because:
> 
> - The density of the log is less than the density of water **[1 mark]**
> 
> Any wording with the same meaning is accepted, for example "water is denser than the wood"

> **[exam-tip]**
> The density of water is 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, which gives you a quick sense-check here. If your answer to part (i) comes out above 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, the log would sink, so go back and check your volume calculation before you explain why it floats.

parts.problemMd:
Identify the unit that is used for mass.

Tick **one** box.

`square` kg

`square` N

`square` m<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
The unit of mass is:

- kg (kilogram); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A student is asked to write definitions for mass and weight.

For each of their answers insert the missing word, selected from the list below.

**force   gravity   kilogram   mass   matter   newton   rest**

(i) Mass is a measure of the quantity of .................... in an object at .................. relative to an observer.

[2]

(ii) Weight is a gravitational ........................ on an object that has ...........................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
The correct definitions of mass and weight are:

(i)

- Mass is a measure of the quantity of **matter** in an object; **[1 mark]**
- at **rest**** **relative to the observer; **[1 mark]**

(ii)

- Weight is a gravitational **force**** **on an object; **[1 mark]**
- that has **mass**; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A student needs to determine the density of a sample of oil.

They measure 0.001 m<sup>3</sup> of oil and find it has a mass of 0.75 kg.

(i) State the equipment the student uses to find the mass of oil.

[1]

(ii) Calculate the density of the oil.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The equipment used to find mass is:

- (Digital) scales; **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate density:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 0.75 kg
- Volume, *V* = 0.001 m<sup>3</sup>

Use the equation for density

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate:

- $ρ=\frac{0.75}{0.001}=750\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

They measure 0.001 m^3 of oil and find it has a mass of 0.75 kg.

Calculate the density of the oil.

- Mass, m = 0.75 kg
- Volume, V = 0.001 m^3
- Use the equation for density
- ρ = m / V
- ρ = 0.75 / 0.001 = 750 kg/m^3

**Extended tier only**

The oil in part (c) is poured into a beaker of water.

Assuming that the liquids do not mix, explain which liquid floats.
parts.solutionMd:
The liquid which will float is:

- <u>Oil</u> (floats on water);** [1 mark]**

Explain why:

- Oil is less dense than water **OR**** **water is more dense than oil (so it sinks); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon.

Gravitational field strength on Earth = 9.8 N/kg

Gravitational field strength on the Moon = 1.6 N/kg

Identify the quantity that is the different for the astronaut on the Moon compared to the Earth.

Tick **one** box.

`square` mass

`square` weight

`square` density
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Weight **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Mass is the amount of matter in an object, so it does not change with location. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass, so it decreases when the astronaut moves to the Moon's weaker gravitational field. Density does not change because neither the astronaut's mass nor their volume changes.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Gravitational field strength on Earth = 9.8 N/kg
Gravitational field strength on the Moon = 1.6 N/kg

The mass of the astronaut is 65 kg on Earth.

(i) Calculate the astronaut’s weight on Earth.

[2]

(ii) Calculate the astronaut’s weight on the Moon

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the astronaut's weight:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass, $m = 65 \text{kg}$
  - Gravitational field strength on Earth, $g_{E} = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$
  - Gravitational field strength on the Moon, $g_{M} = 1 . 6 \text{N/kg}$

(i) Weight on Earth:

- Write down the equation for weight:

$W = m g$

- Substitute the known values using the gravitational field strength on Earth:

$W = 65 \times 9 . 8 = 637 \text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer to two significant figures:

$W =$$640 \text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for substitution into $W = m g$ using $g = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$ **OR** a correct intermediate answer of $637 \text{N}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $640 \text{N}$
> 
> - Accept 637 N
> - Must include the unit N for this mark

(ii) Weight on the Moon:

- Substitute the known values using the gravitational field strength on the Moon:

$W = 65 \times 1 . 6 = 104 \text{N}$

$W =$$100 \text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $100 \text{N}$
> 
> - Accept 104 N
> - Must include the unit N for this mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Weight is a force, so its unit is N, not N/kg — writing the unit of gravitational field strength after a weight loses the mark. Round your final answers to the same number of significant figures as the data; two significant figures is a safe choice in almost every calculation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Gravitational field strength on Earth = 9.8 N/kg
Gravitational field strength on the Moon = 1.6 N/kg
The mass of the astronaut is 65 kg on Earth.
Weight on Earth: W = m × g_E = 65 × 9.8 = 640 N
Weight on the Moon: W = m × g_M = 65 × 1.6 = 100 N

Complete the following sentence.

The astronaut's weight on Earth is more than their weight on the Moon because, although their ..................... is the same, the .......................... force on Earth is ............................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The astronaut's weight on Earth is more than their weight on the Moon because, although their **mass** is the same, the **gravitational** force on Earth is **greater**.
> 
> - mass **[1 mark]**
> - gravitational **[1 mark]**
> - greater **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept larger for the third mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to write weight in the first blank — but weight is the quantity being compared, so it cannot also be the explanation. Always re-read the completed sentence to check it makes sense as a whole.

parts.problemMd: State the piece of equipment that can be used to compare the mass and weight of the astronaut while they are still on Earth.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - A balance **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A balance works by comparing the astronaut with known masses, so it compares mass and weight at the same time. An instrument that only measures one of them, such as a force meter for weight, does not answer the question.

parts.problemMd:
A student wishes to determine the density of a regular-shaped solid block, such as a cube.

State the **two** quantities the student must measure to find the density of the block.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Mass **[1 mark]**
> - Volume **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember that density is calculated using the formula $ρ = \frac{m}{V}$, so you need both mass and volume to determine density. For a regular-shaped solid like a cube, volume can be found by measuring the dimensions (e.g. length, width and height) and calculating, but the question asks for the two quantities needed, not how to measure them.

parts.problemMd:
The student then determines the density of an irregularly shaped stone.

To find the volume, the student lowers the stone into a measuring cylinder containing water.

Fig. 1.1 shows the water level in the measuring cylinder **before** the stone is added.

![Illustration of a graduated cylinder containing liquid at the 22 cm³ mark, with measurement lines in increments of 2 cm³ up to 50 cm³.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/036-illustration-of-a-graduated-cylinder-containing-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

(i) State the volume of water in the measuring cylinder shown in Fig. 1.1.

[1]

(ii) State the name of the curve formed by the water surface in Fig. 1.1.

[1]

(iii) The stone is lowered carefully into the water until it is fully covered.

The new volume reading is 46 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the volume of the stone.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> (i) State the volume of water in the measuring cylinder shown in Fig. 1.1.:
> 
> - $22\text{cm}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> (ii) State the name of the curve formed by the water surface in Fig. 1.1.:
> 
> - Meniscus **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When reading a measuring cylinder, always read from the bottom of the meniscus (the curved water surface) at eye level.

(iii) Calculate the volume of the stone:

$V=V_{f}-V_{i}$

$V = 46 - 22$  **[1 mark]**

$V=$$24\text{cm}^{3}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For displacement method questions, remember that the volume of an irregular object equals the difference between the final and initial water levels. Always show your working clearly, even for simple subtractions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(iii) The stone is lowered carefully into the water until it is fully covered. 

The new volume reading is 46 cm<sup>3</sup>. 

Calculate the volume of the stone.

V = Vf - Vi
V = 46 - 22
V = 24 cm<sup>3</sup>

The mass of the stone is 6.5 g.

Calculate the density of the stone.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the density of the stone:

$ρ=\frac{m}{V}$

$ρ=\frac{6.5}{24}$ **[1 mark]**

$ρ=0.2708...$

$ρ=$ $0.27g/\mathrm{cm}³$** **(2 s.f.)** ****[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember the density formula: $ρ = \frac{m}{V}$. Make sure you use the correct values for mass and volume from the question. Always include units in your final answer—density is typically expressed in g/cm<sup>3</sup> or kg/m<sup>3</sup> depending on the units given.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows a coil of wire.

![cie-2020-31-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/040-cie-2020-31-1.png)

A student measures the length of the coil using a ruler. His measurement is 3.8 cm.

There are 20 turns of wire in the coil. The student uses his measurement to calculate the average thickness of the wire.

(i) Show that the average thickness of the wire is about 0.2 cm.

average thickness of wire = .................................................. cm  [2]

(ii) The student’s measurement of 3.8 cm is inaccurate. Suggest one reason why the measurement is inaccurate.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Show that the average thickness of the wire is about 0.2 cm

List the known quantities:

- Number of turns on the wire = 20
- Length of coil = 3.8 cm

Calculate the average thickness:

- $\mathrm{average} \mathrm{thickness}=\frac{\mathrm{length} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{coil}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{turns} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{wire}}$
- $\mathrm{average} \mathrm{thickness}=\frac{3.8}{20}$ **[1 mark]**
- average thickness = 0.19 cm = 0.2 cm (1 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

(ii) One reason why the measurement is inaccurate is:

**Any one from:**

- The wire(s) are not touching; **[1 mark]**
- The wire could be stretched (in places); **[1 mark]**
- The ruler does not start at zero; **[1 mark]**
- The wire(s) (could) overlap; **[1 mark]**
- Eye is not directly above ruler (when reading from the scale); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The 3.8 cm does not need to be converted into metres (m), since the final answer is required in cm. Since the number of turns of the wire has no units,  *$\frac{3.8}{20}$*still has the units of cm. To know which value to divide by which, have a look at the diagram given in Fig 1.1, the thickness of the wire would be the thickness of one coil.*

> *A 'show that' calculation question often involves rounding your final answer to equal the value you've been asked to show. Remember to show this in your mark scheme by, for example, showing that your final answer is equal to the value requested when rounded to a certain number of significant figures (like is done in this mark scheme). *

parts.problemMd:
The volume of the wire in the coil is 16.6 cm<sup>3</sup> and its mass is 148 g.

Calculate the density of the metal used for the wire in the coil.

density = ............................................. g/cm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the density of the metal used for the wire in the coil:

List the known quantities:

- Volume of the wire, *V* = 16.6 cm<sup>3</sup>
- Mass of the wire, *m* = 148 g

State the equation linking density, volume and mass:

- $\mathrm{density}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{volume}}$ **OR **$ρ=\frac{m}{V}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the density equation, *ρ:*

- $ρ=\frac{148}{16.6}$ **[1 mark]**
- $ρ$* *= 8.9157 = 8.9 g/cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *If you forget whether it's mass or volume on the numerator (or denominator), have a look at the units that you've been required to give your final answer in. This is g/cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* where g (grams) is a unit of mass whilst cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* (centimetres cubed) is a unit of volume. The '/' means 'per', which means the equation must be *$\frac{mass}{volume}$*. Units will always match the equations, so it is a good habit to get into interpreting these if you're stuck in the exam!*

parts.problemMd:
The student has a measuring cylinder and a beaker of water, as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![cie-2020-31-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/041-cie-2020-31-2.png)

Describe how the student can determine the volume of the coil by using the equipment shown in Fig. 1.2.
parts.solutionMd:
The student can determine the volume of the coil by:

- Partially filling the measuring cylinder with water; **[1 mark]**
- Submerging the coil in the water; **[1 mark]**
- Measuring the new volume; **[1 mark]**
- The volume of the wire is the difference/increase in volume; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *This method works because the volume of water **displaced** is equal to the volume of the object, and is a great way of measuring the weight or volume of an irregular object. This is based upon 'Archimedes' principle'.*

parts.problemMd:
A 250 cm<sup>3</sup> beaker containing some liquid is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![q2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/049-q2.png)

(i) A student has a measuring cylinder and a balance.

Describe an experiment to determine the density of the liquid.

[5]

(ii) Suggest the unit of density used by the student.

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the resultant horizontal force acting on the raft and state the direction of this force:

List the known quantities:

- Force acting to the right = 1200 N
- Force acting to the left = 800 N

Deduce the method for calculating the resultant force:

- Resultant force = force acting to the right − force acting to the left

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- Resultant force = 1200 − 800
- Resultant force = 400 N **[1 mark]**

State the direction of the resultant force:

- To the right / forwards; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *A **resultant force** is a single force that describes all of the forces operating on a body. When many forces are applied to an object they can be combined (added) to produce one final force which describes the **combined action** of all of the forces.*

> *This single resultant force determines:*

- *The **direction** in which the object will move as a result of all of the forces*

  - *The **magnitude** of the final force experienced by the object*

> *If we determine that forward acting force is positive and the backward acting force is negative, then the resultant force is:*

> *F** = (+ 1000 N) + (− 800 N)*

> *Which is the same as saying:*

> *F** = 1000 N − 800 N*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(i) The face in contact with the ground is 12.0 cm by 2.0 cm; expected answer 24 cm². (ii) g = 9.8 N/kg; expected answer 8.232 N rounded to 8.2 N; accept 8.23 N; accept 8.4 N if g = 10 N/kg has been used. Award both marks in each sub-part for the correct answer alone.

Fig. 3.1 shows a metal block and its dimensions.

![Diagram of a rectangular block measuring 12.0 cm long, 3.0 cm high, and 2.0 cm from ground; labelled as Fig. 3.1, not to scale.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-3-mass-weight-and-density/assets/038-diagram-of-a-rectangular-block-measuring-12-0-cm.png)

(i)** **Calculate the area of the metal block in contact with the ground.

area = .................................................. cm<sup>2 </sup> [2]

(ii) The mass of the metal block is 0.84kg.

Calculate the weight of the metal block.

weight = ..................................................... N [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the area of the metal block in contact with the ground:

- The face on the ground measures 12.0 cm by 2.0 cm, so:

$\text{area} = \text{length} \times \text{width} = 12 . 0 \times 2 . 0$ **[1 mark]**

$\text{area} =$$24 \text{cm}^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for $\text{length} \times \text{width}$ or $12 . 0 \times 2 . 0$ (accept $12 \times 2$)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $24 \text{cm}^{2}$
> 
> - Do not accept 36 ($12 \times 3$) or 6 ($3 \times 2$): the face on the ground is the 12.0 cm by 2.0 cm face
> - Both marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

(ii) To calculate the weight of the metal block:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass, $m = 0 . 84 \text{kg}$
  - Gravitational field strength, $g = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$
- Write down the equation for weight and substitute the known values:

$W = m g = 0 . 84 \times 9 . 8$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$W = 8 . 232 \text{N} =$$8 . 2 \text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for $W = m g$ in words or symbols, or correct substitution $0 . 84 \times 9 . 8$ (accept $0 . 84 \times 10$)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $8 . 2 \text{N}$
> 
> - Accept 8.23 N or 8.232 N
> - Accept $8 . 4 \text{N}$ if $g = 10 \text{N/kg}$ is used
> - Both marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the diagram to decide which face touches the ground: it is the 12.0 cm by 2.0 cm face, not the 12.0 cm by 3.0 cm one. The current syllabus takes *g* as 9.8 N/kg; this 2022 paper used 10 N/kg, so 8.4 N is also credited here, but in your exam, use 9.8 N/kg unless the paper tells you otherwise.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

*Mass of balloon:*

**Any three from**:

- Let balloon dry; **[1 mark]**
- Use digital scales to find mass of the inflated balloon; **[1 mark]**
- Burst balloon **AND**** **find mass of the empty balloon; **[1 mark]**
- Subtract (balloon + air) − (balloon) to find mass of air; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *An example answer which scores five marks is:*

> *To calculate density you will need mass and volume. *

> *To find the volume of air, fill the balloon and tie the neck. Add water to the bucket then put the balloon in, pushing it down so it is completely under water. Note the new level of the water.*

> *Take out the balloon and use the measuring cylinder to top up the bucket to the same level. The volume of the water needed is the volume of air in the balloon.*

> *Let the balloon dry before weighing.*

> *Find the mass of the balloon using the digital scales. Burst the balloon and find the empty mass. Subtract mass 2 from mass 1 to find the mass of the air.*

> *The statement that 'you do not need to include details of the calculation' indicates that you will not get any marks for doing so. Especially since in part (c) you have already calculated density, so doing so again is not showing the examiner any new skills.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extended Tier Only**

A lake has a layer of ice on its surface. The area of the lake is 1800 m<sup>2</sup> . The ice has a thickness of 0.025 m. The density of ice is 920 kg/m<sup>3</sup> .

(i) Calculate the mass of ice on the lake.

mass = .......................................................... [2]

(ii) At night, the temperature of the ice on the lake falls by 3.5 °C.

The specific heat capacity of ice is 2.1 $\times$ 10<sup>3</sup>  J/kg °C.

Calculate the change in energy as the temperature falls.

energy = .......................................................  J [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the mass of ice:

List the known quantities:

- Area, *A* = 1800 m<sup>2</sup>
- Thickness, *t* = 0.025 m
- Density, *ρ* = 920 kg/m<sup>3</sup>

Calculate the volume, *V*, of the ice:

- $V=At$
- $V=1800\times0.025$
- $V=45m^{3}$

Recall the equation for density and rearrange for mass:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$ **[1 mark]**
- $m=ρV$

Substitute the known quantities:

- $m=920\times45$
- $m=41000kg$ **[1 mark**]

(ii) To calculate the energy change:

List the known quantities:

- Temperature change, Δ*θ* = 3.5 °C
- Mass, *m* = 41 000 kg (from part (a))
- Specific heat capacity, *c* = 2.1 × 10<sup>3</sup>  J/kg °C

Recall the equation for thermal energy transfer:

- $ΔE=mc\mathrm{Δθ}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities:

- $ΔE=41000\times(2.1\times10^{3})\times3.5$
- $ΔE=3.0\times10^{8}$ J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

The following apparatus is available:

- a selection of beams made from different ratios of sand and cement and of various lengths
- triangular blocks to support the beams
- a metre rule
- a selection of loads.

The student takes all the necessary safety precautions. You are **not** required to write about safety precautions.

In your plan, you should:

- explain briefly how to carry out the investigation (you may add to the diagram if it helps your explanation)
- state the key variables to keep constant
- draw a table, or tables, with column headings, to show how to display your readings (you are **not** required to enter any readings in the table)
- explain how you would use the readings to reach a conclusion.
parts.solutionMd:
Plan an experiment to investigate the force required to break different beams:

Identify the variable being tested:

- The distance between the supports / the length of beam **OR **
- The composition of the beam (proportion of sand / cement); **[1 mark]**

Describe a method for the investigation:

- Increase load (in steady increments) until the beam breaks **AND **record the maximum breaking load (force at which the beam breaks); **[1 mark]**
- Repeat for (at least 2 more) different lengths (if testing length) **OR**
- Repeat for (at least 2 more) different beams (if testing composition); **[1 mark]**

Plus any **one **from:

- Collect at least 5 sets of results; **[1 mark]**
- Carry out repeats of individual tests **AND **average the results; **[1 mark]**
- (Conduct a rough initial test then) add small loads until near the breaking load; **[1 mark]**
- Carefully place loads on the beam; **[1 mark]**

Identify the control variables:

**EITHER**

If testing length:

- The position of the load e.g. the centre of the beam **AND**
- The position of the supports
- **AND**
- The composition of the beam;** [1 mark]**

**OR **If testing composition:

- The position of the load e.g. the centre of the beam **AND**
- The distance between the supports **AND**
- The length of the beam; **[1 mark]**

Draw a table to show how to display the readings:

- Table drawn with a column for distance / length **OR **composition **AND**
- A column for (maximum) load **AND **
- Correct units for load (N) and distance / length (cm or m); **[1 mark]**

Explain how the readings can be used to reach a conclusion:

- Compare the maximum breaking load with the variable being tested **OR**
- Plot a graph of maximum breaking load against length; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

> *An example model answer might be:*

- *Test how the length of a beam affects the maximum load required to break it*
- *Control the position of the load by placing it at the centre of the beam each time,** **keep the supports in the same relative position for each beam length and use the same beam composition each time*
- *The method is:*

  - *Carry out an initial test to increase the load until the beam breaks and note this as the rough breaking load *
  - *Repeat, but carefully add loads (in steady increments) until close to the rough breaking load, then add smaller loads*
  - *Record the maximum breaking load (force at which the beam breaks)*
  - *Repeat for 5-6 different beam lengths *
- *Repeat this experiment 3 times for each length and calculate the average breaking load for each beam length*
- *Record this data in a table (as shown above) and plot a graph of maximum breaking load against length*

> *To score the mark about reaching a conclusion, you could make a prediction about the outcome of the experiment to illustrate your point, for example: *

- *If testing beam length, you might conclude: As the length of the beam increases, the maximum breaking load decreases*
- *If testing beam composition, you might conclude: As the proportion of cement in the beam increases, the maximum breaking load increases*

![A spring hanging from a clamp stand next to a vertical metre ruler positioned on a bench.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/031-a-spring-hanging-from-a-clamp-stand-next-to-a-ve.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The student measures the length $L_{0}$ of the unstretched spring. Fig. 1.2 shows the spring next to the metre rule.

![Close up of the top and bottom of the spring against the vertical ruler scale marked from 35 to 51 with millimetre increments.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/032-close-up-of-the-top-and-bottom-of-the-spring-aga.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

(i) By taking scale readings from the metre rule in Fig. 1.2, calculate the unstretched length $L_{0}$ of the spring in cm.

[2]

(ii) State **one** precaution the student should take to obtain an accurate length reading.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Take scale readings from the metre rule:

top reading = 37.0 cm

bottom reading = 48.5 cm

**[1 mark]**

Calculate the unstretched length of the spring:

$L_{0}=\mathrm{bottom} \mathrm{reading}-\mathrm{top} \mathrm{reading}$

$L_{0}=48.5-37.0$

$L_{0}=$ $11.5\text{cm}$** ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct top and bottom readings within 0.1 cm
> 
> 1 mark for correctly calculating $L_{0}=\mathrm{bottom} \mathrm{reading}-\mathrm{top} \mathrm{reading}$
> 
> Accept answers for $L_{0}$ in range 11.3 to 11.7 cm.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (ii) To obtain an accurate length reading, the student should:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Use a set square to ensure the metre rule is vertical
> - Read the scale perpendicularly / at eye level to avoid parallax error
> - Ensure the spring is not oscillating before taking the reading
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When reading lengths from a ruler where the object does not start at zero, remember to subtract the starting position from the end position. Many students make errors by simply reading the bottom value without accounting for where the top of the spring is positioned.
> 
> For precautions relating to measurement accuracy, always think about parallax error and how to minimise it. Mentioning the use of a set square or reading at eye level demonstrates good practical technique.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The student measures the length L₀ of the unstretched spring.

Calculate the unstretched length of the spring:
L₀ = bottom reading - top reading
L₀ = 48.5 - 37.0
L₀ = 11.5 cm

The student hangs various loads $W$ on the spring and measures the new length $L$ each time. The results are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| $W$ / N | $L$ / cm | $e$ / cm |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 14.3 |   |
| 2.0 | 16.7 |   |
| 3.0 | 19.5 |   |
| 4.0 | 22.1 |   |
| 5.0 | 24.9 |   |

Calculate, and record in Table 1.1, the extension $e$ of the spring for each load $W$. Use the equation $e = ( L - L_{0} )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the extension $e$ for each load $W$:

- Unstretched length, $L_{0}=11.5\text{cm}$ (from (a))

$e = ( L - L_{0} )$

- For $W=1.0\text{N}$:

$e=14.3-11.5=2.8\text{cm}$

Record the values of extension $e$ in the table:

| $W$ / N | $L$ / cm | $e$ / cm |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 14.3 | **Final answer:** **2.8** |
| 2.0 | 16.7 | **Final answer:** **5.2** |
| 3.0 | 19.5 | **Final answer:** **8.0** |
| 4.0 | 22.1 | **Final answer:** **10.6** |
| 5.0 | 24.9 | **Final answer:** **13.4** |

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly calculating each value of $e$ by subtracting the value of $L_{0}$ calculated in part (a) from $L$ in each row** AND** recording each value to 1 d.p.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you use your calculated value for the unstretched length $L_{0}$ from the previous part of the question. A common mistake is to use the wrong value or to subtract the values in the wrong order. Remember that extension is always the new length minus the original length, so your answer should be positive if the spring has stretched.

Include the unit.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the gradient $G$ of your line:

![Large triangle drawn on graph between data points (0, 0) and (6, 16). Calculations shown for delta y (16 minus 0) and delta x (6 minus zero).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/035-large-triangle-drawn-on-graph-between-data-point.png)

$G=\frac{16-0}{6-0}$

$G=$ $2.67$(3 s.f.)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

(ii) Calculate a value for the spring constant $k$ of the spring:

$k=\frac{1}{G}$

$k=\frac{1}{2.67}$

$k=$ $0.375$(3 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

- Include the unit:

$\text{N/cm}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Accept equivalent values and corresponding units, e.g. $37.5N/m$

> **[exam-tip]**
> When finding the gradient of a graph, always draw a large triangle that uses as much of the line as possible. This reduces the percentage error in your reading and gives a more accurate gradient. Make sure you clearly mark the triangle on the graph so the examiner can see how you obtained your values. Remember that the gradient has units derived from the y-axis unit divided by the x-axis unit.

parts.problemMd:
A student is using some 50 g masses.

Calculate the weight of one 50 g mass.

weight of 50 g mass = ...................................................... N
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the weight of one 50 g mass:

Recall the equation linking weight, mass and g:

- $g=\frac{W}{m}$  **OR**  $W=mg$ **[1 mark]**

Convert 50 g to kg:

- 1 g = 0.001 kg
- 50 g = 0.001 × 50 = 0.05 kg **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate *W*:

- *W *= 0.05 × 9.81 = 0.49 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
The mass of a small steel ball is 120 g. The volume of the ball is 16.0 cm<sup>3</sup>.

(i) Calculate the density of the steel ball.

density = ............................................... g / cm<sup>3</sup> [3]

(ii) The ball falls to the ground from rest. At a time of 0.2 s after it started to fall, its acceleration is 10 m / s<sup>2</sup>.

State the acceleration of the ball at a time of 0.1 s after it started to fall.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the density of the ball:

List the known quantities:

- mass of the ball = 120 g
- volume of the ball = 16.0 cm<sup>3</sup>

Recall the equation linking density, mass and volume:

- $Density=\frac{mass}{volume}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate density:

- $Density=\frac{120}{16.0}$ **[1 mark]**
- Density = 7.50 g / cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

(ii) The acceleration of the ball at a time of 0.1 s is:

- 9.8 m / s<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *It's really important to remember that, unless we are taking air resistance into account, acceleration is constant at a value of g, 9.8 m / s*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

force = ..................................................... N [1]
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A load is attached to a spring, as shown in Fig. 3.1. Two arrows indicate the vertical forces acting on the load. The spring and the load are stationary.

The load is pulled downwards and then released. The load moves up and down.

Fig. 3.2 represents the vertical forces acting on the load at some time after it is released.

![cie-2019-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/046-cie-2019-4.png)

Calculate the resultant force on the load and state its direction.

resultant force = ........................................................... N

direction = ...............................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the resultant force on the load and state its direction.

List the known quantities:

- Force acting vertically upwards = 7.6 N
- Force acting vertically downwards = 2.8 N

Calculate the resultant force, *F*:

- $F=7.6--2.8$
- *F* = 4.8 N ** [1 mark]**

State its direction:

- Upwards;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The resultant force is the **net** or **overall **force on an object. Here, there are two forces acting in opposite directions on the load, but it can only travel in one direction! *

> *The resultant force is a single force when combining all the forces. An object experience a resultant force if the forces are **unbalanced**. Forces acting in opposite directions are subtracted from one another, and in the same direction are added to one another. *

> *Forces are vectors so have a direction which is positive or negative. It doesn't matter in this case which direction you say is which because the overall force will still be upwards and the magnitude (size) of the force will still be the same (4.8 N).*

![img-bf9374e0ccd8-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/047-img-bf9374e0ccd8-1.jpeg)

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Fig. 1.1 shows an aeroplane accelerating uniformly on a runway.

![1-4-4a-h-aeroplane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/057-1-4-4a-h-aeroplane.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The aeroplane has a mass of 3.1 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg.

From rest, the aeroplane reaches a speed of 70 m/s after 32 s.

Calculate the following quantities

(i) The acceleration of the aeroplane.

acceleration = .................................... [2]

(ii) The resultant force acting on the aeroplane.

resultant force = .................................... [2]
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Initial speed = 0 m/s
- Final speed = 70 m/s
- Time taken, $t$ = 32 s
- Mass, $m$ = 3.1 × 10<sup>6</sup> kg

(i) Calculate the acceleration:

Use the equation for acceleration to calculate:

- $a=\frac{\Delta v}{t}$
- $a=\frac{70-0}{32}$ **[1 mark]**
- $a=2.2m/s^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the resultant force:

Use Newton's second law to calculate:

- $F=ma$
- $F = ( 3.1 \times 10^{6} ) \times 2.2$ **[1 mark]**
- $F=6820000N$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Part (ii) is an error carried forward question, you will see this as 'ecf' on a mark scheme.*

  - *That means that if you calculate the acceleration incorrectly in part (i), you can still gain full marks for part (ii) as long as your calculation is correct for the value you used. *
- *Note that the answer mark in CIE can only be gained with the correct value **AND** the correct units*

parts.solutionMd:
The pilot could decrease the radius of the circular flight path whilst maintaining a constant speed by:

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

A man with a mass of 70 kg steps into an elevator.

(i) State the value of the force exerted on the man by the elevator.

force = .................................... [1]

(ii) Calculate the force required to accelerate the man at 1.6 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

force = .................................... [1]

(iii) Explain why these values are different.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State the value of the force exerted on the elevator by the man:

Use the equation for weight to calculate:

- $W=mg$
- $W=70\times9.8=686N$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the force required to accelerate the man upwards at 1.6 m/s<sup>2</sup>:

Use Newton's second law to calculate:

- $F=ma$
- $F=70\times1.6=112N$ **[1 mark]**

** **

(iii) Explain why these values are different:

- The force required to accelerate the man / in part (ii) is the <u>resultant force</u>; **[1 mark]**
- The total force required to accelerate the man upwards is the weight plus the resultant force / 798 N; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Drawing a diagram, when one is not given in the question, is a good way to get your head around the question. *

![ma-man-in-lift](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-4-effects-of-forces/assets/052-ma-man-in-lift.png)

- *When the man is at rest, there is no change in his motion, therefore there is no resultant force acting on him. The forces are balanced. *
- *In order for the man to be accelerating (there is a change in his motion), there must be a resultant force acting on him.*

  - *This resultant force is the addition of an extra force applied to him, therefore the total force needed to accelerate him is the normal contact force equal to his weight, plus the resultant force.*

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The driving force is equal to the resistive force(s) / the forces are balanced **[1 mark]**
> - The resultant force is zero so there is no acceleration / the speed does not change **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept: "forward force = backward force" or "thrust = drag + friction"
> 
> Do not accept: "there are no forces acting" — forces are present but balanced

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks you to explain constant speed "in terms of forces", the examiner wants you to identify two things:
> 
> (1) the forces are balanced (driving force = resistive forces)
> 
> (2) this means the resultant force is zero, so there is no acceleration
> 
> A common mistake is to say "there are no forces acting" — the forces are still there, they just cancel out. Make sure you link balanced forces to zero resultant force and then to no change in speed.

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the total distance travelled by the cyclist:

- Recall how to use the graph to determine distance:

distance = area under the speed–time graph **[1 mark]**

- Determine the area of each section:

area of triangle (0-8 s) $=\frac{1}{2}\times8.0\times12=48\text{m}$

area of rectangle (8-28 s) $=20\times12=240\text{m}$

area of triangle (28-32 s) $=\frac{1}{2}\times4.0\times12=24\text{m}$

**[1 mark]**

- Determine the total distance by adding the areas:

$\text{total distance}=48+240+24$

$\text{total distance}=$ $312m$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Accept distance = average speed × time taken
> 
> 1 mark for at least two correct area calculations **OR** correct average speed used
> 
> - Accept any valid method, e.g. area of a trapezium, average speed of each section, counting squares, etc.
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $312m$
>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A metre rule is balanced on a pivot by three vertical forces, as shown in Fig. 5.1.

Diagram of a 100 cm lever with a pivot at 40 cm from the left-hand side. A 5.0 N force acts at 40 cm from the pivot on the left-hand side, and the 2.0 N weight of the rule acts at 10 cm from the pivot on the right-hand side (weight acts from the centre of the rule).

Force = 5.0 N
Distance from the pivot = 40 cm
Weight of rule = 2.0 N (acts at 10 cm from the pivot on the right-hand side)
Distance from pivot to F = 100 - 40 = 60 cm

Moment = force × distance from the pivot

The size of force is calculated by:
- Moment of 5.0 N force = 200 N cm
- Sum of the clockwise moments = sum of the anticlockwise moments
- Moment due to 2.0 N = 2.0 × 10 = 20 N cm
- Moment due to F = F × (100 – 40) = 60F N cm
- 20 + 60F = 200
- 60F = 200 – 20 = 180
- F = 180 / 60
- F = 3.0 N

**Extended tier only**

F = .................................................... N
parts.solutionMd:
The size of force is calculated by:

List the known quantities:

- Moment of 5.0 N force = 200 N cm

State the principle of moments:

- Sum of the clockwise moments = sum of the anticlockwise moments; **[1 mark]**

Determine the clockwise moments:

- $moment due to2.0N=2.0\times10=20N\mathrm{cm}$
- $moment due to F = F \times ( 100 - 40 ) = 60 F \mathrm{N} \text{cm}$

Substitute values into the principle of moments equation:

- $20+60F=200$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for the force F:

- $60F=200--20=180$
- $F=\frac{180}{60}$**[1 mark]**
- *F* = 3.0 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Whether a moment is clockwise or anticlockwise is determined by its location about the pivot (to the right or left) and the direction of the force. You can find these by following the direction of the force, and imagining which way the rule would turn if that force was increased. *

> *Don't just blindly use all the distances given. The distance in the moment equation must be the distance **from the pivot**. This means the distance for force F is 100 – 40 = 60 cm and not the 100 cm.*

Rearrange the equation to make the weight of the load the subject:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 2.1 shows a uniform plank AB of length 2.0 m suspended from two ropes X and Y. The weight W of the plank is 210 N. The force in rope X is P. The force in rope Y is Q. Distance from A to P is 1.0 m, from P to B is 1.0 m, from A to B is 2.0 m, and from P to B is 1.5 m. The moment of force P about B is P × 1.5. The equation for the size of a moment is Moment = force × distance OR M = Fd. The moment of W about B is W × 1.0. In equilibrium, the total upward forces equal the total downward forces: P + Q = W. To rearrange the moment equation to make F the subject: F = M/d. To rearrange P + Q = W to make Q the subject: Q = W – P. W = 210 N.

**Extended tier only**

Calculate:

(i) the moment of *W *about B

moment = ...........................................................[1]

(ii) the force *P*

force P = ...........................................................[2]

(iii) the force *Q*.

force Q = ...........................................................[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the moment of *W* about B:

![2b-ms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-5-moments/assets/079-2b-ms.png)

List the known quantities:

- Weight, *W* = 210 N
- Distance from pivot, *d* = 1.0 m

Substitute the known values into the moment equation to calculate:

- $M=F\times d$
- $M=210\times1.0$
- *M* = 210 N m **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the force *P*:

List the known quantities:

- Moment of *P* about *B* = *P* × 1.5 (from part (a))
- Anticlockwise moment = 210 N

Recall the principle of moments:

- The total clockwise moments = the total anticlockwise moments

Rearrange the moment equation to make P the subject:

- $M=Pd$
- $P=\frac{M}{d}$
- $P=\frac{210}{1.5}$ **[1 mark]**
- *P* = 140 N **[1 mark]**

(iii) Calculate the force *Q*:

Set up the equation using the known quantities:

- In equilibrium, the total upward forces equal the total downward forces
- $P+Q=W$

Rearrange to make Q the subject:

- $Q=W-P$

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $Q=210--140$ **[1 mark]**
- *Q* = 70 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The two rules you need to remember when rearranging equations are:*

1. * To undo an operation, do the **opposite** operation (to cancel a multiplication relationship, you need to divide, to cancel a minus you need to add and vice versa)*

A bus is travelling along a straight road. The bus and the driver have a combined mass of 16000 kg when there are no passengers in it. The bus has 73 passengers. The average mass of each of the passengers is 65 kg.

(i) Calculate the total mass of the bus, the driver and the 73 passengers.

mass = ......................................................... [2]

(ii) The fully loaded bus accelerates uniformly from rest to a speed of 14 m / s. The time taken to reach a speed of 14 m / s is 20 s.

Calculate the resultant force on the bus during the acceleration.

force = ......................................................... [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the total mass of the bus, the driver and the 73 passengers:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of bus and driver = 16 000 kg
- Average mass of one passenger = 65 kg
- Number of passengers on bus = 73

Calculate the total mass of the passengers:

- $Totalmassofpassengers=numberofpassengers\times average mass of one passenger$
- $Totalmassofpassengers=65\times73=4700\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the total mass of the bus, the driver and the 73 passengers:

- $Total mass=mass of bus and driver+totalmassofpassengers$
- $Total mass=16000+4700$
- Total mass = 20 700 kg = 21 000 kg (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

** **

(ii) Calculate the resultant force on the bus during the acceleration:

List the known quantities:

- Initial speed, *u *= 0 m / s
- Final speed, *v *= 14 m / s
- Time to accelerate, *t *= 20 s
- Total mass, *m *= 21 000 kg (from part (c) (i))

Calculate the acceleration, *a *of the box:

- $a = \frac{( v - u )}{t}$
- $a = \frac{( 14 - 0 )}{20}$
- *a *= 0.7 m/s<sup>2</sup>

Recall Newton's second law:

- $F=ma$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into Newton's second law to calculate the resultant force, *F*:

- $F=21000\times0.7$
- *F *= 14 700 N = 15 000 N (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

Clockwise moments = Anticlockwise moments

  - Weight from block, providing an anticlockwise moment
  - Weight from plank, providing a clockwise moment
  - Push force from builder, providing a clockwise moment

Clockwise moments = Anticlockwise moments

$\text{80.0 + 3}\text{F}\text{= 600.0}$ **[1 mark]**

$3F=600.0-80.0$

$3F=520.0$

$F=\frac{520.0}{3}$ **[1 mark]**

$F=173.33..$

**Extended tier only**

In a game of tennis, a player hits a stationary ball with his racquet.

(i) The racquet is in contact with the ball for 6.0 ms. The average force on the ball during this time is 400 N.

impulse = ...........................................................[2]

(ii) The mass of the ball is 0.056 kg.

Calculate the speed with which the ball leaves the racquet.

speed = ...........................................................[2]

(iii) State the energy transfer that takes place:

1. as the ball changes shape during the contact between the racquet and the ball

2. as the ball leaves the racquet.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the impulse on the tennis ball:

List the known quantities:

- Average force on the ball, *F *= 400 N
- Time in contact with the ball, *t *= 6.0 ms

Convert the units for time from ms into s:

- There are 1000 ms in 1 second
- So, in 6 ms there are 6 ÷ 1000 = 6 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s

Recall the equation to calculate impulse:

- $Impulse=Ft$**[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities to calculate the impulse on the tennis ball:

- $Impulse = 400 \times ( 6 \times 10^{- 3} )$
- Impulse = 2.4 Ns **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the speed with which the ball leaves the racquet:

List the known quantities:

- Average force on the ball, *F *= 400 N (from part (i))
- Time in contact with the ball, *t *= 6.0 ms (from part (i))
- Mass of ball, *m *= 0.056 kg

Relate the equations for impulse and change in momentum:

- $Impulse=change in momentum$
- $Impulse=mv-mu$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation and rearrange to calculate the final velocity, *v* of the ball:

- $Impulse = m ( v - u )$
- $Impulse = 0.056 \times ( v - 0 )$
- $2.4=0.056v$
- $v=\frac{2.4}{0.056}$
- *v *= 42.85 m/s = 43 m/s (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

(iii) State the energy transfer that takes place:

1. The <u>kinetic energy</u> stored in the racquet undergoes a <u>mechanical energy transfer to elastic energy</u> stored in the ball / strings; **[1 mark]**

2. The <u>elastic energy</u> stored in the ball undergoes a <u>mechanical energy transfer into the kinetic energy</u> stored in the ball; **[1 mark]**

> *Use the tables in the revision notes to clarify the differences between energy stores and transfers. *

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the speed with which the pellet leaves the rifle:

List the known quantities:

- Impulse, *I* = 0.019 Ns
- Mass of the pellet, *m* = 1.1 × 10<sup>–4</sup> kg

Recall the equation linking impulse and momentum:

- $\mathrm{impulse}=\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{momentum}$ (or $\mathrm{impulse}=m\timesΔv$)

  - The bullet stops when it hits the target, so the change in speed is the difference between the initial speed, *v* and zero.
- $\mathrm{impulse}=m\times v$* ***[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to make *u* the subject by dividing both sides by *m* :

- $v=\frac{\mathrm{impulse}}{m}$

Substitute the known quantities and calculate the initial speed:

- $v = \frac{0.019}{( 1.1 \times 10^{- 4} )}$
- $v=172.73m/s$

Write the initial speed to two significant figures and give units:

- *v* = 170 m/s **[1 mark]**

List the known quantities:

- Mass of the pellet, *m *= 1.1 × 10<sup>–4</sup> kg
- Initial speed of the pellet, *v* = 173 m/s (3 s.f.) **OR** 170 m/s (2 s.f.)

Recall the equation for kinetic energy:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation and calculate kinetic energy:

- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 1.1 \times 10^{- 4} ) \times ( 173 )^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=1.646J$

Write the kinetic energy to two significant figures and give the units:

- $E_{k}=1.6J$  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The value of a final answer can sometimes depend on whether you calculated it using a quantity that was rounded or not. In this case you may have used a speed of 170 m/s or of 173 m/s. In this particular question, both give answers which round to 1.6 J.*

> *You will not lose marks for doing one or the other. Generally speaking, it is best practice not to round values until you give your final answer. When calculating the kinetic energy, it is best to use a value of speed that has not been rounded so much (i.e. three significant figures rather than two).*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Trolley A and trolley B are on a horizontal, frictionless bench. Trolley A moves to the right with a constant velocity of 0.15 m/s. Trolley B is stationary.

After the collision, the two trolleys move together with a constant velocity $v$ to the right. The mass of trolley A is $1.2\mathrm{kg}$, and the mass of trolley B is $0.80\mathrm{kg}$.

Calculate $v$.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the velocity of the trolleys after the collision:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass of trolley A, $m_{A}=1.2\mathrm{kg}$
  - Mass of trolley B, $m_{B}=0.80\mathrm{kg}$
  - Velocity of A before collision, $u_{A}=0.15m/s$
  - Velocity of B before collision, $u_{B}=0$
- Recall the principle of conservation of momentum:

$\text{total momentum before}=\text{total momentum after}$ **[1 mark]**

- Apply the principle of conservation of momentum:

$(1.2\times0.15)+(0.80\times0)=(1.2+0.80)\times v$ **[1 mark]**

$0.18=2.0\times v$

$v=\frac{0.18}{2.0}$

$v=$ $0.09\text{m/s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for stating or applying conservation of momentum, e.g. momentum before (collision) = momentum after (collision)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution, e.g. momentum before collision = (1.2 × 0.15) **OR** momentum after collision = (1.2 + 0.80) × v
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $0.09m/s$
> 
> Full marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always start a conservation of momentum question by writing "momentum before = momentum after". This earns a method mark even if you make an arithmetic error later. Remember that trolley B is stationary, so its momentum before the collision is zero — but you must use the combined mass of both trolleys on the right-hand side, since they move together after the collision.

parts.problemMd:

v = 0.09 m/s

The trolleys are brought to rest in $0.50s$ when they collide with the wall.

parts.solutionMd:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass of trolleys, $m=1.2+0.8=2.0\mathrm{kg}$
  - Velocity of trolleys, $v=0.09m/s$ (from (b))
  - Time of collision, $\Delta t=0.50s$
- Recall the equation relating force and change in momentum:

$F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the known quantities into the equation:

$F=\frac{m\Delta v}{\Delta t}$

$F=\frac{2.0\times0.09}{0.50}$

$F=$ $0.36\text{N}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$ **OR** $\frac{2.0\times0.090}{0.50}$ **OR** $\frac{0.18}{0.50}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $0.36N$
> 
> Both marks can be scored for the correct answer alone
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (b)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The trolleys are now moving together (from part (b)), so make sure you use the combined mass and the velocity from part (b). Since they are brought to rest, the change in velocity is $\Delta v=0.09-0=0.09\text{m/s}$.

parts.problemMd:
In a car collision, crumple zones at the front of the car deform during the impact.

Explain how crumple zones reduce injury to the passengers during a collision.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Crumple zone increases the time of the collision **[1 mark]**
> - For the same change in momentum $\Delta ( m v )$, an increased time leads to less force on passenger as $F \Delta t = \Delta ( m v )$ (so less injury) **[1 mark]**
> 
> For the second mark: accept use of $F \Delta t = \Delta ( m v )$ **OR** $F\propto1/\Delta t$

> **[exam-tip]**
> To score both marks, you must explicitly link the crumple zone to increased time and reduced force using the relationship $F=\Delta p/\Delta t$. Since the car comes to rest as a result of the collision, the change in momentum is the same regardless of whether it has a crumple zone or not. Therefore, the only way to reduce the force on the passengers is to increase the time it takes for the collision to occur.

Until the second half of the 20th century, cars were designed as strong rigid boxes, which designers thought would protect passengers in accidents. In fact, although average speeds were much slower than today, passengers were often very badly injured.

Modern cars are designed with safety features including 'crumple zones'. The crumple zones are at the front and rear of the car but do not include the passenger section. In a crash, the crumple zone is designed so that it deforms and bends. This is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![HIVZR74H_1-6-5a-h-momentum-crumple-zone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-6-momentum/assets/016-hivzr74h-1-6-5a-h-momentum-crumple-zone.png)

The use of crumple zones explains why the front and rear of cars are badly damaged during accidents.

Use your knowledge of momentum and impulse forces to suggest why a car with a crumple zone protects the driver and passengers from serious injury better than one which is a strong, rigid box.
parts.solutionMd:
Crumple zones protect a driver from series injury because:

Any **six** from:

- Injuries are caused by forces (to the body); **[1 mark]**
- A <u>moving</u> car / driver has momentum; **[1 mark]**
- When the car stops, momentum is reduced to zero; **[1 mark]**
- In a sudden impact / collision, the momentum is reduced to zero in a very <u>short</u> period of <u>time</u> / <u>more</u> quickly / in <u>less</u> time; **[1 mark]**
- In both the impulse / change in momentum is the <u>same</u>; **[1 mark]**
- $I = m ( v - u )$**[1 mark]**
- $F=\frac{I}{t}$ ; **[1 mark]**
- Force is inversely proportional to time;** [1 mark]**
- Crumple zones <u>increase the time</u> to stop / reduce momentum to zero; **[1 mark]**
- <u>Reduces the force</u> on the driver; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *An example of an answer which scores six marks:*

> *In an accident, the injuries are caused by forces to the body, [1] so reducing the force will reduce the injuries. Force is inversely proportional to the time [1] it takes for momentum to fall to zero, because *$F=\frac{I}{t}$*. [1] Therefore, anything which makes it take longer for the car to stop will reduce injuries.*

> *The change in momentum is the same however long it takes to stop, [1] since **p **=** mv** and since **I = m**(**v - u**) [1] then the impulse is also the same. *

> *As the car is crumpling it is also stopping but taking more time to do so. [1] This reduces the force and the injuries. [1]*

> *In long written answers you may make more points worth one mark than there are marks available. It's better to write more and still only score six, than to write less, and only score three!*

**Both** cars have a driver of mass 70 kg and they **both **crash to a stop from an initial speed of 30 m/s.

At the moment of impact, the front ends of the cars crumple, taking different amounts of time to come to a stop. Car **A** takes 0.3 seconds to stop, while car **B** takes 0.7 seconds to stop.

Using this information, calculate the forces which would be experienced by the **cars **due to the impact.

Force = .................................... N [3]

(ii)

For car **B**

Force = .................................... N [2]
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the forces which would be experienced by the cars due to the impact.

List the known quantities:

- Mass of car **A**, *m*<sub>*A*</sub>* *= 1200 kg
- Mass of car **B**, *m*<sub>*B*</sub>* *= 1500 kg
- Mass of each driver, *m* = 70 kg
- Initial speed of both cars, *v* = 30 m/s
- Time for car **A** to stop, *t*<sub>A</sub> = 0.3 s
- Time for car **B** to stop, *t*<sub>B</sub> = 0.7 s

Recall the relevant equations:

- Momentum, $p=mv$
- Impulse, $I=Δp=mΔv$
- Force, $F=\frac{I}{t}=\frac{mΔv}{t}$

(i) Calculate the force on car **A**, *F*<sub>A</sub>:

- Momentum after the crash = 0
- Momentum before the crash, $p_{A} = ( m_{A} + m ) \times v$ **[1 mark]**
- Change in momentum, `capital delta p _ A = ( 1200 + 70 ) x 30 = 38 100 kg m / s` **[1 mark]**
- Force on **A**, $F_{A}=\frac{mΔv}{t}=\frac{38100}{0.3}=127000N$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the force on car **B**, *F*<sub>B</sub>:

- Momentum after the crash = 0
- Momentum before the crash, $p_{B} = ( m_{B} + m ) \times v$
- Change in momentum, `capital delta p _ B = ( 1500 + 70 ) x 30 = 47 100 kg m / s` **[1 mark]**
- Force on **B**, $F_{B}=\frac{mΔv}{t}=\frac{47100}{0.7}=67000N$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *If you see two similar calculations attracting different marks, as they do here, don't be put off.*

> *Since you are repeating the same skills, the examiner will often only apply the 'easiest' mark once (in this case, recalling the equations). *

[2]

(ii)** **Calculate the average resultant force acting on the ball while it is in contact with the golf club.

[2]

(iii) While the golf club is in contact with the ball, the ball becomes compressed and changes shape.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate final momentum:

List the known quantities:

- Final velocity, *v* = 65 m/s
- Mass of ball, *m* = 0.046 kg

Recall the equation for momentum, *p*:

- *p = mv* **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities:

- *p* = 0.046 × 65
- *p* = 3.0 kg m/s **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the average resultant force:

List the known quantities:

- Initial velocity, *u* = 0 m/s
- Final velocity, *v* = 65 m/s
- Mass of ball, *m* = 0.046 kg
- Time of contact with club, *t* = 5.0 × 10<sup>–4</sup> s

Recall the equation for force in terms of mass, velocity and time:

- $F = \frac{m ( v - u )}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities:

- $F = \frac{0.046 \times ( 65 - 0 )}{5.0 \times 10^{- 4} }$

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A drone is a machine that can fly. Fig. 4.1 shows a drone rising into the air, lifting a camera.

The drone obtains energy from a battery of cells.

When the drone moves, it wastes some energy.

Describe what happens to this energy.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - The wasted energy is dissipated / transferred to the thermal store / as heat / thermal energy **[1 mark]**
> - Of the surroundings / environment / air **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Dissipated' or 'transferred' to the surroundings scores; 'lost', 'used up' or 'destroyed' does not, because energy is conserved

> **[exam-tip]**
> No system in reality will have totally efficient energy transfers. In practice, there will always be wasted energy. This energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings, usually by sound, air resistance, etc which causes the particles in the surroundings (the air, walls, floor, etc) to vibrate. This vibration causes small amounts of heating, so we call it the thermal store of the surroundings. When we refer to this type of energy transfer, we say the energy is dissipated to the surroundings. Dissipated just means spread out, but you must use the correct terminology in your exams. Always name a destination for the wasted energy, e.g. the surroundings, rather than just saying it is 'lost' or 'released'.
> 
> To add this energy transfer to the beaker of water analogy, you can think of the thermal store of the surroundings as a larger, wider beaker (or trough) that catches all the wasted energy.
> 
> ![The image shows three beakers labeled "Chemical," "Kinetic," and "GPE" pouring liquid, along with droplets spilling over into a larger container marked "Thermal store of surroundings." This visually encodes the concept that energy dissipates from these sources into the thermal store of the surroundings.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/assets/019-the-image-shows-three-beakers-labeled-chemical-k.png)

A group of students want to measure their power output when climbing a ladder.

Student A has a mass of 54 kg and takes 15 s to climb the ladder which has a vertical height of 1.8 m.

Calculate the work done in raising the student's body mass as they climb the ladder.

work = ....................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the work done in raising the student:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass, $m = 54 \text{kg}$
  - Vertical height, $h = 1 . 8 \text{m}$
  - Gravitational field strength, $g = 9 . 8 \text{N/kg}$
- Write down the equation for work done:

$W = F d$

- The force needed is equal to the student's weight, $F = m g$, and the distance moved is the vertical height, so:

$W = m g h$

- Substitute the known values:

$W = 54 \times 9 . 8 \times 1 . 8$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$W = 953 \text{J} =$$950 \text{J}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $W = m g h$ (accept $W = F d$ with $F = 54 \times 9 . 8$ shown)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $950 \text{J}$
> 
> - Accept 953 J or 952.56 J
> - Accept $970 \text{J}$ (972 J) if $g = 10 \text{N/kg}$ is used
> - Accept N m as the unit

> **[exam-tip]**
> The work done against gravity is the same as the gain in gravitational potential energy, so $W = m g h$ and $\Delta E_{p} = m g h$ give the same answer — use whichever you remember. Do not divide by the time here: that gives power, which is asked for in the next part.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the power output:

- List the known quantities:

  - Work done, $W = 953 \text{J}$ (from part (a))
  - Time taken, $t = 15 \text{s}$
- Write down the equation for power:

$P = \frac{W}{t}$

- Substitute the known values:

$P = \frac{953}{15}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$P = 63 . 5 \text{W} =$$64 \text{W}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $P = \frac{W}{t}$ (accept $\frac{950}{15}$ or $\frac{972}{15}$)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $64 \text{W}$
> 
> - Accept 63.5 W
> - Accept 63 W (from 950 J) or 65 W (from 972 J)
> - ecf from an incorrect answer to part (a)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Carry the unrounded value from part (a) into this calculation where you can. Using 950 J instead of 953 J still scores here, but rounding twice can push an answer outside the accepted range in other questions. Power is measured in watts (joules per second), so a bare number or a unit of J loses the final mark.

Calculate the total power input of the student to climb the ladder.

power input =  ....................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the total power input:

- List the known quantities:

  - Useful power output, $P_{out} = 64 \text{W}$ (from part (b))
  - Efficiency = 17% = 0.17
- Write down the efficiency equation:

$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}$

- Rearrange to make total power input the subject:

$\text{total power input} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{efficiency}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the known values:

$\text{total power input} = \frac{64}{0.17}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the answer:

$\text{total power input} = 376 \text{W} =$$380 \text{W}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the efficiency equation, or its rearrangement, in words or symbols (accept efficiency written as a percentage: $\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}} \times 100$)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution (accept $\frac{64}{0.17}$, $\frac{64\times100}{17}$, $\frac{63.5}{0.17}$ or $\frac{63}{0.17}$)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $380 \text{W}$
> 
> - Accept 376 W, 374 W (from 63.5 W) or 370 W (from 63 W)
> - ecf from an incorrect answer to part (b)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Convert the percentage to a decimal (17% = 0.17) or keep the × 100 in the equation, but not both. A quick sanity check: the total input must be larger than the useful output, so if your answer comes out smaller than 64 W you have divided the wrong way round.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Fig. 3.1 shows a model of a wind turbine used to demonstrate the use of wind to generate electricity. The wind is blowing towards the model, as shown.

![fan](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/assets/015-fan.png)

The mass of air passing through the circular area swept out by the turbine blades each second is 7.5 kg. The energy in the kinetic store of the air that passes through this circular area each second is 240 J.

(i) Calculate the speed of the air.

speed = ........................................................ [3]

(ii) The moving air drives a generator. State the input power of the air passing through the turbine blades.

input power = ........................................................ [1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the speed of the air:

List the known quantities:

- Kinetic energy, $E_{k}$ = 240 J
- Mass of air, *m* = 7.5 kg

Recall the equation for kinetic energy:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation:

- $2E_{k}=mv^{2}$
- $\frac{2E_{k}}{m}=v^{2}$
- $\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m}}=v$

Substitute the values and calculate:

- $v=\sqrt{\frac{2\times240}{7.5}}$; **[1 mark]**
- *v *= 8.0 m / s; **[1 mark]**

(ii) State the input power:

- Recall that power = the energy per second
- Therefore input power = kinetic energy
- *P* = 240 W; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *When rearranging, the number one rule is "whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other". For example, to go from*

$E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$

> *to*

$2E_{k}=mv^{2}$,

> *we have multiplied the right hand side by 2 to cancel out the fraction. We must also multiply the left side by 2, following the rule above for rearranging. The same applies for each step.*

> *Here, you must choose operations to perform on each side that get you closer to making **v** the subject. On the right hand side, we want to get rid of the factor of **m**, the factor of ½ and the fact that **v** is squared. We can do this by dividing both sides by **m**, so the **m** on the right is cancelled out:*

$2E_{k}=mv^{2}$

$\frac{2E_{k}}{m}=\frac{mv^{2}}{m}$

`(2 E _ k)/(m) = (/ m v ^2)/(/ m)`

> *This leaves us with:*

$\frac{2E_{k}}{m}=v^{2}$

> *The final step is achieved by square-rooting both sides, which cancels out the square term on **v **:*

$\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m}}=\sqrt{v^{2}}$

$\sqrt{\frac{2E_{k}}{m}}=v$
