Fig. 3.1 shows a girl throwing a heavy ball.

![18p4-2b](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/assets/014-18p4-2b.png)

(i) State the energy transfers that take place from when the girl begins to exert a force on the ball until the ball hits the ground and stops moving.

[2]

(ii) The mass of the ball is 4.0 kg. The girl exerts a force on the ball for 0.60 s. The speed of the ball increases from 0 m/ s to 12 m/s before it leaves the girl’s hand.

Calculate:

1. the momentum of the ball on leaving the girl’s hand

momentum = ...........................................................[2]

2. the average resultant force exerted on the ball.

average resultant force = ...........................................................[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The energy transfers that take place are:

- Energy in the <u>chemical</u> energy store (of the girl) is transferred to the <u>kinetic</u> energy store (of the girl as she moves her arm / of the ball as she releases it); **[1 mark]**

**Any one from:**

- Energy in the <u>kinetic</u> store of the girl is transferred (mechanically) to the <u>gravitational potential</u> energy store of the ball (as the girl lifts the ball); **[1 mark]**
- Energy in the <u>gravitational potential</u> energy store of the ball is transferred (mechanically) to the <u>kinetic</u> energy store of the ball (as the ball falls to the ground); **[1 mark]**
- Energy in the <u>kinetic</u> energy store of the ball is dissipated / transferred to the <u>thermal</u> store of the surroundings (as sound and friction); **[1 mark]**

(ii)

1. Calculate the momentum of the ball on leaving the girl’s hand:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 4.0 kg
- Velocity of the ball as it leaves her hand, *v* = 12 m/s

Recall the momentum equation:

- $p=mv$

Substitute the known values into the equation to calculate:

- $p=4.0\times12$* ***[1 mark]**
- *p* = 48 kg m/s **OR** 48 N s **[1 mark]**

2. Calculate the average resultant force exerted on the ball:

List the known quantities:

- Initial speed of the ball, *u* = 0 m/s
- Time, *t* = 0.6 s

Recall the equation for average force in terms of momentum:

- $\mathrm{average} \mathrm{force}=\frac{\mathrm{change} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{momentum}}{\mathrm{time}}$ **OR**
- $F = \frac{ m ( v - u )}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $F = \frac{4.0 ( 12 - 0 )}{0.60} = \frac{4.0 \times 12}{0.60} = \frac{48}{0.60}$
- F = 80 N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *In order to be able to answer questions about energy transfers, you need to learn all the energy **stores** and **transfer pathways** by heart, and practice applying them to different contexts. *

> *For part (ii) 2., the mark scheme here will also score the equation mark for substituting the known values into the correct equation, even if you did not write out the equation before hand. However, often separate marks are awarded for writing out the equation, so it is always best to do this for all questions, and it makes your working out much clearer by showing the examiner which equation you used. *

An electric kettle contains water at a temperature of 19 °C. The kettle has a power rating of 3.0 kW and is switched on for 3.5 minutes.

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the energy supplied to the kettle by the electricity supply:

List the known quantities:

- Time, *t* = 3.5 minutes

Convert the units to standard units:

- 1 kW is 1000 W

  - $P=3.0\mathrm{kW}=3000W$
- 1 minute is 60 seconds

Recall the power equation:

- $P=\frac{E}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange this by multiplying both sides by *t* to make energy, *E*, the subject:

- $E=P\times t$

Substitute in the known values in standard units and calculate energy:

- $E=3000\times210$ **[1 mark]**
- *E* = 630 000 J **OR** 630 kJ **[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the energy gained by the water:

List the known quantities:

- Initial temperature = 19 °C
- Final temperature = 100 °C
- Volume of water, *V* = 1700 cm<sup>3</sup>
- Density of water, *ρ *= 1.0 g/cm<sup>3</sup>
- Specific heat capacity of water, *c* = 4200 J/kg °C

Recall the equation for the change in energy associated with a temperature change:

- $ΔE=m\times c\timesΔT$ **[1 mark]**
- The value of the mass term, *m*, is not yet known

Recall the equation relating mass, volume and density:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$

Rearrange this equation for *m* by multiplying both sides by *V *:

- $m=ρ\times V$

Substitute in the known quantities and calculate *m* :

- $m=1.0\times1700$
- $m=1700g$

  - Note that mass has units grams because the density has units of g/cm<sup>3</sup>

Convert *m* to kg:

- $1000g=1.0\mathrm{kg}$
- $m=\frac{1700}{1000}=1.7\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the temperature difference:

- $ΔT=finalT-initialT$
- $ΔT=100-19=81^{\circ}C$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values into the equation and calculate the change in energy:

- $ΔE=m\times c\timesΔT$
- $ΔE=1.7\times4200\times81$ **[1 mark]**
- Δ*E* = 580 000 J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *The specific heat capacity of water is given with units of J/kg °C, so the value of mass used in the energy change equation must be in units of kg. Make sure your units match when answering a calculation question. *

> *This one has multiple steps. To calculate the change in energy, we need to know mass, specific heat capacity and change in temperature. Some of these quantities are unknown, so we need to use other quantities given in the question to figure these out before we can calculate the change in energy. *

parts.problemMd:
A student uses an electric motor to lift a load. Fig. 4.1 shows the arrangement.

![figure](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-7-energy-work-and-power/assets/007-figure.png)

(i)**   **The motor exerts a force of 25 N on the load. It lifts the load a vertical distance of 2.0 m.

Calculate the work done by the motor on the load.

work done on the load = ...................................................... J [3]

(ii)**  **State the useful energy output of the electric motor when it lifts the load 2.0 m.

useful energy output = ...................................................... J [1]

(ii)  The useful energy output of the motor is less than the energy input to the motor.

Explain why the useful energy output is less than the energy input.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

List the known quantities:

- Force = 25 N
- Distance = 2.0 m

Identify and write down the correct equation for work done:

- $\mathrm{work} \mathrm{done}=\mathrm{force}\times\mathrm{distance}$**  [1 mark]**

Substitute the values given into the question and calculate the answer:

- $\mathrm{work} \mathrm{done}=25\times2.0$ **[1 mark]**
- $\mathrm{work} \mathrm{done} \mathrm{on} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{load}=50J$ **[1 mark]**

(ii)

Since the energy gained by the load is equal to the work done on it by the motor:

- useful energy output = 50 J **OR** same answer given in (a)(i); **[1 mark]**

(iii)

The useful energy output is less than the energy input because:

- Some energy is lost to the surroundings as thermal energy; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In (ii), the question asks you to **state** something. That means you should not need to calculate anything else; the answer must be something you already know. If you are not sure what this is, look back at any previous calculations, as the answer is probably linked to them. In this case, it is the value for work done from part (i).
> 
> In (iii), the question asks for an **explanation**; you need to give a clear reason. Energy is always conserved, so the total energy output is the same as the total energy input. However, not all the energy output is useful energy. You need to describe where energy is being transferred in a non-useful way. Electrical devices heat up when used, and this is the wasteful process, so you need to say that energy is lost to the surroundings (dissipated) due to heating.
> 
> Be specific when you describe energy transfers, making sure to use the correct terms from the specification. You should know about thermal energy, kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and so on.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Show that the gravitational potential energy gained by $50\mathrm{kg}$ of water raised through a height of $12m$ is approximately $5900J$.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the gravitational potential energy gained by the water:

- List the known quantities:

  - Mass of water, $m=50\mathrm{kg}$
  - Height raised, $\Delta h=12m$
  - $g=9.8m/s^{2}$
- Write down the equation for gravitational potential energy:

$\Delta E_{p}=mg\Delta h$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values into the equation:

$\Delta E_{p}=50\times9.8\times12$ **[1 mark]**

$\Delta E_{p}=5880\approx5900\text{J}$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct equation $\Delta E_{p}=mg\Delta h$
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution $50 \times 9 . 8 \times 12$ leading to a final answer of $5880\text{J}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a "show that" question, you must show every step of your working. Avoid just multiplying the given numbers until they arrive at the target answer. Always write down the equation first - this demonstrates to the examiner that you have an understanding of the physics. Then substitute the values, and calculate the answer, making sure you write down the unrounded answer.

The solar panel that powers the pump has an efficiency of 18%.

Calculate the total energy input from the solar panel required to raise this water.

To calculate the total energy input from the solar panel:

- List the known quantities:

  - Useful energy output = $5880J$ (from (b))
  - Efficiency = 18%
- Write down the equation for efficiency

$\text{efficiency} = \frac{ \text{useful \text{energy} output} }{ \text{total \text{energy} input} } \times 100 \%$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the equation and substitute in the values:

$\text{total energy input}=\frac{5880\times100}{18}$

$\text{total energy input}=$ $32700\text{J}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct substitution/rearrangement
> 
> - Accept $\frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}$ **OR** $\frac{5880}{0.18}$ **OR** $\frac{5880\times100}{18}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $32700J$
> 
> - Accept $33000J$ or $32800J$ (from use of 5900 J)
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (b)

parts.problemMd: Suggest **two **advantages of using solar energy to power the water pump, compared to using a diesel generator.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two **from:
> 
> - Solar energy is renewable / will not run out (whereas diesel is non-renewable/finite)
> - No pollution / no carbon dioxide emissions / no greenhouse gases during operation
> - No fuel costs / free energy source (after initial installation)

> **[2 marks]**
>

> 
> Do not accept "better for the environment" without a specific reason

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Suggest" questions require you to apply your knowledge to a given context. For energy resource comparisons, the two safest answers are:
>

> 
> (2) solar does not produce pollution or CO<sub>2</sub> emissions, while diesel does

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

The lifting mechanism raises a box of mass 32 kg through a vertical distance of 2.5 m in 5.4 s.

(i) Calculate the energy transferred to the gravitational potential energy store of the box.

energy = ...........................................................[2]

(ii) The efficiency of the lifting mechanism is 0.65 (65%).

Calculate the input power to the lifting mechanism.

input power = ...........................................................[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the energy transferred to the gravitational potential energy store:

List the known quantities:

- Mass = 32 kg
- Distance lifted = 2.5 m
- Time = 5.4 s

Recall the equation for change in gravitational potential energy:

- $E_{p}=m\times g\timesΔh$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate *E*<sub>*p*</sub>:

- $E_{p}=32\times9.81\times2.5$
- *E*<sub>*p*</sub>* *= 785 J **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the input power:

List the known quantities:

- Time = 5.4 s
- Efficiency = 0.65
- E<sub>p</sub> = 785 J

Calculate output power:

- $power,P=\frac{energy transferred}{time}$
- $P=\frac{785}{5.4}$
- *P* = 145 W **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation linking efficiency, output power and input power, and substitute in values:

- $efficiency=\frac{output power}{input power}$
- $input power=\frac{output power}{efficiency}=\frac{145}{0.65}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate output power:

- Output power = 223 W **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Sometimes you will need to use more than one equation in a calculation. The key to getting maximum marks is to lay everything out clearly to help avoid errors.*

A man is working on a platform. He uses a rope to raise a bag from the ground to the platform as shown in Fig. 4.1.

(i) Name the energy store that energy is usefully transferred to as the bag is lifted at constant speed.

On which bag of materials does the man do more work?

Explain your answer.

[1]

(iii) The man wants to determine his useful power as he lifts one of the bags. He knows the weight of the bag. State the **two** other quantities he needs to know.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Name the energy store of the bag that energy is usefully transferred to as the bag is lifted at constant speed:

- Energy is transferred to the <u>gravitational potential</u> energy store as it is lifted; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Explain which of the two bags the man does more work on, the 100 N bag or the 150 N:

- The man does more work on <u>the second bag / the 150 N bag</u>

**AND**

- Because it has a <u>greater weight / force</u> (moved through the same distance); **[1 mark]**

**   **

(iii) State the two other quantities he needs to know to determine his useful power:

- The man needs to know <u>distance</u> travelled by the bag to determine work done; **[1 mark]**

> *For part (iii), the two quantities needed to determine power can be found from the definition of **power**, and subsequently the definition of **work done.*

- *Power is energy transferred / work done per unit time (*$power=\frac{work done}{time}$)
- *Work is done when a force is used to move an object a distance (*$force\times distance$*)*

> *Combining these gives *$power=\frac{force\times distance}{time}$

> *Therefore, otherwise than weight (the force), the distance and time is needed to determine the power*

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

A rifle fires a bullet of mass 0.020 kg vertically upwards through the air. As it leaves the rifle, the speed of the bullet is 350 m/s.

Calculate

(i) the energy in the kinetic store of the bullet as it leaves the rifle,

energy = ...........................................................[3]

(ii) the maximum possible height that the bullet can reach.

maximum height = ...........................................................[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the energy:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of bullet = 0.020 kg
- Initial speed = 350 m/s

Recall the equation for kinetic energy:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in known values to calculate:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\times0.020\times350^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}$ = 1200 J **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the maximum height:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of bullet, *m* = 0.020 kg
- Initial speed = 350 m/s

Recall the equation for gravitational potential energy:

- $E_{p}=mgh$

Recall the link between $E_{k}$* *and $E_{p}$:

- **All** the energy will be transferred from the kinetic store to the gravitational potential store at maximum height
- $E_{k}=E_{p}=mgh$

Substitute in known values:

- $h=\frac{E_{k}}{mg}=\frac{1200}{0.020\times9.81}$**[1 mark]**

Calculate* h*:

- *h* = 6000 m (1.s.f) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *An object fired upwards will reach a maximum height where velocity will momentarily be 0. This point occurs when all the energy has been transferred from the kinetic store of the bullet to the gravitational potential store. *

> *The transfer of energy between the kinetic and gravitational potential stores are very common.*

- *When an object is lifted, energy is transferred from the kinetic store to the gravitational potential store*
- *When a object is falling, energy is being transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store*

State whether the salmon can make the jump:

Calculate the minimum speed with which a salmon of mass 2.2 kg would have to leave the water in order to reach the height required:

- $\Delta E_{P}=mg\Delta h$
- $\Delta E_{P}=2.2\times9.8\times0.36$
- $\Delta E_{P}=7.76J$ **[1 mark]**

Using the kinetic energy equation:

- $E_{K}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- Rearrange to make $v$ the subject
- $v=\sqrt{\frac{2E_{K}}{m}}$ **[1 mark]**
- The minimum $E_{K}$ required = $E_{P}$ = 7.76 J
- $v=\sqrt{\frac{2\times7.76}{2.2}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $v_{min}=2.65m/s$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the power rating of the man:

Calculate the weight of the load:

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

A solar panel receives energy from the Sun at a rate of 5.0 kW.

Thermal energy is transferred from the solar panel to water with an efficiency of 20%.

Cold water of mass 15 kg enters the solar panel every hour.

The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J / (kg°C).

Calculate the temperature increase of the water.

temperature increase = .....................................................°C
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the temperature increase of the water:

List the known quantities:

- Power of sunlight from the Sun, *P* = 5.0 kW
- Mass of water every hour, *m *= 15 kg
- Time, *t *= 1 hour
- Specific heat capacity of water, *c *= 4200 J / (kg°C)
- Efficiency of solar panel = 20%

Convert the energy from the Sun from kW to W:

- $1000W=1kW$

  - $5.0kW=5\times1000=5000W$

Convert the time from hours into seconds:

- $1hour=60seconds$
- $1minutes=60seconds$

  - $1hour=60\times60=3600s$

Recall the equation to calculate the energy input from the Sun using it's power:

- $energy input=power\times time=Pt$
- $energy input=5000\times3600=1.8\times10^{7}J$

Recall the equation for calculating the energy output of the solar panel using the specific heat capacity of the water, *c*:

- $energy output=mcΔT$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to obtain an expression for energy output:

- $energy output=15\times4200\timesΔT$
- $energy output=63000\timesΔT$

Recall the equation for calculating the efficiency of the solar panel:

- $efficiency = 20 \% = 0.2$
- $efficiency=\frac{energy output}{energy input}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation for efficiency and substitute for each quantity:

- $energy output=efficiency\times energy input$
- $63 000 \times \Delta T = 0.2 \times ( 1.8 \times 10^{7} )$* ***[1 mark]**

Rearrange the expression to calculate the change in temperature:

- $\Delta T = \frac{0.2 \times ( 1.8 \times 10^{7} )}{63 000}$
- Δ*T *= 57 °C **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Your first step in this long question is to remove the k for kW and convert time into seconds. So all units are in their fundamental form. *

> *The question gives you the efficiency of the solar panel, this indicates you must calculate both the input and output energy. Then apply the efficiency and rearrange to obtain the change in temperature. *

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the kinetic energy of this cylinder of sea water:

List the known quantities:

- Radius, $r$ = 5.0 m
- Length, $l$ = 24 m
- Density of sea water, $ρ$ = 1020 kg/m<sup>3</sup>
- Speed of tide, $v$ = 6.0 m/s

Calculate the volume of the cylinder:

- $V=πr^{2}l$
- $V=π\times5.0^{2}\times24$ **[1 mark]**
- $V=1885m^{3}$

Calculate the mass of the cylinder:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$
- $m=ρV=1020\times1885$ **[1 mark]**
- $m=1.92\times10^{6}\mathrm{kg}$

Calculate the kinetic energy:

- $E_{k}=\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$
- $E_{k} = 1 \frac{1}{2} \times ( 1.92 \times 10^{6} ) \times 6.0^{2}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{k}=3.46\times10^{7}$

Give the answer to 2 significant figures and with units:

- $E_{k}=3.5\times10^{7}J$ **[1 mark]**

**   **

(ii) Calculate the time taken for 24 m of water to pass through the turbine at 6.0 m/s:

Rearrange the speed equation:

- $d=vt$
- $t=\frac{d}{v}=\frac{24}{6.0}$
- $t=4.0s$ **[1 mark]**

(iii) Calculate the power transferred to the turbine:

Substitute the known quantities from (i) and (ii) into the power equation:

- $P=\frac{E}{t}=\frac{3.46\times10^{7}}{4.0}=8.65\times10^{6}$
- $P=8.7\mathrm{MW}$ **[1 mark]**

**   **

(iv) The turbine's electrical power output is 7.0 MW. Calculate its efficiency:

Substitute the values into the efficiency equation:

- $\mathrm{efficiency}=\frac{\mathrm{useful} \mathrm{power} \mathrm{output}}{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{power} \mathrm{input}}=\frac{7.0}{8.7}$
- $\mathrm{efficiency}=0.80$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

> *While it is important to give your answers to the correct number of significant figures (2 s.f. here), it is best to use **unrounded** values in calculations.*

> *Rounding multiple values **midway** **through** a long calculation like this can end up having a big impact on the final answer. *

Area of the Earth in sunlight, A_Sun = 2.55 × 10^14 m^2

**Extended tier only**

(i) Under the assumption that there are no clouds obscuring the Sun, calculate the power that each square metre of the Earth receives from the Sun.

[3]

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the power that each square metre of the Earth receives from the Sun, giving its units:

- Power the Earth's surface receives from the Sun, $P_{surface}$ = 1.9 × 10<sup>17</sup> W
- Area of the Earth in sunlight, $A_{Sun}$ = 2.55 × 10<sup>14</sup> m<sup>2</sup>

- $\frac{P_{surface}}{A_{Sun}}=\frac{1.9\times10^{17}}{2.55\times10^{14}}=745.1$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the power transferred to the solar cell, $P_{in}$:

Use the efficiency equation to calculate useful power out, $P_{out}$:

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the weight of the elephant:

List the known quantities:

- Mass, *m* = 4000 kg (from part (a))

Recall the equation for weight:

- $g=\frac{W}{m}$ **OR** $W=mg$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the value of acceleration of free fall:

- *g* = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup>

Substitute the known values into the equation to calculate weight:

- $W=4000\times9.8$ **[1 mark]**
- *W* = 39 200 N **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the pressure the elephant exerts on the ground when it is standing on four feet, including the unit:

List the known quantities:

- Area of one elephant's foot, *A* = 0.125 m<sup>2</sup> (from part (a))
- Weight of the elephant, *W* = 39 200 N (from part (b)(i))

Calculate the total area in contact with the ground:

- Elephants have 4 feet
- $total area=0.125\times4=0.500m^{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation for pressure:

- $pressure=\frac{force}{area}$  **OR**  $P=\frac{F}{A}$  **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values into the equation to calculate pressure:

- The force here is weight, *W* = 39 200 N (from part (i))
- $P=\frac{39200}{0.500}$ **[1 mark]**
- *P* = 78 400 Pa **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

> *Remember that mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object, whereas weight is the force acting on an object with mass in a gravitational field. *

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 4.1 shows a pin. Fig. 4.2 shows a person pushing the pin into a wall.

![pin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-9-pressure/assets/035-pin.png)

The area of the top surface of the pin is 1.8 cm<sup>2</sup>.

The person applies a force of 50 N.

Calculate the pressure exerted on the top surface of the pin.

pressure = ............................................. N / cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pressure exerted on the top surface of the pin:

List the known quantities:

- Area, *a* = 1.8 cm<sup>2</sup>
- Force, *F* = 50 N

Recall the equation for pressure:

- $P=\frac{F}{A}$** [1 mark]**

Substitute the values:

- $P=\frac{50}{1.8}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate and write the answer:

- P = 28 N / cm<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The area of the top surface of the pin is 1.8 cm^2.
The person applies a force of 50 N.
pressure = 28 N / cm^2

The area of the top surface of the pin is 500 times larger than the area of the point.

Calculate the value of the pressure exerted by the point on the wall.

pressure = ............................................. N / cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pressure exerted by the point on the wall:

Use the ratio from the question:

- The area of the point is 500 times smaller (from the question)
- Therefore since $P=\frac{F}{A}$, the pressure must be 500 times larger

Calculate using the ratio:

- Pressure from the point = 500 × 28  = 14 000 N / cm<sup>2 </sup>**[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *They key to this question is to realise that the force is the same at each end of the pin, and that only the pressure changes. This is why pins have a sharp end and a flat end - one easily goes into walls (high pressure) while the other does not easily go into and hurt your thumb (low pressure).*

> *For the final part you may have decided to find the area of the point and then calculate. In this case your working should look like:*

- $areaofpoint=\frac{area of top}{500}$
- $areaofpoint=\frac{1.8}{500}=0.0036cm^{2}$
- $pressurefrompoint=\frac{force}{area}=\frac{50}{0.0036}=13889Ncm^{2}$

> *To take into account alternative methods the examiner would allow a range of answers from 13 500 to 15 000 N / cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

parts.problemMd:

Table 2.1 gives some data about the cylinder and the liquid.

![q2a2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-9-pressure/assets/031-q2a2.jpg)

The cylinder containing liquid is placed on a digital balance that displays the mass in kg.

Calculate the reading shown on the balance.

reading ......................................................kg
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the reading shown on the balance:

List the known quantities:

- Radius, *r *= 3.5 cm
- Depth, *h *= 12.0 cm
- Density, *ρ *= 900 kg/m<sup>3</sup>
- Weight of empty cylinder = 2.5 N

Convert the units for radius and depth from cm into m:

- There are 100 cm in 1 m
- So, for radius there are 3.5 ÷ 100 = 0.035 m
- For depth there are 12 ÷ 100 = 0.12 m

Calculate the volume of the liquid in the cylinder:

- $Volume of cylinder,V=πr^{2}h$
- $V = \pi \times ( 0.035 )^{2} \times 0.12$
- *V *= 4.62 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

Recall the equation for density and rearrange to make mass the subject:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$
- $m=ρV$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the mass of the liquid, *m*:

- $m = 900 \times ( 4.62 \times 10^{- 4} ) = 0.41 \text{kg}$** [1 mark]**

Convert the mass of the cylinder from N into kg:

- $weight,W=mass\times gravity$
- $mass=\frac{weight}{gravity}$
- $mass=\frac{2.5}{9.8}$
- mass = 0.255 kg

Calculate the total mass of the liquid and cylinder as recorded on the balance:

- $Total mass=mass of container+mass of liquid$
- $Total mass=0.255+0.41$
- Total mass = 0.665 kg = 0.67 kg (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *When solving calculation questions:*

- *Convert units into their standard form e.g. kg for mass and m for length*
- *Check each step of your workings at the end*

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

On a particular day, the atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. A bubble of gas forms at a point 5.0 m below the surface of a lake. The density of water is 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>.

Determine

(i) the total pressure at a depth of 5.0 m in the water,

pressure = ...........................................................[3]

(ii) the pressure of the gas in the bubble.

pressure = ...........................................................[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the total pressure at a depth of 5.0 m:

List the known quantities:

- Atmospheric pressure = 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Density of water = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>
- Depth = 5.0 m

Recall the equation for pressure at depth, and substitute in known values:

- $pressure at depth=density\times g\times height$ **OR** $p=ρgh$
- $pressure at depth=1000\times9.81\times5.0$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate pressure at this depth:

- $pressure at depth=50000\mathrm{Pa}$ **[1 mark]**

Combine with atmospheric pressure to give total pressure, *p*:

- $p=atmospheric pressure+pressure at depth$
- $p=100000+50000$
- *p* = 1.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa **[1 mark]**

(ii) State the pressure in the bubble:

- Pressure is constant at constant depth
- Therefore, pressure = 1.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Remember that pressure is constant at a constant depth. The depth is determined by the gravitational field strength (**g**), density of the liquid (**ρ**) and depth (**h**). Don't forget that a question might need you to consider atmospheric pressure as well, especially when it's asked for the **total **pressure.*

> *If an object in a liquid is less dense than that liquid, it will rise up and float on the liquid. It is important to memorise the gas relationships so you can back up your answers!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extended Tier Only**

Fig. 2.1 shows water stored in a reservoir behind a hydroelectric dam.

![Diagram of a hydroelectric power plant, showing water flow from a 150m high reservoir, through a turbine, and into a generator.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-9-pressure/assets/017-diagram-of-a-hydroelectric-power-plant-showing-w.png)

The turbine is 150 m below the level of the water in the reservoir.

Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> <sup> </sup>Pa. The density of water is 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>.

(i) Calculate the total pressure in the water at the turbine.

pressure = ......................................................... [3]

(ii) The turbine has a cross-sectional area of 3.5 m<sup>2</sup>.

Calculate the force exerted on the turbine by the water.

force = .......................................................... [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the total pressure in the water at the turbine:

List the known quantities:

- Atmospheric pressure, $p_{atm}$ = 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- The density of water, $p$ = 1000 kg/m<sup>3</sup>
- Height of water, $\Delta h$ = 150 m
- Gravitational field strength, $g$= 10 N/kg

Use the equation for pressure in a liquid to find the pressure due to the water in the reservoir:

- $p_{water}=pg\Delta h$ **[1 mark]**
- $p_{water}$= 1000 × 10 × 150
- $p_{water}$ = 1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa

Calculate the total pressure by adding the atmospheric pressure:

- Total pressure = $p_{atm}$+ $p_{water}$
- Total pressure = (1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup>) + (1.5 × 10<sup>6</sup>) **[1 mark]**
- Total pressure = 1.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the force exerted on the turbine by the water:

- Pressure = force ÷ area  **OR  **$p=\frac{F}{A}$
- Therefore, force = pressure × area  **OR ** $F=pA$** [1 mark]**

  - Where *p *= 1.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa and *A* = 3.5 m<sup>2</sup>
- Force = (1.6 × 10<sup>6</sup>) × 3.5
- Force = 5.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> N **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

The kinetic energy of the water in the pipe remains constant because:

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 4.1 shows liquid in a cylinder.

![18p4-3a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-9-pressure/assets/025-18p4-3a.png)

The depth of the liquid is 10 cm and the radius of the cylinder is 3.0 cm. The weight of the liquid in the cylinder is 2.5 N.

Calculate the density of the liquid. You can assume that acceleration of free fall is 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>.

density = ...........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the density of the liquid:

List the known quantities:

- Weight, *W* = 2.5 N
- Acceleration of free fall, g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>
- Radius of cylinder, *r* = 3.0 cm = 0.03 m
- Depth of liquid, *h* = 10 cm = 0.1 m

State the equations for density, mass and volume:

- $ρ=\frac{m}{V}$
- Where

  - mass $m$ can be found from $W=mg$
  - volume $V$ can be found from $V=πr^{2}h$

Rearrange the weight equation for mass and substitute in the values:

- $m=\frac{W}{g}$
- $m=\frac{2.5}{10}=0.25\mathrm{kg}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known values to calculate volume:

- $V=πr^{2}h$
- $V = \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 0.03 )^{2} \times 0.1 = 2.8 \times 10^{- 4} \mathrm{m}^{3}$* ***[1 mark]**

Substitute the mass and volume values into the density equation:

- $ρ=\frac{0.25}{2.8\times10^{-4}}$
- $ρ$ = 892.86 = 890 kg/m<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *This question is a **lot** more involved than it looks at first sight. It relies heavily on your recall of equations. Make sure you learn **all** the equations, and understand the links between them. You will be able to apply different equations to find the values you need.*

> *For example, once you understood that you were using the density equation, and to that you needed to know the mass and the volume, you can use the equations for **weight** to find the **mass** and the equation for the **volume** of a **cylinder** to find the volume of the liquid. *

> *Remember that for CIE IGCSE exams, you are **not** given an equation sheet or a data booklet. You will need to recall **all** the equations that you have met throughout your course. It is easier and far more effective to learn them as you study each topic, rather than trying to learn them all just before your exams. *

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Fig. 4.2 shows a device called a manometer that measures the pressure of a gas supply.

![18p4-3b](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/1-motion-forces-and-energy/1-9-pressure/assets/026-18p4-3b.png)

(i) The difference *h* between the two liquid levels is 2.0 cm. The density of the liquid is 800 kg/m<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the difference between the pressure of the gas and atmospheric pressure.

pressure difference = ...........................................................[2]

(ii) A similar device with a tube of smaller cross-sectional area is connected to a gas supply at the same pressure.

State and explain any effect on the value of *h*.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the difference between the pressure of the gas and atmospheric pressure:

List the known quantities:

- Change in height of liquid, Δ*h *= 2.0 cm = 0.02 m
- Density of the liquid, *ρ *= 800 kg/m<sup>3</sup>
- Gravitational field strength, *g* = 10 N/kg

State the equation for pressure in fluids:

- $\Delta p=ρg\Delta h$

Substitute in the known values to calculate the change in pressure:

- $\Delta p=800\times10\times0.02$ **[1 mark]**
- $\Delta p$ = 160 Pa **[1 mark]**

(ii) State and explain any effect on the value of *h:*

State the effect on the value of *h*:

- The value of *h* stays the same; **[1 mark]**

Explain the effect on the value of *h*:

- Because the difference in height does not depend on the cross-sectional area of the tube **OR**
- Because the pressure of the liquid column depends only on height, density and gravitational field strength (because Δ*p* = *ρg*Δ*h*); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Remember that gravitational field strength, **g**, and acceleration of free fall, **g**, are the **same** **thing**. They have different units, but the same value. *

- *gravitational field strength, **g **=** **9.8 N/kg*
- *acceleration of free fall, **g **= 9.8 m/s*<sup>*2*</sup>* *

> *These are the values you should learn, and these are the values you should use,** unless the question tells you otherwise**, as it does in this instance.*

Calculate

(i) the weight of liquid in the container

weight = ...........................................................[1]

(ii) the pressure due to the liquid on the base of the container

parts.problemMd:
When a material is cooled or heated there may be a change of state.

Complete each statement by using words from the box. Each word can be used once, more than once or not at all.

| condensation     evaporation     freezing     melting |
|---|

The change from solid to liquid is called .....................................

The change from liquid to gas is called .....................................

The change from liquid to solid is called .....................................

The change from gas to liquid is called ..................................... .
parts.solutionMd:
Complete each statement by using words from the box:

- The change from solid to liquid is called **melting**; **[1 mark]**
- The change from liquid to gas is called** evaporation / boiling**; **[1 mark]**
- The change from liquid to solid is called** freezing / solidifying;** **[1 mark]**
- The change from gas to liquid is called **condensing**; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *You need to learn and remember the changes in state with increasing and decreasing energy:*

- *A solid will **melt** into a liquid as energy is transferred **to** the substance.*

  - *This change of state happens at the **melting point**.*

- *A liquid will **evaporate** into a gas as energy is transferred **to** the substance.*

  - *This change of state happens at the **boiling point**.*

- *A gas will **condense** into a liquid as energy is transferred **away** from the substance.*

  - *This change of state happens at the **boiling point**. *

- *A liquid will **freeze** into a solid as energy is transferred **away** from the substance.*

  - *This change of state happens at the **melting point**. *

> *Melting** and **freezing** happen at the **melting point**. **Evaporation** and **condensing** happen at the **boiling point**. *

> *Energy is transferred **to** a substance when it is **heated**, and energy is transferred **away** from a substance when it is **cooled**.*

If the volume of the container was not fixed, the gas would expand. parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Air is trapped by a piston in a cylinder. The pressure of the air is 7.1 × 10^5 Pa. The distance from the closed end of the cylinder to the piston is 48 mm. The piston is pushed in until the pressure of the air has risen to 9.0 × 10^5 Pa.

- Initial pressure of the air, p1 = 7.1 × 10^5 Pa
- Final pressure of the air, p2 = 9.0 × 10^5 Pa
- Initial distance, l1 = 48 mm

The equation linking pressure and volume at a constant temperature is:
- pV = constant

The volume that the gas has taken up is the volume of the cylinder. This is equal to its length × cross-sectional area (V = l × A).

**Extended tier only**

Air is trapped by a piston in a cylinder. The pressure of the air is 7.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. The distance from the closed end of the cylinder to the piston is 48 mm.

The piston is pushed in until the pressure of the air has risen to 9.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.

Calculate how far the piston has moved.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate how far the piston has moved

List the known quantities:

- Initial pressure of the air, *p*<sub>1</sub> = 7.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Final pressure of the air, *p*<sub>2</sub> = 9.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Inital distance, *l*<sub>1</sub> = 48 mm

State the equation linking pressure and volume:

- *pV* = constant, therefore, $p_{1}V_{1}=p_{2}V_{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation for the final distance, *l*<sub>2</sub>:

- $V_{2}=\frac{p_{1}V_{1}}{p_{2}}$ where $V=lA$

  - *l* is the length of the cylinder
  - *A* is the cross-sectional area of the cylinder
- $l_{2}A=\frac{p_{1}l_{1}A}{p_{2}}\Rightarrow l_{2}=\frac{p_{1}l_{1}}{p_{2}}$

Substitute the values into the equation to calculate *l*<sub>2</sub>:

- $l_{2} = \frac{( 7.1 \times 10^{5} ) \times 48}{9.0 \times 10^{5} }$ **[1 mark]**
- $l_{2}=37.867\mathrm{mm}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the distance moved, *d *:

- $d=l_{1}-l_{2}=48-37.867=10.1\mathrm{mm}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The volume that the gas has taken up is the volume of the **cylinder**. This is equal to its length × cross-sectional area.*

> *From previous subparts, we know that pressure is **inversely proportional** to volume. This means that as one increases, the other must decrease.*

> *In both cases, 1 and 2, the cross-sectional area **A** is the same as the cylinder itself has not changed, just the distance of the closed end of the cylinder to the piston. You must be confident in using this equation in this form - look out for the 'two scenarios' type of questions which is when you have to use *$p_{1}V_{1}=p_{2}V_{2}$

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The piston in Fig 1.2 is pulled out of the cylinder from position A to position B, without changing the temperature of the air enclosed. Position B is double the length of the distance between position A and the end of the cylinder. The pressure when the piston is at position A is 2.5 × 10^5 Pa.

Distance of position A from the end of the cylinder, l₁ = 25 cm

Boyle's law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
Volume of a cylinder is length × cross-sectional area (V = lA), A is the same in both scenarios
p₂ = (p₁ × l₁) / l₂

**Extended tier only**

The piston in Fig 1.2 is pulled out of the cylinder from position A to position B, without changing the temperature of the air enclosed. Position B is double the length of the distance between position A and the end of the cylinder. The pressure when the piston is at position A is 2.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa.

![2-1-4c-h-boyles-law-piston](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/2-thermal-physics/2-1-kinetic-particle-model-of-matter/assets/035-2-1-4c-h-boyles-law-piston.png)

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the pressure is moved to position B

List the known quantities:

- Initial pressure, *p*<sub>1</sub> = 2.5 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Distance of position A from the end of the cylinder, *l*<sub>1</sub> = 25 cm

Calculate the distance of position B from the end of the cylinder, *l*<sub>2</sub>:

- Position B is double the distance of position A, $2\times25=50\mathrm{cm}$
- $l_{2}=50+25=75\mathrm{cm}$ from the end of the cylinder **[1 mark]**

State Boyle's law:

- $p_{1}V_{1}=p_{2}V_{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation for the pressure distance, *p*<sub>2</sub>:

- $V_{2}=\frac{p_{1}V_{1}}{p_{2}}$ where $V=lA$

  - *l* is the length of the cylinder
  - *A* is the cross-sectional area of the cylinder
- $l_{2}A=\frac{p_{1}l_{1}A}{p_{2}}\Rightarrow l_{2}=\frac{p_{1}l_{1}}{p_{2}}$
- $p_{2}=\frac{p_{1}l_{1}}{l_{2}}$

Substitute the values into the equation:

- $p_{2} = \frac{( 2.5 \times 10^{5} ) \times 25}{75}$ **[1 mark]**
- $p_{2}=8.3\times10^{4}\mathrm{Pa}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Always make sure your answer makes sense at the end. In this case, the temperature isn't changing. Boyle's law states that pressure is inversely proportional to volume. From A to B, the volume increases, so the pressure must decrease. This means **p*<sub>*2*</sub>* must be less than **p*<sub>*1*</sub>* which is the case for our final answer. If you get a value that's greater than **p*<sub>*1 *</sub>*this is an indication you have gone wrong with the maths somewhere!*

> *Remember that the volume of a cylinder is length, **l** × cross-sectional area, **A**. **A** is the same in both scenarios as we are using the same cylinder.*

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Write a conclusion to this experiment and explain your results:

Conclusion:

- The beaker with lid **A **has a greater rate of cooling; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- This is because the temperature change of the beaker with lid **A **from *t *= 0 s to *t *= 180 s is greater than the beaker with lid **B**; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Suggest and explain a change to the **apparatus** that could produce a greater difference between the rates of cooling for lids **A** and **B**:

Suggest a change to the apparatus:

**Any one from:**

- This is because thermal energy only escapes from the surface of the beaker (because plastic is more insulating); **[1 mark]**

- This is because there is a larger surface area from which evaporation can occur; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extended**

In a laboratory at normal room temperature, 200 g of water is poured into a beaker. A thermometer placed in the water has a reading of 22 °C.

Small pieces of ice at 0 °C are added to the water one by one. The mixture is stirred after each addition until the ice has melted. This process is continued until the temperature recorded by the thermometer is 0 °C.

The total mass of ice added to the water is found to be 60 g.

The specific heat capacity of water is 4.2J/(g °C).

Calculate the energy transferred from the water's thermal energy store originally in the beaker.

thermal energy = ...........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the energy transferred from the thermal energy store:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of water = 200 g
- Initial temperature of water = 22 °C
- Final temperature of water = 0 °C
- Specific heat capacity of water = 4.2J/(g °C)

Recall the equation for specific heat capacity:

- $energy transferred=mass\times specific heat capacity\times temperature change$ **OR**** **$Q=mcΔθ$ **OR**** **$E=mcΔT$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate energy, *Q*:

- $Q = 200 \times 4.2 \times ( 22 - 0 )$
- *Q* = 18000 J **[1 mark]**

Be very careful with units - you will often find specific heat capacity is given as J/(kg °C). Make sure that your units for mass match your units for specific heat capacity.

Many text books write energy as ***E*** instead of ***Q, ***and temperature as ***T*** instead of ***θ***.

As long as you are consistent throughout your calculation it's fine to do either.

The immersion heater is powered by the mains at a voltage of 230 V. When the tap is opened, the heater switches on and the current in the heater is 13 A.

thermal energy = ......................................................... [2]

rate = ......................................................... [4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the thermal energy produced by the heater in 60 s:

List the known quantities:

- Voltage of the supply, *V* = 230 V
- Current in the heater, *I* = 13 A
- Time, *t *= 60 s

The thermal energy is equal to the electrical energy transferred:

- *E* = *VIt*
- *E* = 230 × 13 × 60 **[1 mark]**
- *E* = 1.8 × 10<sup>5</sup> J **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the rate at which water at its boiling point emerges from the tap:

Calculate the change in temperature of the water:

- The water enters the tap at 22 °C and leaves the tap at the boiling point of water
- The boiling point of water is 100 °C
- Therefore, Δ*T* = 100 – 22 = 78 °C **[1 mark]**

Determine the equation for the mass of water leaving the tap each second:

- The rate is equal to the amount, or mass, of water, leaving the tap each second, or $\frac{m}{t}$
- Rearrange the equation for specific heat capacity $E=mc\Delta T$ for the mass $m=\frac{E}{c\Delta T}$**[1 mark]**
- Using the equation for power  $P=\frac{E}{t}$ the rate can be found by dividing each side of the equation by time
- Rate =  $\frac{m}{t}$= $\frac{E}{c\Delta Tt}$=  $\frac{E}{t}\frac{1}{c\Delta T}=\frac{P}{c\Delta T}$

Calculate the mass of water leaving the tap each second:

- List the known quantities

  - Power, *P* = *VI* = 230 × 13
  - Specific heat capacity of water, *c* = 4200 J/(kg °C)
- Rate =   $\frac{P}{c\Delta T}$=  $\frac{230\times13}{4200\times78}$ **[1 mark]**
- Rate = 9.1 × 10<sup>–3</sup> kg/s **[1 mark]**

**Total: [6 marks]**

> *You may also gain the marks by calculating the energy transferred in 1 second, then substituting this into **E** = **mc**Δ**T** and rearranging to find mass leaving each second.*

parts.problemMd:
A student heats a $2.0\mathrm{kg}$ aluminium block in an electrical heater of power $48W$. The initial temperature of the block is $20^{\circ}C$. After 20 minutes, the temperature of the block is $45^{\circ}C$.

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium:

- List the known quantities:

  - Power of heater, $P=48W$
  - Time, $t=20\mathrm{min}$
  - Mass of aluminium block, $m=2.0\mathrm{kg}$
  - Temperature change, $\Deltaθ=45-20=25^{\circ}C$
- Convert the time to seconds:

$t=20\times60=1200\text{s}$

- Calculate the energy supplied by the heater:

$E=Pt$

$E=48\times1200=57600\text{J}$ **[1 mark]**

- Use the equation for specific heat capacity to find $c$:

$c=\frac{E}{m\Deltaθ}$ **[1 mark]**

$c=\frac{57600}{2.0\times25}$

$c=$ $1150\text{J/(kg °C)}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for converting the time to seconds (1200 s) **AND** using $E = P t$ to calculate the energy supplied (57 600 J)
> 
> 1 mark for correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $c=\frac{E}{m\Deltaθ}$ or $\frac{57600}{2.0\times25}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $1150\text{J/(kg °C)}$
> 
> - Accept $1152\text{J/(kg °C)}$
> - Accept $\text{J/(kg K)}$ as the unit
> 
> Full marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student heats a 2.0 kg aluminium block in an electrical heater of power 48 W. The initial temperature of the block is 20 °C. After 20 minutes, the temperature of the block is 45 °C.

Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium.

Calculated value: 1150-1152 J/(kg °C)

The accepted value for the specific heat capacity of aluminium is $900\text{J/(kg °C)}$.

Suggest why the student's calculated value is higher than the accepted value.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings **OR** not all thermal energy is transferred to the block **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept: "energy is lost by conduction/convection/radiation to the surroundings"
> 
> Do not accept: "energy is lost" without stating where it is lost to (must mention surroundings or air)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the calculated value ($1152  \text{J/(kg °C)}$) to be higher than the accepted value ($900  \text{J/(kg °C)}$), the energy that was transferred to the block must be less than $57  600  \text{J}$. This makes the numerator too large, so the calculated specific heat capacity is too high. Whenever a "suggest" question asks about experimental error, think about energy losses first — this is the most common source of error in thermal experiments.

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of particles, what happens to the internal energy of the block as its temperature increases.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Particles gain kinetic energy **OR** particles vibrate more / faster **[1 mark]**
> - Internal energy increases (because the kinetic energy of the particles increases) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept "molecules" or "atoms" for "particles"
> 
> Do not accept "particles move faster" without specifying vibration (in a solid, particles vibrate — they do not move about freely)

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a solid, the particles vibrate about fixed positions — they do not move freely like gas particles. When the temperature increases, the particles vibrate more vigorously, which means their kinetic energy increases. Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles, so the internal energy increases. Avoid circular reasoning such as "internal energy increases because it gets hotter" — you must explain the mechanism in terms of particle motion.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended**

Gas of mass 0.23 g is trapped in a cylinder by a piston. The gas is at atmospheric pressure which is 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. Fig. 4.1 shows the piston held in position by a catch.

![sGf1GOLb_q5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/2-thermal-physics/2-2-thermal-properties-and-temperature/assets/029-sgf1golb-q5.png)

The volume of the trapped gas is 1.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.

An electrical heater is used to increase the temperature of the trapped gas by 550 °C.

The specific heat capacity of the gas is 0.72 J / (g °C).

(i) Calculate the energy required to increase the temperature of the trapped gas by 550 °C.

energy = ......................................................... [2]

(ii) The power of the heater is 2.4 W.

1. Calculate how long it takes for the heater to supply the energy calculated in (a)(i).

time = ......................................................... [2]

2. In practice, it takes much longer to increase the temperature of the gas by 550 °C using the heater. Suggest **one **reason for this.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate energy required to raise the temperature:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of gas, *m* = 0.23 g
- Specific heat capacity of the gas, *c* = 0.72 J / (g °C)
- Change in temperature, Δ*T* = 550 °C

Recall the equation linking energy and specific heat capacity:

- $E=mcΔT$* ***[1 mark]**

Substitute the values and calculate:

- $E=0.23\times0.72\times550$
- $E=91.08$

Round the answer to two significant figures and include the units:

- Energy, *E* = 91 J **[1 mark]**

(ii)

**1.** To calculate the time taken to supply the energy:

List the known quantities:

- Energy, *E* = 91 J
- Power, *P* = 2.4 W

Recall the equation for power:

- $P=\frac{E}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make time the subject by multiplying both sides by t and then dividing by P:

- $E=P\times t$
- $t=\frac{E}{P}$

Substitute the values and calculate:

- $t=\frac{91}{2.4}$
- $t=37.92$

Round the answer to two significant figures and include the units:

- Time, *t *= 38 s **[1 mark]**

**2.** Reasons it will take longer than the estimate above:

- Thermal/heat energy also heats up/is dissipated to the cylinder / piston / heater / surroundings; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Since experiments, machinery and electronics always lose energy as thermal energy is dissipated to the surroundings, you can almost guarantee being asked about this in your exam.*

> *You should have done experiments in class where you can feel for yourself that the heat escapes. Other ways of testing this are simply to feel the way your phone, laptop or car gets hot while in use.*

> *The phrase 'thermal energy is dissipated to the surroundings' is a very useful one - be ready to use it!*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Gas of mass 0.23 g is trapped in a cylinder by a piston. The gas is at atmospheric pressure which is 1.0 × 10^5 Pa. The volume of the trapped gas is 1.9 × 10^–4 m^3. An electrical heater is used to increase the temperature of the trapped gas by 550 °C.

When the temperature of the gas has increased by 550 °C, its pressure is 2.9 × 10^5 Pa.

#### Extended

When the temperature of the gas has increased by 550 °C, its pressure is 2.9 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa. The catch is then released allowing the piston to move. As the piston moves, the temperature of the gas remains constant.

(i) State and explain what happens to the piston.

[2]

(ii) Determine the volume of the gas when the piston stops moving.

volume = ......................................................... [3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To state and explain what happens to the piston:

First state the direction of movement:

- The piston moves to the right / away from heater **OR **accelerates (to right); **[1 mark]**

Explain the cause of this movement:

- The pressure of the gas is greater on the left **OR **the resultant force is to the right; **[1 mark]**

(ii) To determine the final volume of gas:

List the known quantities (given in part (a)):

- Initial volume, *V*<sub>*1*</sub> = 1.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m<sup>3</sup>
- Initial pressure, *P*<sub>*1*</sub> = 2.9 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa
- Final pressure, *P*<sub>*2*</sub> =  1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa

Since temperature is constant, use the equation relating pressure and temperature (Boyle's Law):

- $P_{1}V_{1}=P_{2}V_{2}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange by dividing by *P*<sub>*2*</sub> to make final volume *V*<sub>*2*</sub>  the subject:

- $V_{2}=\frac{P_{1}V_{1}}{P_{2}}$

Substitute the values and calculate:

- $V_{2} = \frac{( 2.9 \times 10^{5 ) \times ( 1.9 \times 10^{-4} } )}{( 1.0 \times 10^{5} )}$ **[1 mark]**
- $V_{2}=5.51\times10^{-4}$

Round the answer to two significant figures and include the units:

- Final volume, *V*<sub>*2*</sub> = 5.5 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Don't get confused by the initial and final values for pressure and volume, make sure you understand what is happening to the gas in this question*
- *After the temperature has increased, but before the catch is released, the pressure inside the cylinder, **P*<sub>*1*</sub>* = 2.9 × 10*<sup>*5*</sup>* Pa and the volume has not changed from part a), so **V*<sub>*1*</sub>* = 1.9 × 10*<sup>*–4*</sup>* m*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *When the catch is released, the piston will move, the volume of gas will increase and the pressure will decrease*
- *The piston will stop moving when the pressure inside the cylinder is equal to the pressure outside the cylinder, i.e. atmospheric pressure, so **P*<sub>*2*</sub> =  1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa

- Time, *t* = 90 s

- *x*<sub>2</sub> = 0.067 **[1 mark]**

State the correct unit for both *x*<sub>1</sub> and *x*<sub>2</sub>:

- °C/s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The marks are allocated slightly differently here that what you may be used to. 1 mark is given for the correct values of **x*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **x*<sub>*2*</sub>* and the second mark is given for the correct unit on **both **values.*

> *The way to work out the unit is by looking at the equations for **x*<sub>*1*</sub>* and **x*<sub>*2*</sub>*. *

- *The numerator (top half) of the fraction has units of °C as **θ** is the temperature*
- *The denominator (bottom half) of the fraction has units of s as **t** is the time*

  - *Therefore, the units are °C/s*

> *With all units the '/' means 'per unit'. Therefore, if the unit is for the value on the denominator of a fraction it is always / unit (per unit). E.g. m/s is 'metres **per** second'*

energy loss = .........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Mass of liquid, *m *= 150 g
- Specific heat capacity, *c *= 4.2 J / (g°C)

- Loss of thermal energy, $Q=mcΔθ$* ***[1 mark]**

- $Q = 150 \times 4.2 \times ( 80 - 56 )$ **[1 mark]**

- *Q *= 15 000 J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *To calculate the amount of thermal energy lost you must find the temperature difference.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the energy incident on the solar panel during that day:

List the known quantities:

- Mass of water, $m$ = 250 kg
- Initial temperature = 16 °C
- Final temperature = 38 °C ** **
- Efficiency of panel = 25 % = 0.25
- Specific heat capacity of water, $c$ = 4200 J/kg °C

Calculate the energy transferred to the water, $ΔE$:

- $c=\frac{\Delta E}{m\Deltaθ}$
- $ΔE=mcΔθ$ **[1 mark]**
- `capital delta E = 250 x 4200 x ( 38 - 16 )` **[1 mark]**
- $ΔE=2.31\times10^{7}J$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the energy transferred to the solar panel, $E_{s}$:

- $\mathrm{efficiency}=\frac{\mathrm{useful} \mathrm{energy} \mathrm{out}}{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{energy} \mathrm{in}}=\frac{ΔE}{E_{s}}$
- $E_{s}=\frac{ΔE}{\mathrm{efficiency}}=\frac{2.31\times10^{7}}{0.25}$ **[1 mark]**
- $E_{s}=9.24\times10^{7}$

Give the answer with units and to two significant figures:

- Energy incident on the solar panel = 9.2 × 10<sup>7</sup> J **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

A wave on a rope has a speed of 0.25 m/s and a time period of 2 seconds.

parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Time period = 2.0 s
- Wave speed = 0.25 m/s

(i) To calculate frequency of the wave:

- Use the equation for frequency:

$f=\frac{1}{T}=\frac{1}{2}$ **[1 mark]**

$f=$ $0.5\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the wavelength of the wave:

- Use the wave equation:

$v=fλ$ **[1 mark]**

$λ=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{0.25}{0.5}$ **[1 mark]**

- Write the answer with units:

$λ=$ $0.5m$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A wave of light is passing from air into a clear plastic prism. The wave is refracted.

parts.solutionMd:
State two changes which would make the angle of refraction increase:

Any **two **from:

- Increase the angle of incidence; **[1 mark]**
- Decrease frequency / increase wavelength; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *It is best to learn how the angle of refraction, **r** changes when other variables such as refractive index, **n**, wave speed, **v**, frequency, **f**, and wavelength, **λ **also change. If you cannot remember then use the equation for refractive index:*

$n = \frac{\sin ( i )}{\sin ( r )}$

> *Rearrange the equation to make sin(**r**) the subject:*

$\sin ( r ) = \frac{\sin ( i )}{n}$

> *It is easy to see that:*

- *decreasing the refractive index, **n** then sin(**r**) will increase*
- *increasing sin(**i**) then sin(**r**) will also increase*

> *If **n** decreases then the density of the block decreases. If sin(**i**) increases then the angle of incidence, **i **increases.*

> *Remember that decreasing wave frequency or increasing wavelength increases the angle of refraction.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Green light of frequency 5.7 × 10^14 Hz is travelling in air at a speed of 3.0 × 10^8 m/s.

**Extended tier only**

The refractive index of the transparent solid is 1.3.

(i) The light is incident on the surface of the solid at an angle of incidence of 67°.

Calculate the angle of refraction of the light in the solid.

angle of refraction = ......................................................... [2]

(ii) Determine the wavelength of the green light in the transparent solid.

wavelength = ......................................................... [4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the angle of refraction:

List the known quantities:

- Refractive index, *n* = 1.3
- Angle of incidence, *i* = 67°

Recall the equation linking refractive index with angles of incidence and refraction:

- $n=\frac{\mathrm{sin}i}{\mathrm{sin}r}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make sin *r* the subject:

- $\mathrm{sin}r=\frac{\mathrm{sin}i}{n}$

Calculate to find sin *r* :

- $\mathrm{sin}r=\frac{\mathrm{sin}67}{1.3}=0.7081$

Use sin<sup>−1</sup> to find the value of *r* :

- $\sin ^{- 1} ( 0.7081 ) = 45.1$

Round the answer to two significant figures and include the units

- Angle of refraction, *r* = 45° **[1 mark]**

(ii) To determine wavelength:

List the known quantities:

- Speed of light in air, *v*<sub>*a*</sub> = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s (from part (a))
- Frequency of light, *f* = 5.7 × 10<sup>14</sup> Hz (from part (a))
- Refractive index, *n* = 1.3

Recall the equation linking refractive index with speed in a more dense medium:

- $n=\frac{v_{a}}{v_{g}}$ where *v*<sub>*a*</sub>* *is the speed in the air and *v*<sub>*g*</sub> is the speed in the glass prism; **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make the speed in the solid the subject:

- $v_{g}=\frac{v_{a}}{n}$

Calculate the speed in the solid:

- $v_{g}=\frac{3.0\times10^{8}}{1.3}=2.3\times10^{8}$m/s **[1 mark]**

Recall the wave equation;

- $v=fλ$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make wavelength the subject:

- $λ=\frac{v}{f}$

Substitute the values and calculate:

- $λ=\frac{2.3\times10^{8}}{5.7\times10^{14}}=4.0\times10^{-7}$m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *The final part of this question is quite difficult and has a lot of steps. However, did you notice that two of the four marks are simply for remembering the equations?*

> *Make sure you have memorised all the equations your teacher gives you. Writing them down will usually get you marks, and may help you to see how to solve a problem which you can't easily see a way into.*

Some students determine the focal length of a converging lens by two different methods. They use the apparatus shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Apparatus on a bench: a lamp behind a card with an illuminated triangle on the left, a converging lens in a holder in the middle and a screen on the right. Distance u is marked from the illuminated triangle to the lens and distance v from the lens to the screen.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-2-light/assets/019-apparatus-on-a-bench-a-lamp-behind-a-card-with-a.png)

She moves the screen until a sharp image of the triangle is seen on the screen.

**Method 1**

On Fig. 2.1, the distance *v* between the lens and the screen is $7 . 5 \text{cm}$.

Fig. 2.1 is drawn to 1/5 scale.

(i) Calculate the actual distance *U* between the illuminated triangle and the lens, and the actual distance *V* between the lens and the screen, in the experiment.

*U* = ...............................................................

*V* = ...............................................................

[1]

(ii) Calculate a value $f_{1}$ for the focal length of the lens, using the equation:

`f_{1} = \frac{UV}{\left(U + V\right)}`

$f_{1}$ = .........................................................

[1]

(iii) Briefly describe a technique to obtain an image on the screen that is as sharp as possible in this experiment.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the actual distances *U* and *V*:

- List the known quantities:

  - Distance on the diagram from the illuminated triangle to the lens, $u = 5 . 0 \text{cm}$
  - Distance on the diagram from the lens to the screen, $v = 7 . 5 \text{cm}$
  - The diagram is drawn to 1/5 scale, so 1 cm on the diagram represents 5 cm in the experiment
- Multiply each distance on the diagram by 5:

$U = 5 . 0 \times 5 =$$25 \text{cm}$

$V = 7 . 5 \times 5 =$$37 . 5 \text{cm}$

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both *U* **AND** *V* correct
> 
> - Accept 25.0 cm for *U*
> - Accept 37.5 cm or 38 cm for *V*

(ii) To calculate the focal length $f_{1}$:

- Write down the equation:

parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the magnification *M*:

- List the known quantities:

  - Height of the image, $h_{I} = 2 . 4 \text{cm}$
  - Height of the illuminated triangle, $h_{O} = 1 . 5 \text{cm}$
- Substitute the known values:

$M = \frac{h_{I}}{h_{O}} = \frac{2.4}{1.5}$

- Calculate the answer:

$M =$$1 . 6$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the known values:

`f_{2} = \frac{V}{\left(M + 1\right)} = \frac{37.5}{\left(1.6 + 1\right)} = \frac{37.5}{2.6}`

$f_{2} =$$14 \text{cm}$ **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

The speed of a light wave in air is 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m / s. The refractive index of water is 1.33.

speed = .........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the speed of light in water

List the known quantities:

- Speed of light in air = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m / s
- Refractive index of water, *n *= 1.33

Recall the equation for the refractive index and speed of wave:

- $refractive index,n=\frac{speed in air}{speed in water}$ **[1 mark]**

**OR**

Rearrange the equation and substitute the known quantities:

- $speed in water=\frac{speed in air}{n}$
- $speed in water=\frac{3\times10^{8}}{1.33}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the speed of the wave in water:

- Speed in water = 2.3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m / s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The equation you need to use comes from the definition for refractive index, **n**:*

*The ratio of the speeds of a wave in two different regions*.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the refractive index of the glass:

- Recall the equation for critical angle:

$\mathrm{sin}c=\frac{1}{n}$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange for $n$ and calculate:

$n=\frac{1}{\mathrm{sin}42^{\circ}}$

$n=$ $1.49$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> 1 mark for a correct answer of $1.49$
> 
> - Accept any value that rounds to 1.5
> 
> Working must be shown to gain both marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating refractive index, remember that the refractive index of air is 1, so for materials such as glass or plastic, if your answer is less than 1, you have the formula inverted.

#### Extended

A technician uses an optical fibre in a factory to view a pipe blockage. The blockage is round a bend, shown in Fig. 1.2.

![3-3-5d-m-curved-pipe-optical-fibre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-3-electromagnetic-spectrum/assets/009-3-3-5d-m-curved-pipe-optical-fibre.png)

(i) Calculate the critical angle of the glass.

[3]

(ii) The light does not reach the blockage. Suggest why.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the critical angle of the glass:

Recall the equation for critical angle:

- $n = \frac{1}{\sin ( C )}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for C and substitute the refractive index, $n$:

- $C = \sin ^{- 1} ( \frac{1}{n} )$
- $C = \sin ^{- 1} ( \frac{1}{1.3} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $C=50^{\circ}$ (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

(ii) The light does not reach the blockage. Suggest why:

- The angle of incidence is less than 50°; **[1 mark]**
- At the point where the fibre bends / turns the corner; **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) the light is <u>refracted</u> / leaves the fibre / core; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *50° is a relatively impractical critical angle - if the angle of incidence is less than this, the light will be refracted out of the optical fibre. In reality, a material would be used with a smaller critical angle. *

parts.problemMd:
Calculate the wavelength of X-rays with frequency 1.3 × 10<sup>17 </sup>Hz in a vacuum.

wavelength = ...........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the wavelength:

List the known quantities:

- Frequency, *f* = 1.3 × 10<sup>17 </sup>Hz
- Speed of light, *v* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s

Recall the equation linking speed, wavelength and frequency:

- $speed=frequency\times wavelength$ **OR** $v=f\timesλ$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in known values:

- $λ=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{3.0\times10^{8}}{1.3\times10^{17}}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate *λ*:

- *λ *= 2.31 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m = 2.3 × 10<sup>−9</sup> m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed, 3.0 × 10*<sup>*8*</sup>* m/s.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A vibrating source on a ship produces a sound wave that travels through the ocean. The wave produced is a longitudinal wave.

**Extended tier only**

The frequency of the sound wave is 800Hz.

(i) The speed of sound in air is 330m/s.

State a typical value for the speed of sound in a liquid.

[1]

(ii) Using your value from **(b)(i)**, calculate the wavelength of the sound wave in the ocean.

wavelength = ...........................................................[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State a typical value for the speed of sound in a liquid:

- A value in the range of 900 m/s to 2000 m/s; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Using your value from **(b)(i)**, calculate the wavelength of the sound wave in the ocean:

List the known quantities:

- Frequency, *f* = 800 Hz
- Speed of sound in liquid, *v* = 1000 m/s

Recall the wave equation:

- *v* = *f λ ***OR**** **wave speed = frequency × wavelength

Rearrange the equation to make wavelength the subject:

- $λ=\frac{v}{f}$

Substitute in the known values to calculate the wavelength:

- $λ=\frac{1000}{800}$ **[1 mark]**
- *λ* = 1.25 m **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The two rules you need to remember when rearranging equations are:*

1. *To undo an operation, do the opposite operation (to cancel a multiplication relationship, you need to divide, to cancel a minus you need to add or vice versa)*
2. *Whatever you do to an equation, you need to do it to **both sides*

> *If you need a reminder on how to rearrange the wave equation to solve for wavelength:*

parts.problemMd:
A boat race starts on the sea, but close to land. Fig. 9.1 shows the boats at the start of the race.

![screenshot-2022-10-20-at-10-58-05](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-4-sound/assets/011-screenshot-2022-10-20-at-10-58-05.png)

On the land, a cannon produces a loud bang to start the race. There is a flash of light at the same time as the bang.

(i) At the start of the race, the sailors watch for the flash of light from the cannon.

Suggest why the sailors watch for the flash of light rather than listen for the bang.

[1]

(ii) One of the sailors is 500 m from the cannon. She measures a time difference of 1.6 seconds between seeing the flash of light and hearing the bang.

Calculate the speed of sound.

speed of sound = ................................................ m/s [3]

(iii) The value of the speed of sound obtained in **(a)(ii)** is lower than expected.

Suggest a reason for this difference.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Suggest why the sailors watch for the flash of light rather than listen for the bang:

- Light travels faster than sound; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Light is seen before the bang is heard; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the speed of sound:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from the canon, *d* = 500 m
- Time difference, *t* = 1.6 s

Recall the equation for speed:

- $speed=\frac{distance}{time}$ **OR** $v=\frac{d}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the known quantities:

- $speed=\frac{500}{1.6}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the speed of sound:

- speed*  *= 312.5 m/s **[1 mark]**

**   **

(iii)  Suggest why the value obtained in **(ii) **is lower than expected:

- It is <u>windy</u> (which affects the measurements); **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- The reaction time to start / stop the watch (affects the time measured); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

In part (ii), you may have noticed that the question gives 1.6 s as the time **difference** between the sailor receiving the flash. The flash and the bang occur at the same time, so technically a short time passes between the canon making the sound and the sailor seeing the light.

You would be forgiven for thinking that this must mean that it is incorrect to say that 1.6 s pass between the canon sounding and the sailor hearing it. Isn't it 1.6 s + the time taken for the light to reach the sailor?

This is actually true! However, light travels at a speed of 300 000 000 m / s, so it takes light 0.0000017 s to reach the sailor. So actually the time it takes for the sound to reach the sailor is 1.6000017 s, but this has no effect on our answer to four significant figures!

Essentially, light travels so quickly that we can say that the sailor seeing the flash and the canon making a sound happen at **almost** the exact same time.  The further away the sailor the longer it will take the light and sound to reach them.

parts.solutionMd:
To determine the speed of sound:

[1]

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) State what is meant by the frequency of the source:

- The number of complete oscillations per second; **[1 mark]**

(ii) State the distance moved, in terms of the wavelength, *λ* by a wavefront during n oscillations of the source:

- For each oscillation the wavefront moves one wavelength, *λ *
- Therefore for n oscillations the wavefront moves <u>n × </u><u>*λ*</u> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

(i) The number of complete oscillations per second.

(ii) For each oscillation the wavefront moves one wavelength, λ. Therefore for n oscillations the wavefront moves n × λ.

Use your answers from part (a) to derive the wave equation.
parts.solutionMd:
Use your answers from part (a) to derive the wave equation:

Start with the equation defining velocity and substitute the term stated in (a)(i):

- $v=\frac{d}{t}=\frac{nλ}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the equation which defines frequency in terms of time:

- $f=\frac{1}{t}$ **OR  **$v=f\times nλ$**[1 mark]**

Make n = 1 to find the velocity of one wavefront (since they all have the same speed):

- $v=fλ$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

![3-4-3c-h-cro-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-4-sound/assets/010-3-4-3c-h-cro-1.png)

Each 1 cm division on the horizontal axis of the c.r.o. screen represents 2.0 ms.

Determine the frequency of the sound wave.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the frequency of the sound wave:

Look at the **troughs** to find the time for one full wavelength:

- One wavelength = 3 cm
- Time per cm = 2.0 ms = 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s
- Therefore time period, T = (3 × 2.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup>) = 6.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> s **[1 mark]**

Use the equation for frequency:

- $f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{( 6.0 \times 10^{- 3} )} = 166.7$

Write the answer to 2 sig figs and include the unit:

- $f=170\mathrm{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *You may instinctively look at the crests of the wave pattern to find the wavelength (since a definition you are used to is 'the distance from one crest to the next one'). *

> *However in this diagram the crests are in the middle of the divisions, making it harder to estimate the distance, while the troughs meet the division lines much more clearly.*

parts.problemMd:
A ship uses pulses of sound to determine the depth of the seabed. Each pulse of sound has a wavelength of $3.0\mathrm{cm}$.

The speed of sound in water is $1500m/s$.

(i) Calculate the frequency of the emitted sound.

[2]

(ii) Explain whether the sound from the ship is audible to a human with normal hearing.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the frequency of the emitted sound:

- Write down the wave equation:

$v = f λ$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange for frequency and calculate

$f=\frac{v}{λ}$

$f=\frac{1500}{0.030}$

$f=$ $50000\text{Hz}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $v = f λ$ **OR** $f = \frac{v}{λ}$ **OR** $\frac{1500}{0.030}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 50 000 Hz
> 
> - Accept $5 . 0 \times 10^{4}  \text{Hz}$ or $50  \text{kHz}$
> 
> Both marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

> **[mark-scheme]**
> (ii) The sound is
> 
> - Not audible, because the frequency ($50  000  \text{Hz}$ / $50  \text{kHz}$) is above $20  000  \text{Hz}$ / $20  \text{kHz}$ (the upper limit of human hearing) **OR **the sound is ultrasound **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept: "it is above the range of human hearing"
> 
> Do not accept: "it is not audible" without a reason — must reference the frequency being above the hearing limit

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember to convert the wavelength to metres before substituting: 3.0 cm = 0.030 m. A common error is to substitute 3.0 instead of 0.030, giving 500 Hz — this would be audible, which contradicts the purpose of the sonar equipment. The result (50 kHz) is well above the 20 kHz upper limit of human hearing, so the sound is ultrasound and is not audible. This is deliberate — ultrasound is used for sonar because its short wavelength allows it to detect small features on the seabed.
