parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Speed of sound in water 1500 m/s. Depth at 300 m read from the graph is 70 m; accept 69 m to 71 m. Total distance is twice the depth: 140 m (accept 138 m to 142 m). Expected answer 0.0933 s; accept 0.092 s to 0.095 s, 0.093 s or 0.09 s. A misread depth that is correctly doubled and divided by 1500 earns the second mark by error carried forward. Not doubling the depth (answer 0.047 s) scores a maximum of 1 mark.

Fig. 6.1 shows the graph for the depth of the sea at different distances from the shore.

![Graph showing sea depth from 0 to 80 metres with distance from shore ranging 0 to 350 metres. Line indicates fluctuating depth including points (70,20), (100,40), (150,40), (200,50), (300,70).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/3-waves/3-4-sound/assets/005-graph-showing-sea-depth-from-0-to-80-metres-with.png)

**Fig. 6.1**

When the ship is 300 m from the shore, a pulse of sound is emitted.

Calculate the time it takes for the sound wave to return to the ship.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the time for the pulse to return to the ship:

- Read the depth from the graph:

From the graph, when distance = 300 m, depth = 70 m

- The pulse travels down to the seabed and back, so the total distance is twice the depth:

$\text{total distance} = 2 \times 70 = 140 \text{m}$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange the speed equation for time and substitute:

$\text{time} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{speed}} = \frac{140}{1500}$

$\text{time} = 0 . 0933 \text{s} =$$0 . 093 \text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for reading the depth from the graph **AND** doubling it: total distance = $140 \text{m}$
> 
> - Accept a depth of 69–71 m (total distance 138–142 m)
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $0 . 093 \text{s}$
> 
> - Accept 0.092–0.095 s
> - Accept 0.0933 s or 0.09 s
> - ecf: if the depth is misread but is doubled and divided by 1500 correctly, award this mark
> - If the depth is not doubled (0.047 s), maximum 1 mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> The pulse goes down to the seabed and back, so double the depth before dividing by the speed: forgetting to double gives 0.047 s and loses a mark. Read the depth at exactly 300 m and to the nearest half-square; the seabed is steep there, so a careless read-off shifts your answer.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

To test that the steel rod has been magnetised:

- Place pole of the rod next to a known magnet;
- If one end of the rod repels the magnet then it must also be a magnet as like poles repel;

A piece of steel which is unmagnetised will still be attracted to the magnet. It is whether one end can repel that shows that it's been magnetised.

There are two types of magnets:

- Induced magnets
- Permanent magnets

Induced magnets are always attracted to the magnet that magnetised them. We only see a repulsive force between two permanent magnets when like poles are facing each other. This is caused by the interaction between the magnetic fields.

This only occurs between two permanent magnets, so if we observe this phenomenon, we must have two permanent magnets. 

The ability to attract materials such as iron is not unique to permanent magnets, so this cannot be used to prove that a magnet is permanent.

Explain how the student could test that the steel rod has been magnetised.
parts.solutionMd:
To test that the steel rod has been magnetised:

**Method 1**

- Place pole of the rod next to a known magnet; **[1 mark]**
- If one end of the rod repels the magnet then it must also be a magnet as <u>like poles repel</u>; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

**Method 2**

- Place a **plotting compass** next to the suspected magnetised rod; **[1 mark]**
- If the steel rod has been successfully magnetized, it will produce its own magnetic field; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *A piece of steel which is unmagnetised will still be attracted to the magnet. It is whether one end can repel that shows that it's been magnetised.*

> *There are two types of magnets:*

- *Induced magnets*
- *Permanent magnets*

> *Induced magnets are **always** attracted to the magnet that magnetised them. We only see a repulsive force between two permanent magnets when like poles are facing each other. This is caused by the interaction between the magnetic fields.*

![screenshot-2022-10-24-at-10-43-30](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-1-simple-phenomena-of-magnetism/assets/054-screenshot-2022-10-24-at-10-43-30.png)

> *This only occurs between two permanent magnets, so if we observe this phenomenon, we must have two permanent magnets. *

> *Induced magnets can also magnetise other materials. If a paperclips is magnetised, it can also magnetise other materials, hence why it is possible to pick up a **chain** of paperclips with a single permanent magnet. *

*The ability to attract materials such as iron is not unique to permanent magnets, so this cannot be used to prove that a magnet is permanent. *

A student is given three unknown metal strips and a bar magnet.

The student is also given the following information:

- One strip is magnetic but not magnetised

> 
> **Method**
> 
> - Bring one pole of the bar magnet up to each strip and note the effect, then repeat with the other pole **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Identification**
> 
> - The magnetised strip is attracted by one pole of the magnet **AND** repelled by the other pole **[1 mark]**
> - The magnetic but unmagnetised strip is attracted by both poles of the magnet **[1 mark]**
> - The non-magnetic strip is neither attracted nor repelled by either pole **[1 mark]**

All atoms contain electrons, and electrons act as tiny magnets with a north and a south pole, as shown in Fig. 1.1.

![4-1-5a-h-electron-as-magnet](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-1-simple-phenomena-of-magnetism/assets/032-4-1-5a-h-electron-as-magnet.png)

Metals are collections of many millions of atoms. For non-magnetic materials the electrons are randomly aligned as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![4-1-5a-h-electrons-non-magnetic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-1-simple-phenomena-of-magnetism/assets/033-4-1-5a-h-electrons-non-magnetic.png)

For magnetic materials, the electrons are arranged in groups called domains. Within each domain, the electrons are aligned so that they all point in the same direction, and each domain acts as a magnet itself. Fig. 1.3 shows this arrangement.

![4-1-5a-h-magnetic-domains](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-1-simple-phenomena-of-magnetism/assets/034-4-1-5a-h-magnetic-domains.png)

[3]

[3]

- The individual electrons have different alignments; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Use domain theory to explain why some metals can be magnetised:

- The electrons within the domain have the same alignment; **[1 mark]**

parts.solutionMd:
(i) Determine the gradient G of the graph, showing clearly on the graph how you obtained the necessary information:

Determine the change in y values:

Conductors are materials that allow charge to flow through easily. These tend to be metals, as they have more 'free charges' to flow. Insulators have no free charges, so charge cannot flow easily through it. Think about the materials you see in your everyday life and consider whether they are conductors or insulators.

Conductors heat up easily and allow electricity to flow through them, whilst insulators do not. This is why a frying pan will be made of a conducting material, but the handle will be an insulator, so you do not feel the heat of the pan that needs to be hot to fry food.

parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the electrical energy transferred:

- Total energy transferred = 3.240 × 10<sup>6</sup> J

- 90 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> *Part (ii) states that 3.6 × 10*<sup>*4*</sup>* J of energy are transferred per cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*.*

Fig. 10.1 shows a circuit used by a student to test a metal wire made of nichrome.

The current in the nichrome wire is 0.8 A. The potential difference (p.d.) across the nichrome wire is 4.5 V.

Calculate the resistance of the nichrome wire.

resistance = ..................................................... Ω
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the resistance of the nichrome wire:

List the known quantities:

- Current, *I* = 0.8 A
- Potential difference, *V *= 4.5 V

Recall the equation for Ohm's Law:

- $V=IR$** [1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to make *R* the subject:

- $R=\frac{V}{I}$

Substitute the known values into the equation to calculate resistance:

- $R=\frac{4.5}{0.8}$ **[1 mark]**
- R = 5.6 / 5.625 Ω **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that when stating an equation, you will still get the marks if the equation is given in its rearranged form as long as the rearrangement is correct. *

> *The two rules you need to remember when rearranging equations are:*

1. * To undo an operation, do the opposite operation (to cancel a multiplication relationship, you need to divide, to cancel a minus you need to add etc)*
2. *Whatever you do to an equation, you need to do it to both sides*

parts.problemMd:
An electrical heater has a resistance of 21.8 Ω when connected to a 240 V mains supply.

(i) Calculate the current in the heater.

current = ....................................................... A [3]

(ii) Suggest a rating for the fuse to be fitted to the mains plug for the heater.

fuse rating = ....................................................... A [1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the current in the heater:

List the known quantities:

- Resistance, *R* = 21.8 Ω
- Voltage, *V* = 240 V

Recall the equation linking voltage, current *I*,  and resistance:

- *V *=* I *× *R* **[1 mark]**

Substitute in known values and calculate I:

- $I=\frac{V}{R}=\frac{240}{21.8}$ **[1 mark]**
- *I *= 11.0 A **[1 mark]**

(ii) A suggestion for a fuse to be fitted is:

- The fuse should be greater than the operating current, but not too high above it
- Therefore, any value in the range 12 to 15 A is acceptable; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Fuses should always be rated above the operating current, but not too far above! If the gap is too large then a dangerous current could flow without the fuse breaking. If the fuse rating is under the operating current then the appliance will not work as the fuse will always break.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 7.1 shows a circuit containing a battery of e.m.f. 12 V and three resistors.

A circuit diagram showing a 12-volt battery connected in series with resistor R1 and a parallel combination of resistors R2 and R3. A voltmeter is connected across the parallel combination. R1 has a resistance of 8 ohms, R2 has a resistance of 20 ohms, and R3 has a resistance of 30 ohms.

Show that the combined resistance of R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> is $12Ω$.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the combined resistance of R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub>:

- List the known quantities:

  - Resistance of $R_{2}=20Ω$
  - Resistance of $R_{3}=30Ω$
- Recall the rule for adding resistance in parallel combinations:

$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\frac{1}{R_{3}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute in the values and rearrange for $R$:

$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{30}=\frac{5}{60}$

$R=\frac{60}{5}=12Ω$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for stating the correct formula for parallel resistors, e.g. $\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_{2}} + \frac{1}{R_{3}}$ **OR** $R = \frac{R_{2}\times R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}$
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution, e.g. $\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{5}{60}$ leading to a final answer of $12Ω$
> 
> "Show that" requires the formula to be written before substitution — answer alone scores zero

> **[exam-tip]**
> For two resistors in parallel, a useful check is that the combined resistance of two parallel resistors is always less than the resistance of the smaller individual resistor, so your answer must be less than $20Ω$.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 7.1 shows a circuit containing a battery of e.m.f. 12 V and three resistors.

The voltmeter measures the potential difference (p.d.) across the parallel combination of resistors.

R1 has a resistance of 8 ohms, R2 has a resistance of 20 ohms, and R3 has a resistance of 30 ohms.

Calculate the current in resistor R<sub>1</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the current in resistor R<sub>1</sub>:

- List the known quantities

  - Resistance of parallel resistors, $R_{\mathrm{parallel}}=12Ω$
  - Resistance of $R_{1}=8.0Ω$
  - e.m.f. of battery, $E=12V$
- Calculate the total resistance of the circuit:

$R_{\text{total}}=R_{1}+R_{\text{parallel}}$

$R_{\text{total}}=8.0+12=20Ω$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the current in the circuit using $V=E$ (emf of the battery) and $R=R_{\mathrm{total}}$ (total resistance):

$V=IR$ **[1 mark]**

$I=\frac{E}{R_{\text{total}}}=\frac{12}{20}$

$I=$ $0.60\text{A}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct formula for series resistors **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $R_{\text{total}}=R_{1}+R_{\text{parallel}}$ **OR** $8.0+12$
> 
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct rearrangement **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $V=IR$ **OR** $I=\frac{V}{R}$ **OR** $\frac{12}{20}$
> 
> 1 mark for a final answer of $0.60A$
> 
> Full marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you know the rules for current in series and parallel. The current from the battery is the same as the current through R<sub>1</sub>, because R<sub>1</sub> is in the main (series) part of the circuit. This current then splits between R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> at the parallel junction.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 7.1 shows a circuit containing a battery of e.m.f. 12 V and three resistors.

The voltmeter measures the potential difference (p.d.) across the parallel combination of resistors.

R1 has a resistance of 8 ohms, R2 has a resistance of 20 ohms, and R3 has a resistance of 30 ohms.

Explain how the reading on the voltmeter can be used to determine the p.d. across resistor R<sub>1</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Subtract the voltmeter reading from the e.m.f./battery voltage **OR** p.d. across $R_{1}=12-(\text{voltmeter reading})$ **[1 mark]**
> - The sum of the p.d.s across the components in a series circuit equals the e.m.f. of the battery/supply voltage **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept: "$V_{R_{1}}=12-V_{\text{parallel}}$" stated in words or symbols
> 
> Accept: "the voltages in a series circuit add up to the battery voltage" for the second mark
> 
> Do not accept: just "use $V = I R$" — the question specifically asks how the voltmeter reading is used, not how to calculate from scratch

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question tests whether you understand how potential differences are distributed in a series circuit. The key rule is: the sum of the p.d.s across all components in a series circuit equals the e.m.f. of the battery. Since the voltmeter reads the p.d. across the parallel combination, you can find the p.d. across $R_{1}$ by subtraction. Make sure you state both the method (subtraction) and the reasoning (p.d.s in series add up to the e.m.f.) to secure both marks. Many students lose the second mark by simply writing the equation without explaining why it works.

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

A cylindrical metal wire W<sub>1</sub>, of length $L$ and cross-sectional area *A*, has a resistance of 16 Ω.

A second cylindrical wire W<sub>2</sub>, of length $\frac{L}{2}$ and cross-sectional area 2*A*, is made from the same metal.

Determine

(i) the resistance of *W*<sub>*2*</sub>,

resistance of *W*<sub>*2*</sub> = ...........................................................[2]

(ii) the effective resistance of *W*<sub>*1*</sub> and *W*<sub>*2*</sub> when connected in parallel

resistance of parallel pair = ...........................................................[2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To determine the resistance of W<sub>2</sub>:

List the known quantities:

- Resistance of W<sub>1</sub> = 16 Ω

State the relationships between resistance *R* and area, *A *and length, *L*:

- $R\propto L$ **AND** $R\propto\frac{1}{A}$**[1 mark]**

Calculate resistance of W<sub>2</sub>:

- Area of W<sub>2</sub> is 2*A*, therefore *R* decreases by a factor of 2
- Length of W<sub>2</sub> is $\frac{1}{2}L$, therefore *R* decreases by a factor of 2
- Therefore, overall $R=\frac{16}{4}$
- *R*<sub>2</sub> = 4 Ω **[1 mark]**

(ii) To determine the effective resistance when W<sub>1</sub> and W<sub>2</sub> are connected in parallel:

**METHOD 1**

Recall the equation for resistors in parallel:

- $\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}$ [1 mark]

Substitute in values and calculate *R*:

- $\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{5}{16}$
- $R=\frac{16}{5}$
- *R* = 3.2 Ω **[1 mark]**

**METHOD 2**

Recall the equation for two resistors in parallel:

- $R=\frac{R_{1}\times R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in values and calculate R:

- $R=\frac{16\times4}{16+4}$
- *R* = 3.2 Ω **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *If you have two resistors in parallel you can use the equation*$R=\frac{R_{1}\times R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}$*.If there is more than one resistor in parallel then you need t**o use *$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{R_{2}}+...$

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

There is a current of 0.29 A in an electrical circuit.

Calculate the time taken for a charge of 15 C to flow through the electrical circuit.

time = .........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the time taken:

List the known quantities:

- Current, *I *= 0.29 A
- Charge, *C *= 15 C

Recall the equation for current, charge and time:

- $I=\frac{Q}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to make time, *t *the subject:

- $t=\frac{Q}{I}$

Substitute the known quantities into the equation to calculate the time, *t*:

- $t=\frac{15}{0.29}$ **[1 mark]**
- *t *= 51.72 s = 51.72 s (2 s.f.) **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *The first mark is given for the equation in any form.*

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 8.1 shows a power supply of e.m.f. 10.5 V connected in series with a lamp and a heater.

The p.d. across the lamp is 2.1 V and the current in the lamp is 1.5 A.

![may-june-2020-42-q8](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-2-electrical-quantities/assets/085-may-june-2020-42-q8.jpg)

Calculate:

(i) the resistance of the heater

resistance = ......................................................... [2]

(ii) the power of the heater.

power = ......................................................... [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Calculate the resistance of the heater:

List the known quantities:

- e.m.f. of the power supply = 10.5 V
- p.d. across the lamp = 2.1 V
- Current through the circuit, *I *= 1.5 A

Obtain an expression for the potential difference within the series circuit:

- e.m.f. = sum of potential differences across each component in the circuit
- $10.5=2.1+V$* ***[1 mark]**

Calculate the potential difference across the heater, *V*:

- $V=10.5--2.1=8.4V$

Recall the equation for Ohm's Law:

- $R=\frac{V}{I}$

Substitute the potential difference and current into the equation for Ohm's Law to calculate resistance:

- $R=\frac{8.4}{1.5}$
- *R *= 5.6 Ω **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the power of the heater:

List the known quantities:

- Current in the circuit, *I *= 1.5 A
- p.d. in the heater, *V *= 8.4 V

Recall the electrical power equation:

- $P=IV$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the known quantities into the equation and calculate the power, *P*:

- $P=8.4\times1.5$
- *P =* 12.6 W **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Read the question carefully, if it is asking about the heater make sure you use the information related to the heater. *

parts.problemMd:
**Extended Tier Only**

For each complete oscillation of the ball moving between the plates, a charge of 8.5 × 10<sup>–10 </sup>C is transferred from one plate to the other. The frequency of oscillation is 4.0 Hz.

Calculate the current shown on the sensitive ammeter.

current = ..........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate current:

List the known quantities:

- Charge transferred per oscillation, *Q* = 8.510<sup>–10</sup> C
- Frequency of oscillations, *f* = 4.0 Hz

Recall the equation for the period of oscillation:

- $T=\frac{1}{f}$
- $T=\frac{1}{4}=0.25s$

Recall the equation for current:

- $I=\frac{Q}{t}$ **[1 mark]**
- Every 0.25 s cycle, 8.5$\times$10<sup>–10</sup> C of charge is transferred between plates

Calculate the current:

- $I=\frac{8.5\times10^{-10}}{0.25}$**[1 mark]**
- $I=3.4\times10^{-9}$A  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Here, you needed to recognise that, in order to calculate current, you needed to determine the time over which the charge was transferred. Harder exam questions will often require you to combine knowledge from different parts of the course.*

resistance = ...................................................... Ω [3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) On Fig. 10.1, draw circuit symbols to show each meter correctly connected in the circuit:

- To determine resistance, potential difference and current must be measured

![screenshot-2022-10-17-at-15-40-28](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-3-electric-circuits-and-electrical-safety/assets/073-screenshot-2022-10-17-at-15-40-28.png)

- Correct symbol for the voltmeter; **[1 mark]**
- The ammeter is in <u>series</u> and the voltmeter is in <u>parallel</u> with the lamp; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Calculate the resistance of the lamp:

List the known quantities:

- Current, *I* = 0.25 A
- Potential difference, *V* = 4.5 V

Recall Ohm's Law:

- *V* = *I *× *R  ***OR**** **potential difference = current × resistance* ***[1 mark]**

Rearrange Ohm's Law to make resistance the subject:

- $V=I\times R$
- $R=\frac{V}{I}$

Substitute in the known quantities to the rearranged equation:

- $R=\frac{V}{I}$
- $R=\frac{4.5}{0.25}$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the resistance of the lamp:

- *R* = 18 Ω **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *When rearranging the equation to *$V=I\times R$* to make **R** the subject, multiple maths steps occur that will be shown below. *

> *First, we divide both sides of the equation by the term **I **:*

$V=I\times R$

$\frac{V}{I}=\frac{I\times R}{I}$

> *On the right hand side of the equation, the terms for current, **I** , cancel out:*

`V / I = (/ I x R)/(/ I)`

> *This just leaves the right hand side as **R **:*

$\frac{V}{I}=R$

> *For neatness, we will write the equation the other way around so the subject is on the left:*

$R=\frac{V}{I}$

**Extract:**

A circuit diagram showing a 12-volt battery connected in series with resistor R1 and a parallel combination of resistors R2 and R3. A voltmeter is connected across the parallel combination. R1 has a resistance of 8 ohms, R2 has a resistance of 20 ohms, and R3 has a resistance of 30 ohms.

![A circuit diagram showing a 12-volt battery connected in series with resistor R1 and a parallel combination of resistors R2 and R3. A voltmeter is connected across the parallel combination. R1 has a resistance of 8 ohms, R2 has a resistance of 20 ohms, and R3 has a resistance of 30 ohms.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-3-electric-circuits-and-electrical-safety/assets/052-a-circuit-diagram-showing-a-12-volt-battery-conn.png)

**Fig. 7.1**

The voltmeter measures the potential difference (p.d.) across the parallel

combination of resistors.

Show that the combined resistance of R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> is $12Ω$.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the combined resistance of R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub>:

- List the known quantities:

  - Resistance of $R_{2}=20Ω$
  - Resistance of $R_{3}=30Ω$
- Recall the rule for adding resistance in parallel combinations:

$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{R_{2}}+\frac{1}{R_{3}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute in the values and rearrange for $R$:

$\frac{1}{R}=\frac{1}{20}+\frac{1}{30}=\frac{5}{60}$

$R=\frac{60}{5}=12Ω$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for stating the correct formula for parallel resistors, e.g. $\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_{2}} + \frac{1}{R_{3}}$ **OR** $R = \frac{R_{2}\times R_{3}}{R_{2}+R_{3}}$
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution, e.g. $\frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{5}{60}$ leading to a final answer of $12Ω$
> 
> "Show that" requires the formula to be written before substitution — answer alone scores zero

> **[exam-tip]**
> For two resistors in parallel, a useful check is that the combined resistance of two parallel resistors is always less than the resistance of the smaller individual resistor, so your answer must be less than $20Ω$.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 7.1 shows a circuit containing a battery of e.m.f. 12 V and three resistors.

The voltmeter measures the potential difference (p.d.) across the parallel combination of resistors.

R1 has a resistance of 8 ohms, R2 has a resistance of 20 ohms, and R3 has a resistance of 30 ohms.

Calculate the current in resistor R<sub>1</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the current in resistor R<sub>1</sub>:

- List the known quantities

  - Resistance of parallel resistors, $R_{\mathrm{parallel}}=12Ω$
  - Resistance of $R_{1}=8.0Ω$
  - e.m.f. of battery, $E=12V$
- Calculate the total resistance of the circuit:

$R_{\text{total}}=R_{1}+R_{\text{parallel}}$

$R_{\text{total}}=8.0+12=20Ω$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the current in the circuit using $V=E$ (emf of the battery) and $R=R_{\mathrm{total}}$ (total resistance):

$V=IR$ **[1 mark]**

$I=\frac{E}{R_{\text{total}}}=\frac{12}{20}$

$I=$ $0.60\text{A}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct formula for series resistors **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $R_{\text{total}}=R_{1}+R_{\text{parallel}}$ **OR** $8.0+12$
> 
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct rearrangement **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $V=IR$ **OR** $I=\frac{V}{R}$ **OR** $\frac{12}{20}$
> 
> 1 mark for a final answer of $0.60A$
> 
> Full marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you know the rules for current in series and parallel. The current from the battery is the same as the current through R<sub>1</sub>, because R<sub>1</sub> is in the main (series) part of the circuit. This current then splits between R<sub>2</sub> and R<sub>3</sub> at the parallel junction.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 7.1 shows a circuit containing a battery of e.m.f. 12 V and three resistors.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Subtract the voltmeter reading from the e.m.f./battery voltage **OR** p.d. across $R_{1}=12-(\text{voltmeter reading})$ **[1 mark]**
> - The sum of the p.d.s across the components in a series circuit equals the e.m.f. of the battery/supply voltage **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept: "$V_{R_{1}}=12-V_{\text{parallel}}$" stated in words or symbols
> 
> Accept: "the voltages in a series circuit add up to the battery voltage" for the second mark
> 
> Do not accept: just "use $V = I R$" — the question specifically asks how the voltmeter reading is used, not how to calculate from scratch

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question tests whether you understand how potential differences are distributed in a series circuit. The key rule is: the sum of the p.d.s across all components in a series circuit equals the e.m.f. of the battery. Since the voltmeter reads the p.d. across the parallel combination, you can find the p.d. across $R_{1}$ by subtraction. Make sure you state both the method (subtraction) and the reasoning (p.d.s in series add up to the e.m.f.) to secure both marks. Many students lose the second mark by simply writing the equation without explaining why it works.

Iron by its self, however, is a soft magnet and does not become **permanently** magnetised, whereas steel does.*

parts.problemMd: Two metal rods are thought to be permanent magnets. Describe the test you would carry out to confirm that both rods are permanent magnets.
parts.solutionMd:
Describe the test you would carry out to confirm that both rods are permanent magnets:

- Place the ends / poles together (and repeat by rotating the first magnet to face its other pole towards the second magnet); **[1 mark]**
- Repulsion (will be seen in one orientation and attraction in the other); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *There are two types of magnets:*

- *Induced magnets*
- *Permanent magnets*

*Induced magnets are **always** attracted to the magnet that magnetised them. We only see a repulsive force between two permanent magnets when like poles are facing each other. This is caused by the interaction between the magnetic fields*.

![screenshot-2022-10-24-at-10-43-30](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/065-screenshot-2022-10-24-at-10-43-30.png)

> *This only occurs between two permanent magnets, so if we observe this phenomenon, we must have two permanent magnets. *

> *Induced magnets can also magnetise other materials. If a paperclips is magnetised, it can also magnetise other materials, hence why it is possible to pick up a **chain** of paperclips with a single permanent magnet. *

> *The ability to attract materials such as iron is not unique to permanent magnets, so this cannot be used to prove that a magnet is permanent.  *

parts.problemMd:
The output from the generator is connected to a step-down transformer with a turns ratio of $20:1$. The voltage across the primary coil is $240V$.

Calculate the voltage across the secondary coil.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the output voltage of the transformer:

- List the known quantities:

  - Turns ratio of the primary : secondary coil, $\frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}=\frac{20}{1}=20$
  - Voltage across the primary coil, $V_{p}=240V$
- Write down the transformer equation:

$\frac{V_{p}}{V_{s}}=\frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}$ **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange for $V_{s}$ and substitute in the known values:

$V_{s}=V_{p}\times\frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}=\frac{240}{20}$

$V_{s}=$ $12\text{V}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct substitution into the transformer equation,
> 
> - Accept $V_{p} / V_{s} = N_{p} / N_{s}$ **OR** $V_{s} = V_{p} \times N_{s} / N_{p}$ **OR** $240/20$
> 
> 1 mark for a final answer of $12\text{V}$
> 
> Both marks can be scored for the correct answer alone

parts.problemMd:
A student has a model electric railway. The model railway uses a step-down transformer.

The input voltage is 230 V. The transformer has 1710 turns on the input coil and 90 turns on the output coil.

Calculate the output voltage of the transformer.

output voltage = ....................................................... V
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the output voltage of the transformer:

List the known quantities:

- Input voltage, *V*<sub>p</sub> = 230 V
- Number of turns on input coil, *N*<sub>p</sub> = 1710
- Number of turns on output coil, *N*<sub>s</sub> = 90

Recall the transformer equation:

- $\frac{V_{p}}{V_{s}}=\frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation to make the output voltage, *V*<sub>s</sub>, the subject:

- Flip the equation upside down

  - $\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}=\frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}$
- Multiply both sides by *V*<sub>p</sub>

  - $V_{s}=\frac{N_{s}V_{p}}{N_{p}}$

Substitute in the known values to calculate:

- $V_{s}=\frac{90\times230}{1710}$ **[1 mark]**
- *V*<sub>s</sub> = 12 V **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that when stating an equation, you will still get the marks if the equation is given in its rearranged form as long as the rearrangement is correct.*

- p.d. in secondary coil, *V*<sub>s</sub> = 6.0 V
- Number of turns in the primary coil, *N*<sub>p</sub> = 8000

Recall the transformer equation:

- $\frac{N_{s}}{N_{p}}=\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange this for *N*<sub>s</sub>:

- $N_{s}=N_{p}\times\frac{V_{s}}{V_{p}}$

Recall the ideal transformer equation:

- $I_{p}V_{p}=I_{s}V_{s}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange this for primary current:

- $I_{p}=\frac{I_{s}V_{s}}{V_{p}}$

Substitute the known quantities:

- $I_{p}=\frac{2.0\times6.0}{240}$

> *This equation comes from the fact that, because the transformer is 100% efficient, the electrical power in the primary coil is equal to the electrical power in the secondary coil. parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Explain why the voltage of the supply to the primary coil of a transformer must be alternating.
parts.solutionMd:
The voltage of the supply to the primary coil of a transformer must be alternating because:

- It must produce an alternating / changing magnetic field; **[1 mark]**
- So that a current / voltage is induced (continuously) in the <u>secondary</u> coil / circuit; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *A d.c. voltage will not enable a transformer to work as the induced magnetic field must be continuously changing direction in order to induce a voltage in the secondary coil.*

> *As a sequence of events:*

- *An **alternating current** is supplied to the **primary coil*
- *The **current** is continually **changing direction*

  - *This means it will produce a **changing magnetic field** around the primary coil*

- *The iron core is **easily magnetised**, so the changing magnetic field passes through it*
- *As a result, there is now a **changing magnetic field** inside the **secondary coil*

  - *This changing field **cuts** through the secondary coil and **induces a potential difference*

- *As the magnetic field is continually changing the potential difference induced will be **alternating*

  - *The alternating potential difference will have the **same frequency** as the alternating current supplied to the primary coil*

- *If the secondary coil is part of a **complete circuit** it will cause an **alternating current** to flow*

> *The structure of a transformer is:*

![transformer-commentary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/047-transformer-commentary.png)

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Fig. 10.1 shows a transformer.

![q10b-](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/4-electricity-and-magnetism/4-4-electromagnetic-effects/assets/048-q10b.png)

There are 8000 turns in the primary coil of the transformer. The primary coil is connected to a 240 V mains supply. A 6.0 V lamp connected to the secondary coil operates at full brightness.

(i) Calculate the number of turns in the secondary coil

number of turns = ...........................................................[2]

(ii) The current in the lamp is 2.0A. The transformer operates with 100% efficiency.

Calculate the current in the primary circuit.

current = ...........................................................[2]

(iii) The secondary circuit contains a 6.0 A fuse.

Calculate the maximum number of lamps, identical to the lamp in **(ii)**, that can be connected in parallel in the secondary circuit without blowing the fuse.

number of lamps = ...........................................................[1]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the number of turns in the secondary coil

List the known quantities:

- Number of turns in the primary coil, *N*<sub>p</sub> = 8000
- Voltage in the primary coil, *V*<sub>p</sub> = 240 V
- Voltage in the secondary coil, *V*<sub>s</sub> = 6.0 V

Recall the equation linking primary and secondary numbers of coils and the voltage:

- $\frac{N_{p}}{N_{s}}=\frac{V_{p}}{V_{s}}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for *N*<sub>s</sub>, substitute in values and calculate *N*<sub>s</sub>:

- $N_{s}=\frac{N_{p}\times V_{s}}{V_{p}}=\frac{8000\times6.0}{240}$
- *N*<sub>s</sub> = 200 turns **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the current in the primary circuit:

List the known quantities:

- Voltage in the primary coil, *V*<sub>p</sub> = 240 V
- Voltage in the secondary coil, *V*<sub>s</sub> = 6.0 V
- Current in the secondary circuit,* I*<sub>s</sub> = 2.0 A

Recall the equation linking current and voltage in the primary and secondary coils:

- $I_{p}V_{p}=I_{s}V_{s}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for *I*<sub>p</sub>, substitute in known values and calculate *I*<sub>p</sub>:

- $I_{p}=\frac{I_{s}\times V_{s}}{V_{p}}=\frac{2.0\times6.0}{240}$
- *I*<sub>p </sub>= 0.050 A **[1 mark]**

(iii) To calculate the maximum number of lamps that can be connected in parallel in the secondary circuit:

List the known quantities:

- Current in the secondary circuit,* I*<sub>s</sub> = 2.0 A
- Fuse rating = 6.0 A

Divide the maximum current which can flow through the fuse by current in one lamp:

- Since current adds in parallel: $\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{lamps}=\frac{\mathrm{fuse} \mathrm{rating}}{\mathrm{current} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{one} \mathrm{lamp}}=\frac{6.0}{2.0}$
- Therefore the maximum number of lamps is 3; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Giving the rearranged and substituted values, *$N_{s}=\frac{8000\times6.0}{240}$*is acceptable for the first mark in part (i).*

> *Giving the rearranged and substituted values, *$I_{p}=\frac{2.0\times6.0}{240}$*is acceptable for the first mark in part (ii).*

parts.problemMd:
A radioactive sample is placed close to a detector. The radioactive isotope in the sample has a long half-life. The detector records a count rate of 597 counts/s.

|---|---|
| a sheet of paper | 602 |
| a piece of thin aluminium | 598 |
| a piece of thin lead | 510 |

** Fig. 11.2**

parts.solutionMd:
Explain whether any α-particles, β-particles or γ-rays are emitted by the radioactive sample:

Determine whether α-particles are emitted:

- α-particles are <u>not</u> emitted because the count rate increases with paper (and paper would stop alpha particles reaching the detector); **[1 mark]**

Determine whether β-particles are emitted:

- β-particles are <u>not</u> emitted because the count rate increases with aluminium (and aluminium would stop beta particles reaching the detector); **[1 mark]**

Determine whether γ-rays are emitted:

- γ-rays <u>are emitted</u> because the count rate decreases with lead (and only lead would stop the gamma rays reaching the detector); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In any measurement, there will be a slight difference in the values recorded for any repeated reading. With radioactivity, you also have to account for background radiation, which is typically between 2 and 10 counts per second. So in this question, the slight differences between the count rate measurements, 597, 598 and 602 counts/s, can all be accounted for by variation due to repeat readings or background radiation. In other words, we can accept these values as being the same. When looking for a significant change, the values should be different by >5%.*

parts.problemMd:
Polonium-210 has a half-life of 140 days. A sample of polonium-210 has 8.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> atoms. Calculate the number of polonium-210 atoms remaining in the sample after 280 days.

number of atoms = ......................................................
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the number of polonium-210 atoms remaining in the sample after 280 days:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of polonium-210 = 140 days
- Number of atoms = 8.0 × 10<sup>10</sup>
- Time passed = 280 days

Determine the number of half-lives that pass in 280 days:

- 280 days have passed

  - The half-life of polonium-210 is 140 days
- $140\mathrm{days}\times2=280\mathrm{days}$
- 280 days is <u>two half-lives</u> (of polonium-210); **[1 mark]**

Recall the definition of half-life:

- Half-life is the time taken for half the nuclei of an isotope in a sample to decay

  - Every half-life, the number of polonium nuclei halves

Calculate the number of nuclei after 280 days:

- Two half-lives pass, so the number of atoms, 8.0 × 10<sup>10</sup>, halves twice
- $\frac{8.0\times10^{10}}{2}=4.0\times10^{10}$
- $\frac{4.0\times10^{10}}{2}=2.0\times10^{10}$
- 2.0 × 10<sup>10</sup> atoms of polonium-210 remain; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *The number of nuclei halves after a half-life has passed, but the radioactivity also halves. Activity or count rate of a source is much easier to measure than counting 80 billion atoms, so experiments tend to use use count rate to determine half-life!*

parts.problemMd:
An isotope of barium–137 has a half-life of 3 minutes.

A radioactive source contains 36 mg of this isotope.

Calculate the mass of the isotope that remains in the source after 9 minutes.

mass of the isotope remaining = .................................................. mg
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the mass of the isotope that remains in the source after 9 minutes

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of barium–137 = 3 minutes
- Mass of barium–137 = 36 mg
- Time of calculating the mass remaining = 9 minutes

Determine the number of half-lives in 9 minutes:

- The half life of the source is the time taken for half the nuclei of that isotope to decay
- $number of half-lives=\frac{9}{3}=3$ ** [1 mark]**

Calculate the mass remaining after 9 minutes:

- This means that the mass is halved **three times**
- $massremaining=\frac{36}{2^{3}}=\frac{36}{8}$ ** [1 mark]**
- mass remaining = 4.5 mg** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *3 half-lives means that the mass has been halved **three** times. If the original mass is 36 mg then:*

- *After 1 half-life, this is *$\frac{36}{2}=18mg$
- *After 2 half-lives this is *$\frac{18}{2}=9mg$
- *After 3 half-lives, this is *$\frac{9}{2}=4.5mg$

> *A quicker way to do this, is use the equation *$\frac{original mass}{2^{number of half-lives}}$

- Initial number of radon nuclei = 6.4 × 10<sup>6</sup>

Determine the number of half-lives that have passed:

- 7.6 days is equal to 2 half-lives; **[1 mark]**

- $number ofαparticlesemitted=initial number of radon nuclei-finalnumberofradonnuclei$

- number of  α-particles emitted = 4.8 × 10<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A radioactive nucleus of uranium-235 decays to a nucleus of thorium and emits an α-particle.

The thorium produced by the decay in (a) is also radioactive and has a half-life of 26 hours.

At a certain time, a pure sample of this isotope initially contains 4.8 × 10<sup>9</sup> atoms.

Calculate the number of atoms of this sample that decay in the following 52 hours.

number = ...........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the number of atoms of the sample that decay in the following 52 hours:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of thorium =  26 hours
- Number of atoms in the sample = 4.8 × 10<sup>9</sup> atoms
- Time elapsed = 52 hours

Determine the number of half lives that have passed:

- $number of half-lives=\frac{timeelapsed}{half-life}=\frac{52}{26}$
- Therefore 2 half lives have passed; **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of thorium atoms remaining after 52 hours:

- The number of thorium atoms will halve and then will halve again
- Therefore the number of thorium atoms will decrease by a factor of 4
- $thoriumatomsremaining=\frac{4.8\times10^{9}}{4}$
- Thorium atoms remaining = 1.2 × 10<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**

Determine the number of atoms that have decayed:

- $n u m b e r d e c a y e d = i n i t i a l n u m b e r - n u m b e r r e m a i n i n g = ( 4.8 \times 10^{9} ) - ( 1.2 \times 10^{9} )$
- Number of thorium atoms which have decayed = 3.6 × 10<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 6.0 years.

A sample of this isotope has a mass of 12 mg.

Calculate the mass of this isotope that remains in the sample after 18 years.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate mass remaining:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life, *T*<sub>*1/2*</sub>* *= 6.0 years
- Initial mass, *m*<sub>*0*</sub>* *= 12 mg
- Time passed, *t* = 18 years

Calculate the number of half-lives that have passed:

- $numberofhalflives=\frac{timepassed}{half-life}$
- $numberofhalflives=\frac{18}{6}=3halflives$** [1 mark]**

Calculate the factor by which the mass reduces:

- The mass halves three times
- $\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{8}$

Calculate the new mass, *m*:

- $m=\frac{1}{8}\times m_{0}$ **[1 mark]**
- $m=\frac{1}{8}\times12$
- $m=1.5\mathrm{mg}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Students often find this question tricky. Just remember that for every half-life, the radioactive mass halves (it’s in the name ‘half-life’). In 18 years, three half-lives pass so halve the mass three times. You can either halve the mass three times separately, or you can divide it by 8 and do it all in one.*

**Extended tier only**

A radiation detector in a laboratory records a reading of 10 counts/min. There are no radioactive samples in the laboratory.

(i) Explain why the radiation detector records a reading and suggest a possible source.

[2]

(ii) Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5700 years. There are atoms of carbon-14 in all living organisms.

An archaeologist digs up some ancient wood. In the same laboratory as in **(b)(i)**, a sample of this ancient wood gives a reading of 20 counts/min. An equivalent sample of living wood gives a reading of 80 counts/min. It is suggested that the age of the ancient sample is 11 400 years.

Do a calculation to check whether this suggestion is correct.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) Explain why the radiation detector records a reading and suggest a possible source:

- The radiation detector is recording background radiation; **[1 mark]**

Any **one **from:

Sources of background radiation include:

- Rocks; **[1 mark]**
- Ground; **[1 mark]**
- Buildings; **[1 mark]**
- Food; **[1 mark]**
- Space; **[1 mark]**
- Weapons testing; **[1 mark]**
- Nuclear accidents; **[1 mark]**
- Nuclear waste; **[1 mark]**
- Sun; **[1 mark]**
- Air; **[1 mark]**
- Radon; **[1 mark]**
- Argon; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Check whether the suggestion is correct:

List the known quantities:

- Half-life of carbon-14 = 5700 years
- Background radiation = 10 counts/min
- Sample 1 = 20 counts/min
- Sample 2 = 80 counts/min
- Suggested age of sample = 11 400 years

Remove the background count from the activity for samples 1 and 2:

- Sample 1: $20-10=10$ counts/min

**   AND**

- Sample 2: $80-10=70$ counts/min **[1 mark]**

Calculate the estimated number of half-lives in the sample:

- $Estimatednumberofhalflives=\frac{11400}{5700}=2$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the change in the activity between the samples:

- $Changeinactivity=\frac{activity of sample2}{activity of sample1}$
- $Changeinactivity=\frac{70}{10}=7$
- Sample 2 is 7 times as active as sample 1

Calculate the actual number of half-lives in the sample:

- After 1 half-life the activity is half as much

  - $1\times2=2$
- After 2 half-lives the activity is $\frac{1}{4}$ as much

  - $2\times2=4$
- After 3 half-lives the activity is $\frac{1}{8}$ as much

  - $4\times2=8$
- Hence, the number of half-lives of the sample is:

  - > 2 **OR **just less than 3; **[1 mark]**

Identify whether the suggestion is correct:

- There are more than 2 half-lives in the sample
- So the age of the sample must be > 11 400 years;
- **So the suggestion is incorrect; [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *With each half-life, the activity of the sample decreases by a further ½. The relationship between activity and time is exponential, as shown on the graph.*

parts.solutionMd:
Recall the definition of half-life:

- The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time taken for the count rate to halve

Calculate half the initial count rate:

- *initial count rate *= 1246 counts per second
- Half of this is 1246 ÷ 2 = 623 counts per second

Estimate the time at which count rate is 623 counts per second:

- From the table, count rate is 621 counts per second after 2.5 minutes have passed

Estimate the half-life:

- half-life = 2.5 minutes **[1 mark] **

> *You can use multiple values to double check that your estimate of half-life is correct. For example, after 1 minute has passed, the count rate of the sample is 941 counts per second. Half of this is 470.5 counts per second.*

> *While we do not have this exact value on the table, 468 counts per second is on the table and is very close to 470.5 counts per second (and we are only **estimating** the half-life). The count rate is 468 counts per second after 3.5 minutes have passed, so from 1 minute to 3.5 minutes the count rate has halved, thus **confirming** that our half-life is 2.5 minutes.*

parts.problemMd:
The innermost planets of the solar system are rocky compared to the outer planets.

(i) State the source of the heavier elements making up the inner planets.

[1]

(ii) State the name of the process which led to the formation of the inner planets and explain their formation.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) The source of the heavier elements is:

- A supernova (explosion); **[1 mark]**

**    **

(ii) The process which formed the inner planets:

- Is called the <u>accretion model</u> of the solar system; **[1 mark]**

**Any four from:**

- Dust / a disc cloud of matter (left from the formation of the Sun); **[1 mark]**
- Contained elements created in a <u>supernova</u>; **[1 mark]**
- <u>Gravity caused the disc to spin / rotate</u> around the Sun; **[1 mark]**
- <u>Gravitational attraction / gravity</u> caused the dust / (small) particles to <u>join / clump together</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Forming an <u>accretion disc</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Near the Sun the <u>temperature was high</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore the inner planets are made of materials with <u>high melting points</u> (such as metals); **[1 mark]**

**An example of an answer which would score five marks is:**

- The accretion model **[1 mark] **of the solar system.
- This says that the dust left over after the Sun formed **[1 mark] **contained many heavy elements formed in a supernova explosion **[1 mark].**
- First the dust made a disc which rotated around the Sun due to gravity **[1 mark]. **
- Slowly the dust started to clump together due to gravitational attraction between the particles **[1 mark]. **
- The inner planets are rocky because the temperature near the sun meant that only elements with high melting points existed as solids **[1 mark].**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

**Extended tier only**

Use data from the graph to calculate

(i) The distance travelled by Jupiter in one orbit.

distance = ............................... million km [3]

(ii) The time taken for Jupiter to complete one orbit, giving your answer in days.

orbital period = ................................ days [3]
parts.solutionMd:
(i) To calculate the distance travelled in one orbit:

List the known quantities:

- Radius of orbit, *r*  = 800 million km (from the graph) **[1 mark]**

![file-000-34](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/6-space-physics/6-1-earth-and-the-solar-system/assets/011-file-000-34.png)

Recall the equation for the circumference of a circle:

- $c=2πr$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute the radius and calculate:

- $c=2\timesπ\times800\mathrm{million}$
- $c=5027\mathrm{million}$

Round the answer to two significant figure and write the units

- Distance travelled by Jupiter in one full orbit = 5 000 million km **[1 mark]**

(ii) To calculate the time taken to complete one orbit:

List the known quantities:

- Distance travelled in one orbit, d = 5 000 million km (from part (i))
- Orbital speed, *s* = 13 km/s (from the graph) ![file-000-35](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/3b2ce8da700b80f51700fb34fc721c90d6654d6b/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-physics-23/6-space-physics/6-1-earth-and-the-solar-system/assets/012-file-000-35.png)

Use the equation linking speed, distance and time:

- $speed=\frac{distance}{time}$ **OR**** **$s=\frac{d}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange to make time the subject:

- ** **$t=\frac{d}{s}$

Substitute the values and calculate to get a time in seconds:

- Leave the distance in km as the orbital speed is given in km/s
- $t=\frac{5000000000}{13}$
- $t=384.6\mathrm{million} \mathrm{seconds}$ **[1 mark]**

To convert seconds to days divide by (seconds × minutes × hours):

- $t = \frac{384 600 000}{( 60 \times 60 \times 24 )} = 4451$

Round the answer to two significant figures:

- Orbital period of Jupiter = 4500 days **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *For part (ii) if you didn't spot that you could use the equation for speed, you may have used the equation for orbital speed, in which case your calculation should look like this:*

> *Recall the equation relating orbital speed, radius and orbital period, **T **:*

> $v=\frac{2πr}{T}$* [1 mark]*

> *Rearrange to make T the subject:*

- $T=\frac{2πr}{v}$* *

> *Substitute the values and calculate:*

- $T=\frac{2\timesπ\times800000000}{13}=387000000seconds$*[1 mark]*

> *Convert seconds to days:*

- $T = \frac{387 000 000}{( 60 \times 60 \times 24 )} = 4478 = 4500 days$*[1 mark]*

> *Hopefully you are getting confident with standard form. In that case you should be writing 5000 million = 5000 × 10*<sup>*6*</sup>*, for example, which will make your calculations neater and easier to follow. *

> *If you aren't confident with standard form yet you can get away without using it at GCSE, but we do recommend you try as you will really need it if you continue on to A-level sciences or maths.*

parts.problemMd:
The speed of light is $3.0\times10^{8}m/s$.

Calculate the distance, in metres, of one light-year.

Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the distance of one light-year:

- List the known quantities:

  - Speed of light, $v=3.0\times10^{8}m/s$
  - Time, $t=1\mathrm{year}$
- Calculate the number of seconds in one year

$1 \text{year} = 365 \times 24 \times 3600 = 3 . 15 \times 10^{7} \text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the known quantities into $d = v \times t$:

$d = ( 3.0 \times 10^{8} ) \times ( 3.15 \times 10^{7} )$ **[1 mark]**

$d=$ $9.5\times10^{15}\text{m}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly converting 1 year to seconds
> 
> - Accept 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s or 3.16 × 10<sup>7</sup> s (using 365.25 days)
> - Do not accept if days, hours or minutes are not all converted
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $d=vt$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 9.5 × 10<sup>15</sup> m
> 
> - Must be given to 2 s.f. as stated in the question

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating large distances in astronomy, always convert time into seconds first before multiplying by the speed of light. A common error is to forget one of the conversion steps (days → hours → minutes → seconds), giving an answer that is many orders of magnitude too small.

$t=\frac{d}{v}$

$t=\frac{4.0\times10^{16}}{3.0\times10^{8}}$

$t=1.33\times10^{8}\text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

- Convert to years:

$t=\frac{1.33\times10^{8}}{3.15\times10^{7}}$ **[1 mark]**

$t=$ $4.2\text{years}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct substitution into $t = d / v$ **OR** correct time in seconds
> 
> - Accept 1.3 × 10<sup>8</sup> s or 1.33 × 10<sup>8</sup> s
> 
> 1 mark for correct conversion to years
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of 4.2 years

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question tests your ability to work with very large numbers in standard form. Remember to convert your final answer into the units asked for — here the question asks for the time 'in years', so you must convert from seconds back to years using the same conversion factor from part (b).

Table 10.1 shows the orbital radius and orbital period for three planets in the Solar System.

**Table 10.1**

| Planet | Average orbital radius / × 10<sup>6</sup> km | Orbital period / Earth years |
|---|---|---|
| Mercury | 57.9 | 0.24 |
| Earth | 150 | 1.00 |
| Jupiter | 778 | 11.86 |

The orbit of Earth is approximately circular.

Calculate the average orbital speed of the Earth.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average orbital speed of the Earth:

- List the known quantities:

  - Orbital radius of Earth, $r=150\times10^{6}\text{km}$
  - Orbital period of Earth, $T=1.00\mathrm{year}$
- Convert the orbital radius to metres:

$r=150\times10^{6}\times10^{3}=150\times10^{9}\text{m}$

- Convert the orbital period to seconds:

$T=365\times24\times3600=3.15\times10^{7}\text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the orbital speed:

$v=\frac{2πr}{T}$ **[1 mark]**

$v = \frac{2 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 150 \times 10^{9} )}{3.15 \times 10^{7} }$

$v = 3 . 0 \times 10^{4}  \text{m/s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct conversion of time to seconds
> 
> - Accept $365\times24\times3600$ **OR** $3.15\times10^{7}\text{s}$
> 
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $v=2πr/T$ **OR** $( 2 \mathrm{\pi } \times 150 \times 10^{6} ) \div ( 365 \times 24 \times 3600 )$ **OR** $9.42\times10^{11}/3.15\times10^{7}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $3.0\times10^{4}\text{m/s}$
> 
> - Accept: use of $T = 3 . 2 \times 10^{7}  \text{s}$ giving $v = 2 . 9 \times 10^{4}  \text{m/s}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> A very common mistake is to use the radius instead of the circumference — remember, the planet travels the full circumference in one orbital period, not just one radius.

parts.problemMd:
A galaxy is at a distance of $9 . 0 \times 10^{7}$ light-years from the Earth. The current value of the Hubble constant is $2.2\times10^{-18}$ per second.

Calculate the speed at which this galaxy is moving away from the Earth.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the speed at which this galaxy is moving away from the Earth:

- List the known quantities:

  - Distance of galaxy from Earth, $d=9.0\times10^{7}$ light-years
  - Hubble constant, $H_{0}=2.2\times10^{-18}$ per second
- Recall the value of a light-year and convert the distance to metres:

1 light-year = $9.5\times10^{15}m$ **[1 mark]**

$d = ( 9.0 \times 10^{7} ) \times ( 9.5 \times 10^{15} )$

$d=8.55\times10^{23}\text{m}$

- Apply Hubble's law to calculate speed:

$v=H_{0}d$ **[1 mark]**

$v = ( 2.2 \times 10^{- 18} ) \times ( 8.55 \times 10^{23} )$

$v=1881000$

$v=$ $1.9\times10^{6}\text{m/s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for stating 1 light-year = $9.5\times10^{15}m$ **OR** correct conversion to metres
> 
> - Accept $9 . 0 \times 10^{7} \times 9 . 5 \times 10^{15}$ **OR** $8 . 55 \times 10^{23}  \text{m}$
> 
> 1 mark for correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $v=H_{0}d$ **OR** $2 . 2 \times 10^{-18} \times 8 . 55 \times 10^{23}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $1.9\times10^{6}\text{m/s}$
> 
> - Accept: $1880\text{km/s}$ or $1.88\times10^{6}\text{m/s}$ or $1900\text{km/s}$ or $1.9\times10^{3}\text{km/s}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sometimes you may be given the values of a light year ($9.5\times10^{15}m$) and the Hubble constant ($2.2\times10^{-18}$ per second) in a question, but not always. If you are taking the extended paper, you must learn them as you could be expected to recall either value.

parts.solutionMd:
To estimate the missing masses by referring to the data:

**Method 1 - Using mass and surface gravity:**

(i) Mercury:

- The <u>diameter is approximately one third</u> that of Earth;** [1 mark]**
- If the <u>mass was the same</u> the gravitational field strength would be <u>much larger</u> / approximately nine times as large; **[1 mark]**
- However gravitational field strength is <u>approximately one third</u> that of Earth, suggesting mass is much <u>smaller</u>; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Venus:

- However gravitational field strength is <u>less than one third</u> that of Earth, suggesting mass is <u>much smaller</u>;** [1 mark]**

**Method 2 - Using density and diameter:**

(i) Mercury:

- The <u>density is very similar </u>to Earth’s;** [1 mark]**
- The <u>diameter is approximately one third</u> that of Earth, so the volume is much smaller;** [1 mark]**
- Therefore, the mass is much <u>smaller</u> than Earth’s; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Venus:

- The density is similar / slightly smaller than Earth’s;** [1 mark]**
- The <u>diameter is similar / slightly smaller</u> as Earth, so the volume is similar / slightly smaller;** [1 mark]**
- Therefore, the mass is <u>very similar / slightly smaller</u> than Earth’s;; **[1 mark]**

(iii) Mars:

- The density is much <u>smaller</u> than Earth’s;** [1 mark]**
- The <u>diameter is approximately half</u> that of Earth, so the volume is much smaller; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the mass is <u>much smaller </u>than Earth’s;** [1 mark]**

> *A question like this, where you must refer to the data, don’t be tempted to guess, or write down information you can remember. You need to work through it step by step and make it clear how the data supports your conclusion.*

> *There are two different ways that you can think about this. The first uses surface gravity and diameter. The second uses density and diameter. Density is defined as density = mass / volume, so mass = density × volume. And because planets are (roughly) spherical, volume depends on diameter*<sup>*3*</sup>*. Therefore, mass depends on density × diameter*<sup>*3*</sup>*  (which means even a small change in diameter can make a big difference to mass).*

> *For Mercury and Venus, the densities are quite similar to Earth’s, so diameter (and therefore volume) is the main factor affecting mass. For Mars, both a smaller diameter and a lower density support the conclusion that its mass is much smaller than Earth’s.*

Fig. 1 shows Jupiter and the orbits of two of its moons, Ganymede and Europa. The positions of the two moons are marked for various dates. The radius of Europa's orbit is 671 000 km. The radius of Ganymede's orbit is 1 070 000 km.

**Extended tier only**

Describe and explain how the distance between Europa and Ganymede changes during three orbits of Europa.
parts.solutionMd:
Describe how the distance between Europa and Ganymede changes during three orbits of Europa:

*Data from the diagram:*

**Any two from:**

- Smallest separation on 4 / 20th June **AND** distance = 399 000 km;** [1 mark]**
- Largest separation on 12 / 28th June **AND **distance = 1 741 000 km; **[1 mark]**
- Separation increases after 4th June; **[1 mark]**

*Description:*

**Any one from:**

- Distance between moons increases and then decreases as they orbit; **[1 mark]**
- Distance increases from a minimum on 4th June to a maximum on 12th June, back to a minimum on 20th June and maximum on 28th June; **[1 mark]**
- Distance change is not linear; **[1 mark]**

*Explanation:*

**Any two from:**

- Europa is closer (to Jupiter) / Ganymede is further (from Jupiter); **[1 mark]**
- Europa moves faster / Ganymede moves more slowly; **[1 mark]**
- Europa has a shorter orbital period **/ **Ganymede has a longer orbital speed; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *There are more marks available for using data (quantitative description) than 'wordy' observation (qualitative description) because, as scientists, we must learn to rely on data to form our conclusions.*

parts.problemMd: Explain the term *galactic redshift*.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain the term *galactic redshift*:

- An<u> increase</u> in the observed <u>wavelength</u> of <u>light</u> emitted from <u>distant galaxies</u>; **[1 mark]**
- When <u>compared</u> to the wavelength of similar light <u>on Earth</u>;** [1 mark]**
- Galactic redshift is evidence that the Universe is <u>expanding</u>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

Explain why galactic redshift is considered as evidence supporting the Big Bang theory:

- If the Universe is expanding, then it must have been closer together in the past; **[1 mark]**
- The expansion of the Universe can be extrapolated back to its point of origin (known as the Big Bang); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

> *If the Universe is expanding at a measurable rate, then it makes sense that if we were able to rewind this expansion we would find a point in time where the Universe existed at a single point in time and space (called a singularity). This is the point at which the Big Bang is thought to have occurred. By doing this, scientists have been able to estimate the age of the Universe to be about 13.7 billion years old.*

**Extended tier only**

The Hubble constant is estimated to be 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> per second.

Calculate the age of the Universe in years.

1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the age of the universe in years.

List the known quantities:

- The Hubble constant, *H*<sub>0</sub> = 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> per second
- 1 year = 3.15 × 10<sup>7</sup> s
- Age of the universe = $\frac{1}{H_{0}}$ (from part b)

Substitute the values into the age of the universe equation:

- $AgeoftheUniverse=\frac{1}{2.2\times10^{-18}}$**[1 mark]**
- $AgeoftheUniverse=4.54\times10^{17}s$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the age from seconds into years:

- $AgeoftheUniverse=\frac{4.54\times10^{17}}{3.15\times10^{7}}$ **[1 mark]**
- $AgeoftheUniverse=1.4\times10^{10}\mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *Only high mass stars become red supergiants, explode as a supernova and then go on to become either a neutron star or a black hole.*

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

Galaxy A is 150 000 × 10<sup>9 </sup>m away.

Calculate its recession velocity.

Hubble constant = 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> per second.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the recession velocity of Galaxy A

List the known quantities:

- Distance, *d* = 150 000 × 10<sup>9 </sup>m
- Hubble constant = 2.2 × 10<sup>–18</sup> per second

State the equation linking distance and recession velocity:

- $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange for recession velocity, *v*:

- $v=H_{0}d$ **[1 mark]**

Substitute in the values:

- $v = ( 2.2 \times 10^{- 18} ) \times ( 150 000 \times 10^{9} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $v=3.3\times10^{-4}m/s$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problemMd:

A galaxy C is twice as far as galaxy A.

Determine the recession velocity of galaxy C.
parts.solutionMd:
Determine the recession velocity of galaxy C

List the known quantities:

- Recession velocity of Galaxy A = 3.3 × 10<sup>–4</sup> m/s (from part c)

Calculate the recession velocity of galaxy C:

- Galaxy C velocity = 2 × (3.3 × 10<sup>–4</sup>) **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extended tier only**

The speed of electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s

Show that one light-year is equal to 9.5 × 10<sup>15</sup> m.
parts.solutionMd:
List the known quantities:

- Speed of light, *c* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s
- Time,* t* = 1 year

Calculate the time for 1 year in seconds:

- *t* = 1 year = 365 × 24 × 60 × 60 = 3.1536 × 10<sup>7</sup> s
- *t* = 3.1536 × 10<sup>7</sup> s **[1 mark] **

State the equation linking speed, distance, and time:

- $v=\frac{s}{t}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the equation for distance and calculate:

- $s=vt$
- $s = 1 \text{light} \text{year} = ( 3.0 \times 10^{8} ) \times ( 3.1536 \times 10^{7} )$ **[1 mark]**
- $s=9.46\times10^{15}=9.5\times10^{15}m$

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *1 light year is defined as the distance travelled in space by light in one year.*

> *If the speed of light is given in m/s, this means to get the distance in m, we need the time to be in s. The time we are given in 1 year, but this needs to be converted.*

parts.problemMd:
Table 10.1 shows the orbital radius and orbital period for three planets in the Solar System.

**Table 10.1**

| Planet | Average orbital radius / × 10<sup>6</sup> km | Orbital period / Earth years |
|---|---|---|
| Mercury | 57.9 | 0.24 |
| Earth | 150 | 1.00 |
| Jupiter | 778 | 11.86 |

The orbit of Earth is approximately circular.

Calculate the average orbital speed of the Earth.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average orbital speed of the Earth:

- List the known quantities:

  - Orbital radius of Earth, $r=150\times10^{6}\text{km}$
  - Orbital period of Earth, $T=1.00\mathrm{year}$
- Convert the orbital radius to metres:

$r=150\times10^{6}\times10^{3}=150\times10^{9}\text{m}$

- Convert the orbital period to seconds:

$T=365\times24\times3600=3.15\times10^{7}\text{s}$ **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the orbital speed:

$v=\frac{2πr}{T}$ **[1 mark]**

$v = \frac{2 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 150 \times 10^{9} )}{3.15 \times 10^{7} }$

$v = 3 . 0 \times 10^{4}  \text{m/s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct conversion of time to seconds
> 
> - Accept $365\times24\times3600$ **OR** $3.15\times10^{7}\text{s}$
> 
> 1 mark for the correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $v=2πr/T$ **OR** $( 2 \mathrm{\pi } \times 150 \times 10^{6} ) \div ( 365 \times 24 \times 3600 )$ **OR** $9.42\times10^{11}/3.15\times10^{7}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $3.0\times10^{4}\text{m/s}$
> 
> - Accept: use of $T = 3 . 2 \times 10^{7}  \text{s}$ giving $v = 2 . 9 \times 10^{4}  \text{m/s}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> A very common mistake is to use the radius instead of the circumference — remember, the planet travels the full circumference in one orbital period, not just one radius.

> You can verify the relationship from the data: Mercury is closest to the Sun and orbits fastest (largest circumference-to-period ratio), while Jupiter is furthest and orbits slowest. The explanation links to gravitational field strength — further from the Sun, the gravitational field is weaker, so the gravitational pull on the planet is smaller. A weaker pull means the planet needs a lower speed to remain in a stable orbit; if it moved too fast, it would spiral outwards.
> 
> Make sure you link the weaker gravitational field to the effect on orbital speed — simply saying "less gravity" without explaining why this leads to a lower speed will not earn the second mark.

parts.problemMd:
A galaxy is at a distance of $9 . 0 \times 10^{7}$ light-years from the Earth. The current value of the Hubble constant is $2.2\times10^{-18}$ per second.

Calculate the speed at which this galaxy is moving away from the Earth.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the speed at which this galaxy is moving away from the Earth:

- List the known quantities:

  - Distance of galaxy from Earth, $d=9.0\times10^{7}$ light-years
  - Hubble constant, $H_{0}=2.2\times10^{-18}$ per second
- Recall the value of a light-year and convert the distance to metres:

1 light-year = $9.5\times10^{15}m$ **[1 mark]**

$d = ( 9.0 \times 10^{7} ) \times ( 9.5 \times 10^{15} )$

$d=8.55\times10^{23}\text{m}$

- Apply Hubble's law to calculate speed:

$v=H_{0}d$ **[1 mark]**

$v = ( 2.2 \times 10^{- 18} ) \times ( 8.55 \times 10^{23} )$

$v=1881000$

$v=$ $1.9\times10^{6}\text{m/s}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for stating 1 light-year = $9.5\times10^{15}m$ **OR** correct conversion to metres
> 
> - Accept $9 . 0 \times 10^{7} \times 9 . 5 \times 10^{15}$ **OR** $8 . 55 \times 10^{23}  \text{m}$
> 
> 1 mark for correct equation **OR** correct substitution
> 
> - Accept $v=H_{0}d$ **OR** $2 . 2 \times 10^{-18} \times 8 . 55 \times 10^{23}$
> 
> 1 mark for a correct final answer of $1.9\times10^{6}\text{m/s}$
> 
> - Accept: $1880\text{km/s}$ or $1.88\times10^{6}\text{m/s}$ or $1900\text{km/s}$ or $1.9\times10^{3}\text{km/s}$

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sometimes you may be given the values of a light year ($9.5\times10^{15}m$) and the Hubble constant ($2.2\times10^{-18}$ per second) in a question, but not always. If you are taking the extended paper, you must learn them as you could be expected to recall either value.

parts.problemMd:

Calculate the distance of 50 light-years in metres.

*Speed of light* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s.
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the distance of 50 light-years

List the known quantities:

- Distance = 50 light-years
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s

State the equation linking speed, distance and time:

- $speed=\frac{distance}{time}\Rightarrow distance=speed\times time$ **[1 mark]**

Convert 1 year into seconds:

- $1year=365\times24\times60\times60=31536000s$ **[1 mark]**
- The time is the number of seconds in 1 year

Substitute values into the distance equation:

- $distance = 1 light year = ( 3.0 \times 10^{8} ) \times 31 536 000$
- $1light year=9.46\times10^{15}m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate 50 light years:

- $50 l i g h t y e a r s = 50 \times ( 9.46 \times 10^{15} ) = 4.7 \times 10^{17} \mathrm{s}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *To calculate the number of seconds in a year, remember:*

- *1 year = 365 days*
- *1 day = 24 hours*
- *1 hour = 60 minutes*
- *1 minute = 60 seconds*

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

1 light year = 9.46 × 10^15 m

Redshift measurements show that a galaxy is receding from Earth at a speed of 32 000 km/s.

Use Hubble's Law to calculate how many light-years the galaxy is distant from the Solar System.

Take the Hubble constant to be 2.2 × 10<sup>-18</sup> per second.
parts.solutionMd:
Use Hubble's Law to calculate how many light-years the galaxy is distant from the Solar System

List the known quantities:

- 1 light year = 9.46 × 10<sup>15</sup> m (from part b)
- The Hubble constant, *H*<sub>0</sub> =  2.2 × 10<sup>-18</sup> per second
- Speed of the galaxy, *v* = 32 000 km/s

State the equation for the Hubble constant:

- $H_{0}=\frac{v}{d}$ **[1 mark]**

Rearrange the Hubble constant equation for the distance, *d:*

- $d=\frac{v}{H_{0}}$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the speed from km/s into m/s:

- 1 km = 1000 m = 1 × 10<sup>3</sup> m
- 32 000 km/s = 32 000 × 10<sup>3</sup> m/s **[1 mark]**

Substitute the values into the distance equation, *d*:

- $d=\frac{32000\times10^{3}}{2.2\times10^{-18}}=1.45\times10^{25}m$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the distance into light years:

- 1 light year = 9.46 × 10<sup>15</sup> m
- $d=\frac{1.45\times10^{25}}{9.46\times10^{15}}=1.5\times10^{9}\mathrm{light} \mathrm{years}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

> *Units are **really** important in this topic!*

> *You could also convert 1 light year into km, and keep the speed of the galaxy **v** in km - this will also get you the same final answer. *

> *Make sure to look at previous sub-parts if you are missing any values. Make sure to use the unrounded value where possible. Only round your final answers (preferably to 2 s.f).*

parts.problemMd:

Scientists measure the wavelength of the radio waves from galaxy A travelling at 260 km/hr away from Earth to be 63.2 m. Sometime later, the wavelength is measured to be 63.4 m. **Extended tier only**

Scientists measure the wavelength of the radio waves from galaxy A travelling at 260 km/hr away from Earth to be 63.2 m. Sometime later, the wavelength is measured to be 63.4 m.

The wavelength of the radio waves from galaxy B is initially measured to be 63.4 m and at the same time later, measured to be 63.8 m.

velocity of galaxy B  = ...................................... m/s
parts.solutionMd:
Calculate the distance of galaxy B in light years

- Initial wavelength of galaxy A = 63.2 m
- Final wavelength of galaxy A = 63.4 m
- Initial wavelength of galaxy B = 63.4 m
- Final wavelength of galaxy B = 63.8 m
- Recession velocity of galaxy A = 260 km/hr

Calculate the change in wavelength (red-shift) of both galaxies A and B:

- $\Deltaλ_{A}=63.4-63.2=0.2m$

**AND**

- $\Deltaλ_{B}=63.8-63.4=0.4m$ **[1 mark]**

Calculate the velocity of galaxy B:

- The change in wavelength of galaxy B is double that of galaxy A, therefore the velocity is also doubled
- velocity of galaxy B = $260\times2=520\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{hr}$ **[1 mark]**

Convert the velocity into m/s:

- 1 km = 1000 m = 1 × 10<sup>3</sup> m
- 1 hour = 60 × 60 = 3600 s
- $520\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{hr}=\frac{520\times10^{3}}{3600}$**[1 mark]**
- velocity of galaxy B = 144 m/s **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

> *The answer line for the question states that the velocity must be in m/s, so this **must** be converted from km/hr.*

> *The change in wavelength is equal to the amount of **redshift**. From Hubble's law, the velocity and the amount of redshift are **directly proportional**. This is because the greater the redshift, the further away an object is. *
